worked_examples.statement: Drawing a pie chart. Draw a pie chart for the transport data (Bus $12$, Walk $10$, Car $6$, Cycle $8$; total $36$ students).
knowns: frequencies 12, 10, 6, 8; total 36
unknowns: the four sector angles
reasoning: Find the value of one student in degrees: $360^\circ\div36=10^\circ$ per student.
Multiply each frequency by $10^\circ$: bus $12\times10=120^\circ$, walk $10\times10=100^\circ$, car $6\times10=60^\circ$, cycle $8\times10=80^\circ$.
Check the angles sum to $360^\circ$: $120+100+60+80=360$ ✓.
worked_examples.solution: Sector angles: Bus $120^\circ$, Walk $100^\circ$, Car $60^\circ$, Cycle $80^\circ$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Finding 'degrees per item' first turns every pie-chart question into a single multiplication per category, with a built-in check (the angles must sum to $360^\circ$).
worked_examples.common_mistake: Dividing $360^\circ$ by the number of CATEGORIES ($4$) instead of by the total number of items ($36$), which gives an equal $90^\circ$ for every category regardless of its actual frequency.

assets.caption: Pie chart of the transport data: each sector's angle is proportional to its frequency, and the four angles sum to $360^\circ$.
assets.purpose: Reuse the legacy pie-chart figure with plain TikZ, replacing the legacy \degree macro with $^\circ$ in math mode (legacy-macro safety).

worked_examples.statement: Reading a pie chart. $200$ students chose their favourite subject. The pie chart has sectors of $90^\circ$ (mathematics), $135^\circ$ (science), $72^\circ$ (art) and $63^\circ$ (history). How many students chose each subject?
knowns: total 200 students; sector angles 90, 135, 72, 63 (sum 360)
unknowns: frequency of each subject
reasoning: Each degree represents $\dfrac{200}{360}$ students, or equivalently use $\text{frequency}=\dfrac{\text{angle}}{360}\times200$ for each sector.
Maths: $\tfrac{90}{360}\times200=50$. Science: $\tfrac{135}{360}\times200=75$. Art: $\tfrac{72}{360}\times200=40$. History: $\tfrac{63}{360}\times200=35$.
Check the four frequencies sum to the stated total: $50+75+40+35=200$ ✓.
worked_examples.solution: Maths $50$, Science $75$, Art $40$, History $35$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Reading a pie chart is the exact reverse of drawing one: instead of frequency$\to$angle, it is angle$\to$frequency, using the same proportion the other way round.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Using the angle itself as the number of students (e.g. writing 'science $=135$ students'), forgetting that the angle must first be converted using the chart's total.

worked_examples.statement: Drawing and reading a stem-and-leaf diagram. The marks of $20$ students in a test are $47,52,38,61,45,52,49,58,66,43,52,39,71,55,48,60,44,57,62,50$. Draw an ordered stem-and-leaf diagram with a key. Find the mode, median and range, and the number of students who scored at least $60$.
knowns: 20 test marks from 38 to 71
unknowns: mode, median, range, and count scoring ≥ 60
reasoning: The stems are the tens digits $3,4,5,6,7$. Write each mark's last digit (leaf) into its stem's row, then reorder each row's leaves into increasing order.
Count the leaves across all rows ($2+6+7+4+1=20$) to confirm no value was lost.
Mode: the value occurring most often across all the leaves is $52$ (appearing three times).
Median: with $n=20$, the median is the mean of the $10$th and $11$th ordered values; counting along the rows, both land on $52$.
Range: largest $-$ smallest $=71-38=33$.
At least $60$: count every leaf in the rows for stems $6$ and $7$: $4+1=5$ students.
worked_examples.solution: Mode $=52$, median $=52$, range $=33$; $5$ students scored at least $60$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Because the leaves are written in increasing order, the mode (a leaf repeated within one row), the median (count to the middle position) and a threshold count (count a whole tail of rows) are all read directly, with no need to re-sort anything.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Finding the median from the UNORDERED stems as written first, before sorting the leaves within each row, which can land on the wrong value if two leaves in a row are out of order near the middle position.

assets.caption: Ordered stem-and-leaf diagram of the 20 test marks: the tens digit forms the stem, the units digit the leaf, the two columns separated by a vertical line, with the leaves of each row in increasing order and a key.
assets.purpose: Model a correctly drawn stem-and-leaf diagram: Stem and Leaf columns divided by a vertical rule, ordered leaves and an explicit key, as required by the syllabus.

worked_examples.statement: Which chart? Choose a suitable diagram for each situation, with a reason. (a) How a household budget is shared between rent, food and travel. (b) Comparing the favourite fruit of two classes. (c) Showing all the individual test marks of a class while keeping the exact values visible.
reasoning: (a) The question is about PROPORTIONS of a single whole (the budget) — the chart built exactly for that is the pie chart.
(b) The question needs GROUP vs GROUP comparison, category by category — the chart built for that is a dual bar chart.
(c) The question explicitly needs every individual value KEPT, not just summarised — the only chart here that preserves every value is a stem-and-leaf diagram.
worked_examples.solution: (a) A pie chart (shows shares of a whole). (b) A dual bar chart (compares two groups category by category). (c) A stem-and-leaf diagram (keeps every individual value visible).
worked_examples.interpretation: Choosing a chart is a matching problem: identify what the question actually needs to show (proportions? group comparison? individual values?) and pick the one chart purpose-built for that need.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Defaulting to a bar chart for every situation, including (a) and (c), where a pie chart or a stem-and-leaf diagram respectively does the specific job asked for far better.

worked_examples.statement: Reading and completing a pictogram. The pictogram shows the number of cars a garage sold in four months. (a) Write down the number of cars sold in January, in February and in March. (b) In April the garage sold $55$ cars. How many symbols are needed for the April row?
knowns: the key: one whole symbol represents $10$ cars
January $3$ symbols, February $4\tfrac12$ symbols, March $2\tfrac12$ symbols
April: $55$ cars sold
unknowns: the three monthly frequencies, and the number of symbols for April
reasoning: Read the key first. One whole symbol stands for $10$ cars, so a half symbol stands for $\tfrac12\times10=5$ cars.
January has $3$ whole symbols: $3\times10=30$ cars.
February has $4$ whole symbols and a half: $4\times10+5=45$ cars.
March has $2$ whole symbols and a half: $2\times10+5=25$ cars.
April works the other way round. Drawing a pictogram means dividing by the key value: $55\div10=5.5$, so April needs $5$ whole symbols and one half symbol.
worked_examples.solution: (a) January $30$ cars, February $45$ cars, March $25$ cars. (b) $5\tfrac12$ symbols.
worked_examples.interpretation: Reading a pictogram is multiplying by the key; drawing one is dividing by the key. A half symbol is always half of the KEY value, never half a car.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Counting the symbols and giving that count as the frequency — saying February is $4\tfrac12$ instead of $45$ — because the key was never used.

assets.caption: Pictogram of the garage's car sales. One whole symbol represents 10 cars, so a half symbol represents 5; the April row has still to be drawn.
assets.purpose: Give the student an actual pictogram to read, with whole and half symbols and a key, which no other item in the lesson does.

guided_exercises.statement: A survey of $25$ students' favourite ice-cream flavour gives: vanilla $9$, chocolate $7$, strawberry $5$, mint $4$. (a) What is the modal flavour? (b) What fraction of students chose strawberry or mint?
hints: The modal flavour is simply the one with the highest frequency — no calculation needed, just identify the largest number.
For the fraction, add the two relevant frequencies first, then divide by the total number of students.
guided_exercises.answer: (a) Vanilla (b) $\dfrac{9}{25}$.
guided_exercises.full_solution: (a) The highest frequency, $9$, belongs to vanilla, so vanilla is the mode. (b) Strawberry and mint together: $5+4=9$ out of $25$ students: $\dfrac{9}{25}$ (already in lowest terms).
common_errors: In (b), dividing by $4$ (the number of flavours) instead of $25$ (the number of students).

guided_exercises.statement: A pie chart represents the $45$ members of a drama club. The sector for 'acting' is $120^\circ$. How many members chose acting, and what angle would represent $9$ members?
hints: First find how many degrees ONE member is worth, using the total $45$ and the full circle $360^\circ$.
Use that 'degrees per member' value twice: once to convert $120^\circ$ into a number of members, and once to convert $9$ members into an angle.
guided_exercises.answer: $15$ members chose acting; $9$ members corresponds to $72^\circ$.
guided_exercises.full_solution: One member is worth $360^\circ\div45=8^\circ$. Acting: $120^\circ\div8^\circ=15$ members. For $9$ members: $9\times8^\circ=72^\circ$.
common_errors: Dividing $120^\circ$ by $360^\circ$ and stopping there (giving a fraction, $\tfrac13$) instead of continuing to convert that fraction into an actual number of members using the total $45$.

guided_exercises.statement: The ages, in years, of $12$ people at a small event are $34,41,28,36,45,33,29,38,42,31,37,44$. Draw an ordered stem-and-leaf diagram with a key, and find the median and the range.
hints: The stems here are the tens digit of each age: list them out first ($2,3,4$) before placing any leaves.
Once every row's leaves are in increasing order, count to the middle position for the median (here, with $12$ values, you need the mean of the $6$th and $7$th).
common_errors: Forgetting to re-sort the leaves within a row into increasing order before counting along for the median, which can shift which value lands in the 6th or 7th position.

exercises.statement: Eye colours of $30$ students: brown $14$, blue $8$, green $5$, grey $3$. (a) Draw a bar chart. (b) How many more have brown eyes than blue? (c) What fraction have green eyes?
exercises.answer: (a) Bars of heights $14,8,5,3$ on a labelled scale from $0$. (b) $6$. (c) $\dfrac{5}{30}=\dfrac{1}{6}$.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Draw four equal-width bars with equal gaps, heights $14,8,5,3$, labelled axes, scale from $0$. (b) $14-8=6$. (c) $\dfrac{5}{30}=\dfrac{1}{6}$.
common_errors: Drawing the bars with gaps of unequal width, or starting the frequency axis above $0$.

exercises.statement: Books read in a month: Ana $12$, Ben $6$, Cara $9$, Dan $15$. Using a symbol to represent $6$ books, how many symbols (including part symbols) are needed for each person?
exercises.answer: Ana $2$, Ben $1$, Cara $1\tfrac12$, Dan $2\tfrac12$.
exercises.full_solution: Divide each frequency by $6$: Ana $12\div6=2$; Ben $6\div6=1$; Cara $9\div6=1.5=1\tfrac12$; Dan $15\div6=2.5=2\tfrac12$.
common_errors: Rounding $1.5$ or $2.5$ symbols to the nearest whole symbol instead of drawing the exact half symbol the key allows.

exercises.statement: In a survey of $72$ people, favourite fruit: apple $24$, banana $18$, orange $21$, pear $9$. Calculate the angle of each sector for a pie chart and check that they add up to $360^\circ$.
exercises.answer: Apple $120^\circ$, banana $90^\circ$, orange $105^\circ$, pear $45^\circ$ (sum $360^\circ$ ✓).
exercises.full_solution: One person is worth $360^\circ\div72=5^\circ$. Apple $24\times5=120^\circ$; banana $18\times5=90^\circ$; orange $21\times5=105^\circ$; pear $9\times5=45^\circ$. Check: $120+90+105+45=360$ ✓.
common_errors: Using the wrong total (e.g. $360\div4$ categories) instead of $360\div72$ people when finding degrees per unit.

exercises.statement: A pie chart shows how $240$ pupils travel to a sports fixture. The sector for football is $105^\circ$ and the sector for tennis is $45^\circ$. How many pupils are in each sector? What angle would represent $60$ pupils?
exercises.answer: Football $70$ pupils, tennis $30$ pupils; $60$ pupils corresponds to $90^\circ$.
exercises.full_solution: Football: $\tfrac{105}{360}\times240=70$. Tennis: $\tfrac{45}{360}\times240=30$. For $60$ pupils: $\tfrac{60}{240}\times360^\circ=90^\circ$.
common_errors: Using $105^\circ$ or $45^\circ$ directly as a number of pupils instead of converting through the $\tfrac{\text{angle}}{360}\times\text{total}$ relationship.

exercises.statement: The heights, in cm, of $15$ plants are $23,31,25,42,38,31,27,45,33,29,36,41,24,32,39$. Draw an ordered stem-and-leaf diagram with a key. Find the median, the mode and the range.
exercises.answer: Median $=32$, mode $=31$, range $=22$.
exercises.full_solution: Stems $2,3,4$: row $2$: $3,4,5,7,9$; row $3$: $1,1,2,3,6,8,9$; row $4$: $1,2,5$. Key: $2\mid3$ means $23$ cm. With $n=15$, the median is the $8$th ordered value, which is $32$. The mode is $31$ (appears twice). Range $=45-23=22$.
common_errors: Taking the median as the value in the MIDDLE ROW of the stem-and-leaf table instead of counting to the actual middle POSITION across all 15 ordered values.

exercises.statement: Results of two classes in a test: Class A: grade A $4$, B $9$, C $12$, D $5$. Class B: grade A $6$, B $8$, C $9$, D $7$. (a) How many students are in each class? (b) Draw a dual bar chart. (c) How many more students in Class B than Class A got grade A?
exercises.answer: (a) $30$ each. (b) Paired bars for each grade. (c) $2$.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Class A: $4+9+12+5=30$. Class B: $6+8+9+7=30$. (b) Draw four pairs of bars (A, B grade by grade) with heights A: $4,9,12,5$; B: $6,8,9,7$. (c) $6-4=2$.
common_errors: Adding both classes' grade-A frequencies together ($4+6=10$) instead of finding the DIFFERENCE between them, since the question asks 'how many more'.

exercises.statement: A shop records drinks and snacks sold: Monday $12$ drinks, $8$ snacks; Tuesday $15$ drinks, $10$ snacks; Wednesday $9$ drinks, $6$ snacks. (a) Draw a composite bar chart. (b) On which day were the most items sold, and how many?
exercises.answer: (a) Stacked bars: Monday $20$, Tuesday $25$, Wednesday $15$. (b) Tuesday, $25$ items.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Each day's bar is drinks stacked with snacks on top: Monday $12+8=20$; Tuesday $15+10=25$; Wednesday $9+6=15$. (b) The tallest stacked bar is Tuesday, with a combined total of $25$.
common_errors: Comparing only the drinks (or only the snacks) across days instead of the COMBINED total each composite bar actually shows.

exercises.statement: The number of siblings of $30$ students: $0$: $6$, $1$: $11$, $2$: $8$, $3$: $3$, $4$: $2$. Draw a bar chart and find how many students have at least $2$ siblings.
exercises.answer: Bars of heights $6,11,8,3,2$; at least $2$ siblings: $13$ students.
exercises.full_solution: At least $2$ means $2$, $3$ or $4$ siblings: $8+3+2=13$.
common_errors: Including only the '$2$ siblings' frequency ($8$) and forgetting to also add the frequencies for $3$ and $4$ siblings.

exercises.statement: A bar chart of sales has a vertical axis that starts at $90$ instead of $0$. Explain why this is misleading.
exercises.answer: Because the bar heights are no longer proportional to the actual sales figures, small real differences look exaggerated.
exercises.full_solution: When the axis starts above $0$, every bar is really showing 'value minus $90$' rather than the actual value, so the VISUAL heights no longer scale in proportion to the real numbers — a small real difference between two values can be stretched to look like a huge one on the truncated axis.
common_errors: Describing the fault only as 'it looks wrong' without explaining the actual mechanism (heights no longer proportional to the real values).

exercises.statement: A pie chart represents $150$ people. The sector for cycling is $48^\circ$. How many people cycle?
exercises.answer: $20$ people.
common_errors: Computing $\dfrac{360}{48}\times150$ by inverting the fraction, instead of angle-over-$360$ times total.

exercises.statement: Two pie charts show the favourite subjects of two schools, one with $200$ students and one with $500$. In both, the art sector is $72^\circ$. Ali says the same number of students chose art in each school. Is he right? Explain, with calculations.
exercises.answer: No: $40$ students in the first school but $100$ in the second.
exercises.full_solution: First school: $\tfrac{72}{360}\times200=40$. Second school: $\tfrac{72}{360}\times500=100$. The same angle represents the same PROPORTION ($20\%$) in each chart, but a different actual number, because the two charts have different totals. Ali is wrong.
common_errors: Assuming an identical angle in two different pie charts must mean an identical number of people, without checking that the two charts have different totals.

exercises.statement: The masses of nine parcels, in kg, are $3.4,3.9,4.1,4.4,4.4,4.7,5.0,5.2,5.8$. Draw a stem-and-leaf diagram with a suitable key, and find the median and range.
exercises.answer: Median $=4.4$ kg; range $=2.4$ kg.
exercises.full_solution: Stems $3,4,5$: row $3$: $4,9$; row $4$: $1,4,4,7$; row $5$: $0,2,8$. Key: $3\mid4$ means $3.4$ kg. With $n=9$, the median is the $5$th value, $4.4$ kg. Range $=5.8-3.4=2.4$ kg.
common_errors: Using whole-number stems (e.g. stem $3$ meaning '$30$-something') instead of the decimal-aware key needed here ('$3\mid4$ means $3.4$ kg').

exercises.statement: A pie chart has four sectors in the ratio $4:3:2:1$. (a) Find the four angles. (b) The largest sector represents $48$ people. Find the total, and the number in each of the other sectors.
exercises.full_solution: (a) $10$ equal parts make up $360^\circ$, so each part is $36^\circ$: angles $144^\circ,108^\circ,72^\circ,36^\circ$. (b) $144^\circ\leftrightarrow48$ people, so $1^\circ\leftrightarrow\tfrac13$ person: total $=360\times\tfrac13=120$. The other sectors: $108^\circ\to36$, $72^\circ\to24$, $36^\circ\to12$.
common_errors: Dividing $360^\circ$ by $4$ (the number of sectors) rather than by the total number of RATIO PARTS ($4+3+2+1=10$) when finding the angle per part.

exercises.statement: Ninety students are asked how they revise: on their own, with friends, or using online videos, in the ratio $5:3:1$. Draw the sectors of a pie chart (give the angles) and explain how you would make a pictogram with a key of $10$ students.
exercises.answer: Angles $200^\circ$, $120^\circ$, $40^\circ$; pictogram counts $5,3,1$ symbols.
exercises.full_solution: $9$ equal parts make up both $90$ students and $360^\circ$: each part is $10$ students and $40^\circ$. 'On their own' ($5$ parts): $50$ students, $200^\circ$. 'With friends' ($3$ parts): $30$ students, $120^\circ$. 'Online videos' ($1$ part): $10$ students, $40^\circ$. For the pictogram with a key of $10$ students per symbol: $5$, $3$ and $1$ symbols respectively, each a whole number — a convenient key for this data.
common_errors: Choosing a pictogram key that does NOT divide every frequency into a whole number or exact half of symbols (e.g. a key of $7$ here), which the strategy explicitly warns against.

exam_questions.statement:
$120$ people were asked their preferred holiday type. The results are: beach $42$, city $30$, mountain $24$, other $24$.
(a) Calculate the angle of the sector for each holiday type. [3]
(b) Draw a fully labelled pie chart to show this information. [2]
exam_questions.answer: (a) Beach $126^\circ$, city $90^\circ$, mountain $72^\circ$, other $72^\circ$ (sum $360^\circ$). (b) A circle divided into these four labelled sectors.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) One person is worth $360^\circ\div120=3^\circ$. Beach: $42\times3=126^\circ$. City: $30\times3=90^\circ$. Mountain: $24\times3=72^\circ$. Other: $24\times3=72^\circ$. Check: $126+90+72+72=360$ ✓. (b) Draw a circle, a starting radius, then measure $126^\circ$, $90^\circ$, $72^\circ$, $72^\circ$ around it in turn with a protractor, labelling each sector with its category and angle.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for finding $360\div120=3^\circ$ per person (or equivalent fraction method); M1 for at least two correct angles; A1 for all four angles correct and summing to $360^\circ$
(b) M1 for a circle with sectors in roughly the correct proportions, each angle measured from a common radius; A1 for every sector correctly labelled (category and angle or value).
common_errors: Dividing $360^\circ$ by $4$ (the number of categories) instead of by $120$ (the number of people), which gives every category an equal share regardless of its actual frequency.

exam_questions.statement:
The table shows the number of trains that arrived on time and late at a station over three days.
$$\begin{array}{l|ccc}
 & \text{Mon} & \text{Tue} & \text{Wed}\\\hline
\text{On time} & 18 & 22 & 16\\
\text{Late} & 6 & 4 & 9
\end{array}$$
(a) Draw a composite (stacked) bar chart for this data. [2]
(b) A student reads the Tuesday bar and says 'the late trains section reaches $26$, so $26$ trains were late on Tuesday.' Explain the student's error and give the correct number. [2]
exam_questions.answer: (a) Stacked bars: Monday total $24$, Tuesday total $26$, Wednesday total $25$. (b) The student read the TOP of the bar, not the height of the late section; the correct number of late trains is $4$.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Each day's bar stacks 'on time' with 'late' on top: Monday $18+6=24$; Tuesday $22+4=26$; Wednesday $16+9=25$. (b) The late section does not start at $0$ — it starts where the on-time section ends, at $22$. Its actual height (and frequency) is $26-22=4$, not the top of the whole bar, $26$.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for three stacked bars with on-time as the lower section; A1 for all three bars reaching the correct combined totals ($24,26,25$)
(b) M1 for identifying that the upper section must be found by subtracting the lower section's height; A1 for the correct value, $4$.
common_errors: Reading the top of a stacked bar as the frequency of its upper section, instead of subtracting the lower section's height first.

exam_questions.statement:
The ages, in years, of $16$ actors auditioning for a play are:
$22,35,19,41,28,33,45,24,31,38,26,29,42,27,36,23$.
(a) Draw an ordered stem-and-leaf diagram for this data, with a key. [3]
(b) Find the median age and the range. [2]
(c) A director wants actors within $5$ years of the median. Find how many of the $16$ actors qualify. [1]
exam_questions.answer: (a) Stems $1,2,3,4$ with ordered leaves and a key. (b) Median $30$, range $26$. (c) $7$ actors (ages $25$ to $35$ inclusive: $26,27,28,29,31,33,35$).
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for correct stems; M1 for all 16 leaves placed; A1 for leaves ordered within each row and a correct key
(b) M1 for identifying the 8th and 9th ordered values; A1 for median $=30$ and range $=26$ both correct
(c) B1 for a sensible count of actors within the stated window of the median, consistent with the candidate's own median value.
common_errors: Taking the median as the value belonging to the middle STEM ROW rather than counting to the actual 8th/9th positions across all 16 ordered values.

exam_questions.statement:
A pictogram shows the number of pizzas a cafe sold on four days. The key is: one symbol represents $8$ pizzas.
Monday is drawn with $3$ symbols, Tuesday with $4\tfrac12$ symbols and Wednesday with $1\tfrac14$ symbols. The Thursday row has not been drawn.
(a) Work out the number of pizzas sold on Monday and on Wednesday. [2]
(b) On Thursday the cafe sold $52$ pizzas. Work out the number of symbols needed for the Thursday row. [2]
(c) The cafe thinks of redrawing the pictogram with a key of one symbol representing $10$ pizzas. Explain why that key would be a poor choice for Monday's figure. [1]
exam_questions.answer: (a) Monday $24$ pizzas, Wednesday $10$ pizzas. (b) $6\tfrac12$ symbols. (c) $24\div10=2.4$, which is neither a whole number of symbols nor an exact half, so Monday would need an awkward fraction of a symbol.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Multiply the number of symbols by the key value. Monday: $3\times8=24$ pizzas. Wednesday: $1\tfrac14\times8=8+2=10$ pizzas (a quarter symbol is $\tfrac14\times8=2$ pizzas). (b) Drawing a row means dividing by the key value: $52\div8=6.5$, so Thursday needs $6$ whole symbols and one half symbol, written $6\tfrac12$ symbols. (c) A good key turns every frequency into a whole number of symbols, or an exact half. With a key of $10$, Monday's $24$ pizzas would need $24\div10=2.4$ symbols, and four tenths of a symbol can be neither drawn nor read accurately.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for multiplying a symbol count by the key value $8$ (e.g. $3\times8$ or $1.25\times8$); A1 for both Monday $=24$ and Wednesday $=10$
(b) M1 for $52\div8$; A1 for $6\tfrac12$ symbols (accept 'six whole symbols and a half symbol')
(c) B1 for $24\div10=2.4$, so the row would need a fraction of a symbol that is not a whole one or a half
common_errors: Giving the number of symbols as the frequency (Monday $=3$ pizzas) instead of multiplying by the key value.
Treating the quarter symbol in the Wednesday row as a half, giving $12$ pizzas instead of $10$.

challenge_questions.statement: A pie chart shows the favourite drink of $120$ people. Its four sectors have angles $2x^\circ$, $3x^\circ$, $4x^\circ$ and $(x+30)^\circ$. (a) Find $x$ and write down the four angles. (b) Find the number of people in each sector. (c) The chart is published without the total. Explain what a reader can and cannot work out from it.
challenge_questions.answer: (a) $x=33$; the angles are $66^\circ$, $99^\circ$, $132^\circ$ and $63^\circ$. (b) $22$, $33$, $44$ and $21$ people. (c) Only the proportions, not the numbers: the total has to be given separately.
challenge_questions.full_solution: (a) The sector angles of any pie chart add up to $360^\circ$, so $2x+3x+4x+(x+30)=360$, giving $10x+30=360$, $10x=330$ and $x=33$. The angles are $2\times33=66^\circ$, $3\times33=99^\circ$, $4\times33=132^\circ$ and $33+30=63^\circ$. Check: $66+99+132+63=360$ ✓. (b) With $120$ people in $360^\circ$, each person is worth $360\div120=3^\circ$, so each sector holds (angle)$\div3$ people: $66\div3=22$, $99\div3=33$, $132\div3=44$, $63\div3=21$. Check: $22+33+44+21=120$ ✓. (c) The angles fix only the share of the whole that each drink takes ($66^\circ$ is $\tfrac{66}{360}$, or about $18\%$). Without the total of $120$ the reader cannot turn any share into a number of people, because the same chart would serve $120$ people or $1200$.

challenge_questions.statement: The test marks of $11$ girls are $34,41,45,47,52,55,58,61,63,67,72$ and the marks of $11$ boys are $28,33,38,42,44,49,51,56,59,65,74$. Draw a back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram (girls' leaves to the left of the stems, boys' to the right) with a single key. Use it to compare the two sets of marks, giving one average and one measure of spread.
challenge_questions.answer: Girls: median $55$, range $38$. Boys: median $49$, range $46$. The girls scored higher on average and their marks were less spread out.
challenge_questions.full_solution:
Use one set of stems (the tens digits $2,3,4,5,6,7$) down the middle. Girls' leaves are written to the left, increasing away from the stem; boys' leaves to the right, increasing away from the stem.

Girls: stem $3$: $4$; stem $4$: $1,5,7$; stem $5$: $2,5,8$; stem $6$: $1,3,7$; stem $7$: $2$ — eleven leaves in all.

Boys: stem $2$: $8$; stem $3$: $3,8$; stem $4$: $2,4,9$; stem $5$: $1,6,9$; stem $6$: $5$; stem $7$: $4$ — eleven leaves in all.

Key: $4\mid 1$ means $41$ marks (and it applies to both sides).

With $n=11$ on each side, the median is the $6$th value. For the girls that is $55$; for the boys it is $49$. The ranges are $72-34=38$ for the girls and $74-28=46$ for the boys. So the girls' marks were higher on average (median $55$ against $49$) and more consistent (range $38$ against $46$). A comparison must name both the average and the spread, and must say which group each figure belongs to.

challenge_questions.statement: In School A, $240$ students were asked their favourite sport and the swimming sector of the pie chart was $75^\circ$. In School B, $180$ students were asked the same question and the swimming sector was $120^\circ$. (a) How many students altogether chose swimming? (b) The two sets of results are combined into one pie chart for all $420$ students. Find the angle of the swimming sector, to the nearest degree. (c) Explain why this angle is not the mean of $75^\circ$ and $120^\circ$.
challenge_questions.answer: (a) $50+60=110$ students. (b) $94^\circ$ to the nearest degree. (c) Because the two schools have different totals, so the combined share is a weighted average, pulled towards the larger school.
challenge_questions.full_solution: (a) School A: $\tfrac{75}{360}\times240=50$ students. School B: $\tfrac{120}{360}\times180=60$ students. Altogether $50+60=110$ students chose swimming. (b) In the combined chart, $110$ out of $420$ students chose swimming, so the sector is $\tfrac{110}{420}\times360=94.28\ldots^\circ$, which is $94^\circ$ to the nearest degree. (c) The mean of $75^\circ$ and $120^\circ$ is $97.5^\circ$, which would be right only if the two schools were the same size. School A is the larger ($240$ against $180$) and has the smaller share of swimmers, so it carries more weight in the combined chart and pulls the angle below the halfway value.

challenge_questions.statement: A pictogram shows the number of bicycles a shop sold in four months. March is drawn with $4$ whole symbols, April with $2\tfrac12$, May with $3\tfrac12$ and June with $6$. Altogether $288$ bicycles were sold. (a) How many bicycles does one symbol represent? (b) How many were sold in each month? (c) The same data is redrawn as a pie chart. Find the angle of the June sector. (d) Explain why a key of $20$ bicycles per symbol would have been a poor choice here.
challenge_questions.answer: (a) $18$ bicycles per symbol. (b) March $72$, April $45$, May $63$, June $108$. (c) $135^\circ$. (d) With a key of $20$, March would need $3.6$ symbols and May $3.15$ — neither a whole symbol nor an exact half.
challenge_questions.full_solution: (a) The pictogram uses $4+2\tfrac12+3\tfrac12+6=16$ symbols in total, and those $16$ symbols stand for $288$ bicycles, so one symbol represents $288\div16=18$ bicycles. (b) Multiply each symbol count by $18$: March $4\times18=72$; April $2.5\times18=45$; May $3.5\times18=63$; June $6\times18=108$. Check: $72+45+63+108=288$ ✓. (c) June's share is $\tfrac{108}{288}$ of the whole, so its sector is $\tfrac{108}{288}\times360=135^\circ$. (d) A key should turn every frequency into a whole number of symbols or an exact half. With a key of $20$: March $72\div20=3.6$, April $45\div20=2.25$, May $63\div20=3.15$, June $108\div20=5.4$ — every one of them an awkward fraction that cannot be drawn or read accurately. The key of $18$ was chosen precisely because it does not do this.

challenge_questions.statement: Decide which chart type (bar chart, pie chart, pictogram, stem-and-leaf) is best for each purpose and justify: (a) the share of a school's budget spent on each department; (b) the heights of $15$ plants where the actual values matter; (c) comparing boys' and girls' favourite sports.
challenge_questions.answer: (a) Pie chart (b) Stem-and-leaf (c) Dual bar chart.
challenge_questions.full_solution: (a) Pie chart: the question is explicitly about SHARES of a single whole (the budget). (b) Stem-and-leaf diagram: it is the only option here that keeps every individual plant height visible. (c) Dual bar chart: it compares two named groups (boys, girls) category by category (each sport).

mcq.stem: A pictogram uses one symbol to represent $4$ books. A row shows $2\tfrac12$ symbols. How many books does this represent?

options.why_wrong: This counts the two whole symbols correctly ($2\times4=8$) but treats the half symbol as worth only $1$ book, instead of half of the key value ($\tfrac12\times4=2$ books).
This rounds $2\tfrac12$ UP to $3$ whole symbols before multiplying, instead of using the exact value $2.5$.
This is the number of SYMBOLS, not the number of books it represents — it still needs multiplying by the key value, $4$.

mcq.explanation: $2\tfrac12\times4=10$ books: the half symbol contributes half of $4$, i.e. $2$ books, plus $2\times4=8$ from the two whole symbols.

mcq.stem: In a composite bar chart, the 'boys' section of a bar (the lower section) reaches $9$, and the whole stacked bar (boys$+$girls) reaches $22$. How many girls does the upper section represent?

options.why_wrong: This reads the TOP of the whole stacked bar as if it were the girls' frequency alone, without subtracting the boys' section underneath it.
This is the BOYS' frequency (the lower section), not the girls' — the two sections have been confused.
This adds the two given numbers ($22+9$) instead of subtracting them, which cannot be right since the girls' section is only PART of the total height $22$.

mcq.explanation: The girls' section starts where the boys' section ends (at $9$) and finishes at the top of the bar ($22$), so its frequency is $22-9=13$.

mcq.stem: A pie chart of $90$ people has a sector of $100^\circ$ for 'cats'. How many people chose cats?

options.why_wrong: This uses the angle itself as the number of people, ignoring that an angle must first be converted using the total.
This computes $360\div100$, inverting the correct ratio $\tfrac{\text{angle}}{360}$.
This finds $360^\circ\div90=4^\circ$ per person correctly, but then MULTIPLIES $100\times4$ instead of dividing: the number of people is $100\div4=25$.

mcq.explanation: $\dfrac{100}{360}\times90=25$ people.

mcq.stem: Pie chart X ($80$ people) and pie chart Y ($240$ people) both have a sector of $90^\circ$ for 'tea'. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The same NUMBER of people chose tea in both charts, since the angle is the same
options.why_wrong: An equal angle in two charts with DIFFERENT totals never means an equal number of people — it means an equal proportion, and the actual numbers ($20$ vs $60$) are different here.

options.text: Chart X has more people choosing tea, since its sector looks the same size on a smaller chart
options.why_wrong: The physical size the chart is drawn at has no bearing on the actual number of people represented; only the stated total and the angle matter.

options.text: Nothing can be concluded about either chart from this information
options.why_wrong: Quite the opposite: knowing both totals and the shared angle lets you calculate and compare the exact number of tea-drinkers in each chart ($20$ and $60$).

options.text: The same PROPORTION (a quarter) chose tea in both charts, but Y has more people choosing tea in total

mcq.explanation: $\tfrac{90}{360}=\tfrac14$ in both charts (same proportion), but $\tfrac14\times80=20$ in X and $\tfrac14\times240=60$ in Y — different actual numbers, because the totals differ.

mcq.stem: A newspaper bar chart shows company profits of \$96,000 and \$99,000 as two bars, with the vertical axis starting at \$95,000. What is the main problem with this chart?

options.text: The second bar looks about four times as tall as the first, even though the real increase is only about $3.1\%$
There is no problem, since both values are plotted at their correct heights above \$95,000
options.why_wrong: Plotting the raw values accurately above a non-zero baseline is exactly what makes the chart visually misleading, even though no individual number is 'wrong'.

options.text: The bars should be different widths to show the different profit amounts
options.why_wrong: Bar WIDTH is never used to encode a value in a standard bar chart; only the height does, and changing widths would introduce a new, different kind of distortion.

options.text: The chart needs a title before it can be considered misleading
options.why_wrong: A missing title is a separate, genuine fault, but it is not what causes THIS chart's specific exaggeration of the size of the increase.

mcq.explanation: Starting the axis at \$95,000 means the bars show heights of $1$ and $4$ units above the baseline for values that only really differ by about $3.1\%$ ($\tfrac{99-96}{96}\times100$), visually exaggerating a small real change.

flashcards.front: Sector angle in a pie chart
flashcards.back: $\text{sector angle}=\dfrac{\text{frequency}}{\text{total}}\times360^\circ$; reversed, $\text{frequency}=\dfrac{\text{angle}}{360^\circ}\times\text{total}$.

flashcards.front: Two pie charts both have a $90^\circ$ sector, but different totals. Do they represent the same NUMBER of items?
flashcards.back: No. The same angle always means the same PROPORTION, never automatically the same number, unless the totals also happen to match.

flashcards.front: In a composite (stacked) bar chart, can you read the top section's frequency straight off the vertical axis?
flashcards.back: No — only the BOTTOM section starts at $0$. Every section above it needs the height where it starts subtracted first.

flashcards.front: Dual bar chart vs composite bar chart — what does each show best?
flashcards.back: Dual: compares two groups category by category (bars side by side). Composite: shows the combined total per category (bars stacked).

flashcards.front: What does the key of a pictogram give you?
flashcards.back: The number of items that ONE whole symbol represents; part symbols represent the matching fraction of that number.

flashcards.front: What makes a good key for a pictogram?
flashcards.back: One where every frequency becomes a whole number of symbols or exactly a half — an awkward key (like fifths) makes the pictogram hard to draw and read.

flashcards.front: What are the two parts of a stem-and-leaf value, and how are they ordered?
flashcards.back: Stem (leading digit(s)) and leaf (last digit); the leaves in each row must be written in increasing order, with a key explaining how to read a stem-leaf pair.

flashcards.front: How do you read the mode and median from an ordered stem-and-leaf diagram?
flashcards.back: Mode: the value (stem and leaf together) that occurs most often — look for the leaf repeated most within one row. Median: count along the ordered rows to the middle position (or the mean of the two middle positions).

flashcards.front: Can a bar chart be numerically accurate and still misleading?
flashcards.back: Yes — if the vertical axis doesn't start at $0$, correctly-plotted bars can still exaggerate small real differences, because the heights are no longer proportional to the actual values.

flashcards.front: Which chart suits 'share of a whole' data, like a household budget?
flashcards.back: A pie chart — built specifically to show proportions of a single total.

flashcards.front: Which chart keeps every individual data value visible?
flashcards.back: A stem-and-leaf diagram — unlike a bar chart or pie chart, it lists every value, split into stem and leaf.

flashcards.front: A pie chart's sector angles sum to $359^\circ$ instead of $360^\circ$. What does this tell you?
flashcards.back: A rounding or arithmetic slip has occurred somewhere in computing the angles — the angles must always sum to exactly $360^\circ$ (within the small tolerance allowed for protractor measurement).

misconceptions.incorrect_model: In a composite (stacked) bar chart, the top of each coloured section can be read directly as that section's frequency.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: In a simple (non-stacked) bar chart, the height you read IS the frequency, so it feels natural to apply the same rule once bars are stacked, without noticing that the upper section now starts from a non-zero baseline.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner reads the upper (e.g. girls') section of a stacked bar reaching height $22$ as 'the girls' frequency is $22$', when the boys' section underneath already accounts for part of that height.
misconceptions.correct_model: Only the BOTTOM section of a composite bar can be read directly from $0$. Every section above it must be found by subtraction: that section's frequency $=$ (height where it ends) $-$ (height where it starts, i.e. where the section below it ends).
misconceptions.remediation: Before reading any stacked bar, ask 'does this section start at $0$?' If not, subtract the starting height first, every single time, with no exceptions.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A bigger sector angle in a pie chart always means a bigger NUMBER of items.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Within a single pie chart (one fixed total), a bigger angle genuinely does mean a bigger number, so the rule 'bigger angle = bigger number' works perfectly until two DIFFERENT pie charts (with different totals) are compared.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner claims that an identical sector angle in two pie charts of different totals represents 'the same number of people', or that a bigger angle in chart A versus a smaller one in chart B must mean more people in A.
misconceptions.correct_model: An angle in a pie chart fixes a PROPORTION of that chart's own total, not an absolute count. The same angle in two charts with different totals represents different numbers of people; comparing angles across two different pie charts tells you nothing about the actual numbers unless the totals are also compared.
misconceptions.remediation: Always convert the angle to an actual number using that chart's own total ($\text{frequency}=\frac{\text{angle}}{360}\times\text{total}$) before comparing two different pie charts — never compare raw angles across charts with different totals.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A bar chart is automatically fair and accurate as long as the bars are the right heights.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners focus on getting the numerical heights of the bars correct, without separately checking the one other feature (where the vertical axis starts) that can distort the visual impression even when every height is numerically correct.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner does not flag a bar chart whose vertical axis starts at, say, $90$ instead of $0$, even though the bar heights plotted are numerically accurate.
misconceptions.correct_model: A bar chart can be numerically correct and still visually misleading: if the vertical axis does not start at $0$, small real differences are stretched to look huge, because the bar heights are no longer proportional to the actual values. Always check where the axis starts before trusting a visual impression of 'how much bigger'.
misconceptions.remediation: Recompute the TRUE percentage difference between two bars directly from their actual values (ignoring the picture), and compare it with how different the bars LOOK on the truncated axis, to expose the gap between appearance and reality.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reading the top of a stacked (composite) bar as the frequency of its upper section.
common_mistakes.why: The habit of reading a bar's height directly carries over from simple bar charts, where that method is correct.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always ask 'does this section start at $0$?' first; if not, subtract the height where it starts before treating a reading as a frequency.

common_mistakes.mistake: Comparing raw sector angles across two different pie charts as if equal angle meant equal number of items.
common_mistakes.why: Within a single pie chart, bigger angle genuinely does mean a bigger number, so the rule feels universal until a second chart (with a different total) is introduced.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Convert every angle to an actual number using that chart's OWN total before comparing two different pie charts.

common_mistakes.mistake: Drawing or trusting a bar chart whose vertical axis does not start at $0$.
common_mistakes.why: The individual bar heights can still be numerically correct, so the chart 'checks out' unless the axis starting point is specifically inspected.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Before interpreting any bar chart's visual impression, check explicitly where the vertical axis starts.

exam_notes: When asked to 'draw' a pie chart, show the degrees-per-item (or per-unit) working explicitly, and label every sector with both its category and its angle or value — an unlabelled, accurately-drawn pie chart can still lose marks.
For a composite bar chart question, always state the subtraction you used to find an upper section's frequency, not just the final number — the method mark sits in showing total-minus-lower-section.
'Which chart is most suitable?' answers need a REASON tied to what the data needs to show (proportions, group comparison, or individual values kept), not just the chart's name.
In a stem-and-leaf question, a bare correct diagram with no stated key can lose a mark — always write the key explicitly, even when it seems obvious from context.

summary.big_idea: Every chart turns a frequency into a visual stand-in — bar height, number of symbols, sector angle, or row of leaves — so reading or drawing any chart is really the single skill of converting between frequency and that stand-in, done correctly and checked at the end.
key_points: Bar chart: height $=$ frequency, equal widths, labelled axes, scale from $0$. Dual: bars side by side. Composite: stacked, subtract to read any section above the bottom one.
Pictogram: the key fixes the value of one whole symbol; part symbols are the matching fraction of it.
Pie chart: $\text{angle}=\frac{\text{frequency}}{\text{total}}\times360^\circ$; the same angle in two different charts means the same proportion, not the same number, unless the totals also match.
Stem-and-leaf: leaves ordered within each row, with a key; mode, median and shape read directly, with every individual value kept.
Choose the chart that matches the question: pie for proportions of a whole, dual bar for group comparison, stem-and-leaf to keep every value; check axes start at $0$ and angles sum to $360^\circ$.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Identify which visual quantity stands for frequency in the chart you are using (height, symbols, angle, or leaf-row), convert carefully in the direction the question needs, and always run the chart's own check (frequencies sum to the total; angles sum to $360^\circ$; axis starts at $0$) before trusting the answer.

objectives.statement: Calculate the mean, median, mode and range of a list of data, and find a missing value from a given mean.
Calculate the mean, median and mode of data given in a frequency table, using running totals to locate the median.
Decide which average (mean, median or mode) is most appropriate for a given situation, and justify the choice.
Find the lower quartile, upper quartile and interquartile range of a list of data.
Estimate the mean of grouped data using mid-class values, and identify the modal class.

prerequisites.statement: Add a list of numbers and divide accurately, including with a calculator and by hand.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The mean is nothing more than total divided by count; every error in this lesson that looks conceptual is usually just an arithmetic slip in the total or the count.

prerequisites.statement: Order a list of numbers from smallest to largest.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The median, the mode's position and both quartiles are all defined in terms of an ORDERED list; none of them can be found correctly from data as originally given.

prerequisites.statement: Read a simple and a grouped frequency table (Lesson 9.1).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Finding an average 'from a frequency table' or 'from grouped data' in this lesson assumes fluent reading of the table structures built in the previous lesson.

diagnostic_items.question: Why must data be ordered before the median is found?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: The median is DEFINED as the middle value's position in an ordered list; the number that happens to sit in the middle of the data as originally written down has no particular meaning and is not the median.

common_wrong_answers.answer: It doesn't really matter, as long as you pick a number from the middle of the list somewhere.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Treats the median as a rough, approximate idea ('somewhere in the middle') rather than a precisely defined position that only makes sense once the data is sorted.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that the learner understands the median as a POSITION in sorted data, not a vague sense of 'a middling value'.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Give a short unordered list and ask for 'the middle value as written'; then sort it and show the actual median is a completely different number, making the necessity of ordering concrete.

diagnostic_items.question: Can the mean of a set of whole numbers be a decimal? Can the median?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Yes to both. The mean of $1$ and $2$ is $1.5$; the median of $1$ and $2$ (an even-sized list) is also $1.5$, the average of the two middle values.

common_wrong_answers.answer: No — if the data is whole numbers, the mean and median must also be whole numbers.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Assumes a result must share the 'type' of the data it was calculated from, missing that both division (for the mean) and averaging two middle values (for an even-sized median) can produce a non-whole-number result even from whole-number data.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Tests whether the learner has internalised that both the mean (division) and the even-$n$ median (averaging two values) can easily produce decimals, even from entirely whole-number data.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Compute the mean and median of a short even-sized whole-number list (e.g. $4,6,7,9$) together, and point out that the DIVISION in each calculation is exactly why a decimal can appear.

diagnostic_items.question: A shopkeeper wants to know which size of T-shirt to order most of. Which average is appropriate?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: The mode: it is the only average that answers 'which single value occurs most often', which is exactly what 'order most of' needs.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The mean, because that's the 'main' average people usually use.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Defaults to the mean as a general-purpose choice without checking whether it actually answers the specific question being asked — here, an 'average' T-shirt size (e.g. a mean of $11.4$) is meaningless for a stocking decision.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that the learner selects an average based on what the QUESTION needs, not habit or familiarity.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Ask directly: 'can you actually order $11.4$ of a T-shirt size?' Since the answer is no, the mean cannot be the right tool here — only a real, occurring value (the mode) can answer a stocking question.

diagnostic_items.question: Why is the mean of grouped data only an estimate?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Grouping hides the exact individual values inside each class; the calculation has to ASSUME every value equals the class midpoint, which is rarely exactly true, so the result is an estimate rather than the true mean.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Because the calculation method itself is less accurate than normal division.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Blames the arithmetic method rather than the actual cause, which is that the underlying DATA needed for an exact mean is simply no longer available once it has been grouped.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Tests whether the learner locates the source of the inaccuracy correctly (lost individual data) rather than vaguely blaming the calculation.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Compute the exact mean of a small raw data set, then group the same data and compute the midpoint-based estimate, to show the two numbers differ and why.

theory_blocks.title: One typical value, one measure of spread
theory_blocks.body: An **average** answers 'what is a typical value?'; a **measure of spread** answers 'how much do the values vary?' Two very different data sets can share exactly the same average, so a genuinely useful summary always needs [[blue:BOTH: one measure of average, and one measure of spread]]. This pairing — never an average alone — is exactly what Lesson 9.4 will ask you to use when comparing two data sets.
