theory_blocks.title: The three averages and the range
theory_blocks.body:
For a set of $n$ data values:

- **Mean** $=\dfrac{\text{sum of all the values}}{\text{number of values}}$.
- **Median** $=$ the middle value when the data is arranged **in order**: the $\tfrac{n+1}{2}$th value in the ordered list. If $n$ is even, this position falls between two values, so the median is the mean of the two middle values.
- **Mode** $=$ the value that occurs most often (there may be no mode, or more than one).
- **Range** $=$ largest value $-$ smallest value.

theory_blocks.title: Three errors that break every average
theory_blocks.body:
- Finding the median WITHOUT ordering the data first — the middle number of the list as originally written is meaningless.
- Giving the range as two numbers ('$5$ to $10$') or as a middle value, rather than the single number largest $-$ smallest.
- Reporting the mode as the FREQUENCY instead of the value: if $5$ occurs three times, the mode is $5$, not $3$.

theory_blocks.title: Working backwards from the mean
theory_blocks.body: Because mean $=$ total $\div$ number of values, rearranging gives **total $=$ mean $\times$ number of values**. This single rearrangement is the key to every 'missing value' or 'combined group' problem: find the total(s) you know, and use subtraction or addition to find what's missing.

theory_blocks.title: Sanity-checking an average
theory_blocks.body: The mean always lies between the smallest and the largest data value — if your mean is bigger than the biggest value (or smaller than the smallest), an arithmetic slip has been made. For an odd number of values, the median is the single middle value; for an even number, it is the mean of the two middle values. Always confirm your ordered list still contains all $n$ original values.

theory_blocks.title: Averages from a frequency table
theory_blocks.body: When many values repeat, they are shown in a **frequency table**: the frequency $f$ tells how many times each value $x$ occurs. Every average can still be found, but each $x$-value must be weighted by how often it actually occurs.

theory_blocks.title: Method for a frequency table
theory_blocks.body:
1. Add a row $f\times x$ and total both the $f$ row and the $f\times x$ row.
2. **Mean** $=\sum fx\div\sum f$.
3. **Median**: find the position $\tfrac{n+1}{2}$ (where $n=\sum f$), then use RUNNING totals of frequency to see which $x$-value that position falls in.
4. **Mode**: the $x$-value with the largest frequency.

theory_blocks.title: Frequencies are weights, not something to ignore
theory_blocks.body: Do not add the $x$-values and divide by the number of columns (categories). The mean of $0,1,2,3,4$ averaged this naive way is $2$, but the data is almost never spread evenly across those values — the frequencies act as [[blue:**weights**]], and the true mean uses $\sum fx\div\sum f$, not a plain average of the $x$-values.

theory_blocks.title: Choosing between mean, median and mode
theory_blocks.body:
| Average | Advantages | Disadvantages |
|---|---|---|
| Mean | Uses every value; most commonly used; needed for totals. | Distorted by extreme values (outliers). |
| Median | Not affected by extreme values; easy to find from ordered data. | Ignores the size of most values. |
| Mode | Works for non-numerical data; easy to find. | May not exist, or may not be unique; ignores other values. |

theory_blocks.title: Giving a reason, not just a name
theory_blocks.body: Exam questions often ask 'which average would be most suitable, and why?' Always give the average AND a reason connected to the actual data: the mode for the most popular size to stock; the median when there is an outlier; the mean when every value matters or a total is needed.

theory_blocks.title: Exam guidance for this lesson
theory_blocks.body: Non-calculator papers use short lists, where every step of a mean/median/mode calculation should be shown explicitly for method marks. On calculator papers a built-in statistics function may be used, but writing out $\sum fx$ and $\sum f$ (or the ordered list for a median) still earns method marks even if the final value is then read off a calculator. Give non-exact answers to $3$ significant figures, and always show the ordered list when finding a median or quartiles.

theory_blocks.title: Quartiles and the interquartile range
theory_blocks.body:
The range uses only the two most extreme values, so a single outlier can make it huge. A better measure of spread looks only at the MIDDLE half of the data. Arrange the $n$ values in order; the median $Q_2$ splits the data into a lower half and an upper half.

- **Lower quartile** $Q_1=$ median of the lower half (a quarter of the data lie below it).
- **Upper quartile** $Q_3=$ median of the upper half (a quarter of the data lie above it).
- **Interquartile range** $\mathrm{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1$: the spread of the middle $50\%$ of the data.

When $n$ is odd, do NOT include the median itself in either half.

theory_blocks.title: Reading quartiles another way
theory_blocks.body: Quartiles can also be read from a cumulative frequency curve (Lesson 9.6), which is the usual method for large, grouped data sets. For a short LIST of raw data (the situation in this lesson), the method above — taking the medians of the two halves — is the one to use.

theory_blocks.title: Estimating the mean of grouped data
theory_blocks.body: When data is grouped into classes, the individual values are no longer known, so the mean can only be ESTIMATED. The method assumes every value in a class equals the class's **mid-class value** (midpoint). The **modal class** is the class with the highest frequency (for equal class widths).

theory_blocks.title: Method for estimating a grouped mean
theory_blocks.body:
1. Add a column for the midpoint $x$ of each class: $\tfrac12(\text{lower boundary}+\text{upper boundary})$.
2. Add a column $f\times x$ and total it.
3. Estimated mean $=\dfrac{\sum fx}{\sum f}$.

theory_blocks.title: Two ways a grouped-mean estimate goes wrong
theory_blocks.body: Dividing $\sum fx$ by the NUMBER OF CLASSES instead of by $\sum f$ (the total frequency); or using the class FREQUENCY instead of the class MIDPOINT as the value $x$ in that row. Also, never call the result simply 'the mean' — always say 'ESTIMATED mean', since the true value depends on data that grouping has hidden.

theory_blocks.title: Going further: the normal distribution and the 68-95-99.7 rule
theory_blocks.body:
Many real data sets — heights, measurement errors, test scores — cluster symmetrically around their mean in a characteristic bell-shaped pattern called the **normal distribution**. Two measures together completely describe this shape: the mean from this lesson, and the **standard deviation** (a measure of spread that goes beyond IGCSE; a more precise cousin of the range, found from every value's distance from the mean).

For data that follows a normal distribution closely, a strikingly consistent pattern holds, often called the [[blue:68–95–99.7 rule]]: about $68\%$ of values lie within $1$ standard deviation of the mean, about $95\%$ lie within $2$ standard deviations, and about $99.7\%$ lie within $3$ standard deviations. So if a set of test scores has mean $65$ and standard deviation $8$, roughly $68\%$ of students scored between $57$ and $73$, and almost every student (99.7%) scored between $41$ and $89$.

This is why standard deviation, not just the range, matters so much in statistics beyond GCSE: it does not only measure spread, it unlocks a precise, predictable description of WHERE most of the data sits. This idea underlies quality control in manufacturing and most of the inferential statistics studied at A-level and university.

keywords.definition: The sum of all the data values divided by the number of values.
The middle value of a data set once it has been arranged in order (the mean of the two middle values if there is an even number of values).
The value that occurs most often in a data set.
The largest value in a data set minus the smallest value.
The median of the lower half of an ordered data set; a quarter of the data lie below it.
The median of the upper half of an ordered data set; a quarter of the data lie above it.
The upper quartile minus the lower quartile; the spread of the middle 50% of the data.
The class interval with the highest frequency in a grouped frequency table.
The value halfway between a class's lower and upper boundary, used to estimate the mean of grouped data.
A data value that is far removed from the rest of the data, which can strongly distort the mean and range.

worked_examples.statement: Odd number of values. Nine students scored these marks in a quiz: $8,5,9,6,5,7,10,5,8$. Find the mean, median, mode and range.
knowns: 9 quiz marks
unknowns: mean, median, mode, range
reasoning: Order the marks first: $5,5,5,6,7,8,8,9,10$.
Mean: add all nine values and divide by $9$: $\dfrac{5+5+5+6+7+8+8+9+10}{9}=\dfrac{63}{9}$.
Median: with $n=9$ (odd), the median is the $5$th ordered value.
Mode: the value occurring most often across the ordered list.
Range: largest $-$ smallest from the ordered list.
worked_examples.solution: Mean $=7$, median $=7$, mode $=5$, range $=5$.
worked_examples.interpretation: With the data ordered once, all four summary statistics come from reading or adding that same ordered list — ordering is the one step that unlocks every later calculation.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Finding the median from the original, unordered list of marks, which can land on a completely different (and wrong) value.

worked_examples.statement: Even number of values. The times, in minutes, that eight people waited at a clinic were $12,15,11,18,14,15,20,13$. Find the median and the mean.
knowns: 8 waiting times
unknowns: median, mean
reasoning: With $n=8$ (even), the median is the mean of the $4$th and $5$th ordered values.
Add all eight times for the mean's numerator, then divide by $8$.
worked_examples.solution: Median $=\dfrac{14+15}{2}=14.5$ minutes; sum $=118$, mean $=\dfrac{118}{8}=14.75$ minutes.
worked_examples.interpretation: An even-sized data set always needs TWO middle values averaged together for the median, which is exactly why a median can be a decimal even from whole-number data.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Taking just one of the two middle values (e.g. only the $4$th) as the median instead of averaging both the $4$th and $5$th.

worked_examples.statement: Finding a missing value. The mean of five numbers is $8$. Four of the numbers are $6,9,7,12$. Find the fifth.
knowns: mean of 5 numbers = 8
four of the numbers: 6, 9, 7, 12
unknowns: the fifth number
reasoning: Use total $=$ mean $\times$ number of values: the total of all five numbers is $5\times8$.
Add the four known numbers to find how much of that total is already accounted for.
Subtract the known sum from the required total to find the missing number.
worked_examples.solution: Total $=5\times8=40$. Known sum $=6+9+7+12=34$. Fifth number $=40-34=6$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Every 'missing value from a mean' problem is really just total $=$ mean $\times$ count, followed by ordinary subtraction — no new technique beyond that single rearrangement.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Dividing $8$ (the mean) by $5$ (the count) rather than multiplying, which reverses the rearrangement needed to recover the total.

worked_examples.statement: Frequency table. A class of $30$ pupils recorded how many brothers and sisters each has: $x=0,1,2,3,4$ with frequencies $f=5,9,8,5,3$. Find the mode, median, mean and range.
knowns: x values 0-4 with frequencies 5,9,8,5,3, total 30
unknowns: mode, median, mean, range
reasoning: Add a row $f\times x$: $0,9,16,15,12$, totalling $52$.
Mode: the largest frequency is $9$, belonging to $x=1$.
Median: $n=30$, so the median position is between the $15$th and $16$th values; running totals of frequency are $5,14,22,\ldots$, so both the $15$th and $16$th values fall in the group $x=2$.
Mean: $\dfrac{\sum fx}{\sum f}=\dfrac{52}{30}$.
Range: largest $x$ value minus smallest, $4-0$.
worked_examples.solution: Mode $=1$ sibling; median $=2$; mean $=\dfrac{52}{30}=1.73$ (3 s.f.); range $=4$.
worked_examples.interpretation: A frequency table's mean needs the $f\times x$ weighting, but its median still comes from the same running-total logic used to locate a position in any ordered list — the frequencies just make the 'list' compact.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Computing the mean as the mean of the five DISTINCT $x$-values ($0,1,2,3,4\to2$), ignoring the frequencies entirely.

worked_examples.statement: Choosing an average. Five workers in a small firm earn \$18\,000, \$19\,500, \$20\,000, \$21\,000 and \$21\,500 a year. The owner earns \$120\,000. The owner claims 'the average salary is over \$36\,000'. Which average is she using, and is it fair?
knowns: 5 worker salaries + 1 owner salary
unknowns: which average gives $\approx\$36\,700$; whether it fairly represents a typical salary
reasoning: Add all six salaries (including the owner's) and divide by $6$ to test whether this matches the owner's claimed figure.
Separately, find the median of all six salaries (order them and average the two middle values) to see what a 'typical' salary looks like.
Compare: does the owner's own huge salary pull one average much further from the typical worker's pay than the other?
worked_examples.solution: Total $=220\,000$ over $6$ people: mean $\approx\$36\,700$, matching the owner's claim. Median $=\dfrac{20\,000+21\,000}{2}=\$20\,500$, which is far closer to what almost everyone actually earns. The owner's salary is an outlier that inflates the mean; the median gives a fairer picture of a typical worker's pay.
worked_examples.interpretation: The owner has technically told the truth about the mean while using it to mislead — recognising WHICH average best represents 'typical' is as important as being able to calculate any of them.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Accepting the mean at face value as 'the average' without checking it against the median, especially when a data set contains one very extreme value.

guided_exercises.statement: Find the mean, median, mode and range of $9,4,7,9,6,3,9,8$.
hints: Order the eight values first: write them out from smallest to largest before doing anything else.
With $8$ values (even), remember the median needs TWO middle values averaged together.
guided_exercises.answer: Mean $=6.875$, median $=7.5$, mode $=9$, range $=6$.
guided_exercises.full_solution: Ordered: $3,4,6,7,8,9,9,9$. Mean $=\dfrac{3+4+6+7+8+9+9+9}{8}=\dfrac{55}{8}=6.875$. Median $=\dfrac{7+8}{2}=7.5$ (4th and 5th values). Mode $=9$ (appears three times). Range $=9-3=6$.
common_errors: Reporting the mode's frequency (3) instead of the actual repeated value (9).

guided_exercises.statement: A survey of $25$ families recorded the number of cars owned: $x=0,1,2,3$ with frequencies $f=4,12,7,2$. Find the mean (to 3 s.f.), median and mode.
hints: Add an $f\times x$ row and total it before attempting the mean.
For the median, use running totals of frequency to find where the $13$th value ($\tfrac{n+1}{2}=13$) falls.
guided_exercises.answer: Mean $\approx1.28$, median $=1$, mode $=1$.
guided_exercises.full_solution: $f\times x$: $0,12,14,6$, total $32$; $\sum f=25$. Mean $=32\div25=1.28$. Running totals: $4,16,23,25$; the $13$th value falls in the $x=1$ group (since the running total reaches $16$ there), so median $=1$. The largest frequency, $12$, belongs to $x=1$, so mode $=1$.
common_errors: Using $\tfrac{n}{2}=12.5$ and rounding incorrectly instead of correctly locating the $13$th value ($\tfrac{n+1}{2}$) via the running totals.

guided_exercises.statement: Find the median, lower quartile, upper quartile and interquartile range of $4,9,11,13,15,18,20,22,25$.
hints: With $n=9$ (odd), find the median first, then split the remaining 8 values into a lower half of 4 and an upper half of 4 (excluding the median itself).
Each half has an EVEN number of values, so each quartile needs two middle values averaged.
guided_exercises.full_solution: $n=9$, median is the 5th value: $15$. Lower half (excluding $15$): $4,9,11,13$, median $Q_1=\tfrac{9+11}{2}=10$. Upper half: $18,20,22,25$, median $Q_3=\tfrac{20+22}{2}=21$. $\mathrm{IQR}=21-10=11$.
common_errors: Including the median value $15$ itself in one of the two halves when $n$ is odd, which shifts both quartiles.

exercises.statement: For the data $4,7,5,9,7,3,7,8$ find the mean, median, mode and range.
exercises.answer: Mean $=6.25$, median $=7$, mode $=7$, range $=6$.
exercises.full_solution: Ordered: $3,4,5,7,7,7,8,9$. Mean $=50\div8=6.25$. Median $=\tfrac{7+7}{2}=7$ (4th and 5th values). Mode $=7$ (appears three times). Range $=9-3=6$.
common_errors: Finding the median from the unordered list as given.

exercises.statement: Find the median, mode, range and mean (3 s.f.) of $12,15,9,18,15,11$.
exercises.answer: Median $=13.5$, mode $=15$, range $=9$, mean $=13.3$.
exercises.full_solution: Ordered: $9,11,12,15,15,18$. Median $=\tfrac{12+15}{2}=13.5$. Mode $=15$ (appears twice). Range $=18-9=9$. Mean $=80\div6=13.333\ldots\approx13.3$.
common_errors: Rounding the mean too early during the division instead of at the final 3 s.f. step.

exercises.statement: The number of goals scored in $20$ matches is: goals $0,1,2,3,4$ with frequencies $4,7,6,2,1$. Find the mean, median, mode and range.
exercises.answer: Mean $=1.45$, median $=1$, mode $=1$, range $=4$.
exercises.full_solution: $f\times x$: $0,7,12,6,4$, total $29$. Mean $=29\div20=1.45$. Running totals: $4,11,17,19,20$; the median position ($10.5$th, mean of 10th and 11th) falls where the running total first reaches $11$, i.e. at $x=1$: median $=1$. Mode: largest frequency $7$ at $x=1$. Range $=4-0=4$.
common_errors: Averaging the five goal VALUES ($0,1,2,3,4\to2$) instead of weighting by frequency for the mean.

exercises.statement: The mean of six numbers is $9.5$. Five of them are $8,12,7,10,9$. Find the sixth.
exercises.full_solution: Total $=6\times9.5=57$. Known sum $=8+12+7+10+9=46$. Sixth number $=57-46=11$.
common_errors: Dividing $9.5$ by $6$ instead of multiplying to recover the total.

exercises.statement: The mean of four numbers is $12$. A fifth number is added and the mean becomes $13$. Find the fifth number.
exercises.full_solution: Original total $=4\times12=48$. New total $=5\times13=65$. Fifth number $=65-48=17$.
common_errors: Using $4$ (the old count) instead of $5$ (the new count) when recovering the new total.

exercises.statement: The midday temperatures ($^\circ$C) on seven days were $14,17,15,19,21,17,13$. Find the range, the median, the mode and the mean (3 s.f.).
exercises.answer: Range $=8$, median $=17$, mode $=17$, mean $=16.6$.
exercises.full_solution: Ordered: $13,14,15,17,17,19,21$. Range $=21-13=8$. Median (4th value) $=17$. Mode $=17$ (appears twice). Mean $=116\div7=16.571\ldots\approx16.6$.
common_errors: Reporting two values as 'the mode' when only one value (17) actually repeats.

exercises.statement: Which average (mean, median or mode) is most suitable for (a) the most popular flavour of ice cream in a shop; (b) the typical house price in a town where one house is a huge mansion? Give a reason for each.
exercises.answer: (a) Mode (non-numerical/categorical, most popular). (b) Median (the mansion is an outlier that would inflate the mean).
exercises.full_solution: (a) 'Most popular flavour' is exactly the mode's definition — the value (flavour) occurring most often; the mean and median don't even make sense for categorical data. (b) House prices with one extreme outlier are best summarised by the median, since the mean would be pulled upward by the mansion and no longer represent a typical house.
common_errors: Suggesting the mean for (b) without recognising that a single extreme value distorts it away from what 'typical' should mean.

exercises.statement: Five whole numbers in ascending order have mode $3$, median $4$, mean $5$ and range $7$. Find them.
exercises.full_solution: Median $4$ means the 3rd (middle) value is $4$. Mode $3$ means $3$ is the most frequent value, so the first two values are both $3$ (to repeat and stay $\le4$ in order). Range $7$ with smallest $3$ gives largest $=3+7=10$. Total $=5\times5=25$; known so far $3+3+4+10=20$, so the fourth value is $25-20=5$. Full list: $3,3,4,5,10$.
common_errors: Assuming the mode value only needs to appear once, missing that 'mode' specifically requires it to be the MOST frequent value.

exercises.statement: A class of $20$ students has a mean mark of $60$ and another class of $30$ students has a mean mark of $70$. Find the mean mark of all $50$ students.
exercises.full_solution: Total marks $=20\times60+30\times70=1200+2100=3300$. Combined mean $=3300\div50=66$.
common_errors: Averaging the two given means directly ($\tfrac{60+70}{2}=65$), ignoring that the two classes have different sizes.

exercises.statement: The numbers of pets owned by $30$ pupils are: pets $0,1,2,3,4$ with frequencies $8,12,6,3,1$. Find the mean (3 s.f.), median and mode.
exercises.answer: Mean $=1.23$, median $=1$, mode $=1$.
exercises.full_solution: $f\times x$: $0,12,12,9,4$, total $37$. Mean $=37\div30=1.2333\ldots\approx1.23$. Running totals: $8,20,26,29,30$; the median (mean of 15th and 16th values) falls in the $x=1$ group. Mode: largest frequency $12$ at $x=1$.
common_errors: Using $n=5$ (the number of distinct pet counts) instead of $n=30$ (the actual number of pupils) when finding the median's position.

exercises.statement: For $12,7,15,9,11,20,14,8,16,10,13$ find the median, the lower and upper quartiles, the IQR and the range.
common_errors: Including the median (12) in one of the two halves before finding the quartiles.
Splitting the 10 values into halves of unequal size instead of two equal halves of 5 each.

exercises.statement: The masses $m$ kg of $40$ parcels are grouped: $0<m\le2$ freq $5$, $2<m\le4$ freq $11$, $4<m\le6$ freq $16$, $6<m\le8$ freq $8$. (a) Write down the modal class. (b) Calculate an estimate of the mean. (c) Explain why it is only an estimate.
exercises.answer: (a) $4<m\le6$. (b) $4.35$ kg. (c) The actual masses inside each class are unknown; the calculation assumes every value equals its class midpoint.
exercises.full_solution: (a) The highest frequency, $16$, belongs to $4<m\le6$. (b) Midpoints $1,3,5,7$: $\dfrac{5(1)+11(3)+16(5)+8(7)}{40}=\dfrac{174}{40}=4.35$ kg. (c) Grouping hides the exact mass of each parcel, so the midpoint is only an assumption, not the true value — the estimate is only as good as that assumption.
common_errors: Using the class WIDTH ($2$) instead of the class MIDPOINT as $x$ in the $f\times x$ calculation.

exercises.statement: A frequency table has $x=1,2,3,4,5$ with frequencies $3,7,10,6,4$. Find the mean (3 s.f.), the median, the quartiles and the IQR.
exercises.full_solution: $\sum f=30$, $f\times x$: $3,14,30,24,20$, total $91$. Mean $=91\div30=3.0333\ldots\approx3.03$. Running totals: $3,10,20,26,30$. Median (mean of 15th and 16th, both in the $x=3$ group): $3$. $Q_1$ (8th value, in the $x=2$ group, since running total reaches $10$ there): $2$. $Q_3$ (23rd value, in the $x=4$ group, since running total reaches $26$ there): $4$. IQR $=4-2=2$.
common_errors: Using $\tfrac n4=7.5$ directly as a data value instead of using it to locate the correct POSITION via the running totals.

exercises.statement: The IQR of a data set is $14$ and its upper quartile is $31$. Find the lower quartile.
exercises.full_solution: $\mathrm{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1$, so $Q_1=Q_3-\mathrm{IQR}=31-14=17$.
common_errors: Adding instead of subtracting ($31+14=45$), reversing the IQR formula's rearrangement.

exercises.statement: Consider $2,15,16,17,18,19,20,60$. Find the range and the IQR, and say which is a better description of the spread of most of the data.
exercises.answer: Range $=58$; $Q_1=15.5$, $Q_3=19.5$, IQR $=4$. The IQR is better.
exercises.full_solution: Range $=60-2=58$. Lower half: $2,15,16,17$, $Q_1=\tfrac{15+16}{2}=15.5$. Upper half: $18,19,20,60$, $Q_3=\tfrac{19+20}{2}=19.5$. IQR $=19.5-15.5=4$. The range is hugely distorted by the two outliers ($2$ and $60$); the IQR describes the spread of the middle, typical values far better.
common_errors: Concluding the range is more informative simply because it is a bigger, more dramatic-looking number.

exercises.statement: In a grouped table the classes are $0<x\le10$, $10<x\le20$, $20<x\le30$ with frequencies $4$, $f$, $6$. The estimated mean is $16$. Find $f$.
common_errors: Forgetting that the TOTAL frequency on the right-hand side also contains $f$ (it is $10+f$, not a fixed number), leading to an unsolvable or wrong equation.

exam_questions.statement:
The number of pages read each evening by a student over $10$ days was:
$14,22,18,14,30,16,14,20,25,17$.
(a) Find the mean, median, mode and range of this data. [4]
(b) The student says 'my mean reading is about 19 pages, so that's a fair way to describe my typical evening'. Comment on whether the mean or median better represents a typical evening here, giving a reason. [2]
exam_questions.answer: (a) Mean $=19$, median $=17.5$, mode $=14$, range $=16$. (b) Both are reasonably close here (no extreme outlier), so either is defensible; the median is slightly less affected by the one higher value (30).
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Ordered: $14,14,14,16,17,18,20,22,25,30$. Sum $=190$, mean $=190\div10=19$. Median $=\tfrac{17+18}{2}=17.5$ (5th and 6th values). Mode $=14$ (appears three times). Range $=30-14=16$. (b) The mean ($19$) and median ($17.5$) are reasonably close, since there is no single extreme outlier in this data; either average gives a fair summary, though the median is marginally less pulled by the single higher value of $30$.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for ordering the data; A1 for mean $=19$; A1 for median $=17.5$; B1 for mode $=14$ and range $=16$ both correct (accept split marks if only one of mode/range is correct)
(b) B1 for a comparison that states both values numerically; B1 for a reason connected to the presence/absence of an outlier in THIS specific data set (not a generic statement).
common_errors: In (a), finding the median from the data in the order given, rather than from the ordered list.

exam_questions.statement:
The table shows the number of emails received by $40$ employees in one day.
$$\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
\text{Emails},\ x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4\\\hline
\text{Frequency},\ f & 6 & 10 & 14 & 7 & 3
\end{array}$$
(a) Calculate the mean number of emails per employee. [3]
(b) Find the median number of emails. [2]
(c) State the modal number of emails. [1]
(d) One employee says 'the mean is $1.775$, which isn't a whole number, so it must be wrong.' Explain why the employee is mistaken. [1]
exam_questions.answer: (a) Mean $=1.775$. (b) Median $=2$. (c) Mode $=2$. (d) A mean doesn't have to be one of the actual data values or a whole number — it is a calculated average, not a data value itself.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) $f\times x$: $0,10,28,21,12$, total $71$. Mean $=71\div40=1.775$. (b) $\sum f=40$; median is the mean of the 20th and 21st ordered values. Running totals: $6,16,30,37,40$; both the 20th and 21st values fall in the $x=2$ group (since the running total passes $20$ only once it reaches $30$ at $x=2$): median $=2$. (c) Largest frequency is $14$, at $x=2$: mode $=2$. (d) The mean is an ARITHMETIC AVERAGE, computed by dividing a total by a count; there's no requirement for it to equal one of the original data values or be a whole number.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for a correct $f\times x$ row; M1 for $\sum fx=71$ and $\sum f=40$; A1 for mean $=1.775$
(b) M1 for correct running totals used to locate the 20th/21st values; A1 for median $=2$
(c) B1 for mode $=2$
(d) B1 for a correct explanation that a mean need not be a whole number or an actual data value.
common_errors: In (b), using $n\div2=20$ as the median's position directly (a single value) instead of recognising that an even $n$ needs the MEAN of the 20th and 21st values.

exam_questions.statement:
The times, in minutes, taken by $11$ runners to complete a race are:
$42,38,51,45,49,36,55,47,40,53,44$.
(a) Find the median time. [1]
(b) Find the lower quartile and upper quartile. [2]
(c) Calculate the interquartile range, and explain what it tells you about the race times. [2]
exam_questions.answer: (a) Median $=45$. (b) $Q_1=40$, $Q_3=51$. (c) IQR $=11$ minutes; the middle half of the runners finished within an $11$-minute window.
exam_questions.full_solution: Ordered: $36,38,40,42,44,45,47,49,51,53,55$ ($n=11$). (a) Median (6th value) $=45$. (b) Lower half (first 5): $36,38,40,42,44$, $Q_1=40$. Upper half (last 5): $47,49,51,53,55$, $Q_3=51$. (c) IQR $=51-40=11$ minutes: the middle $50\%$ of runners (excluding the fastest and slowest quarters) all finished within an $11$-minute spread of each other.
mark_scheme: (a) B1 for median $=45$
(b) M1 for correctly splitting into two halves of 5, excluding the median; A1 for both $Q_1=40$ and $Q_3=51$ correct
(c) M1 for IQR $=11$; A1 for a contextual interpretation referencing 'the middle half of the runners' or equivalent, not just the bare number.
common_errors: Including the median (45) in the lower or upper half before finding the quartiles, which shifts both $Q_1$ and $Q_3$.

challenge_questions.statement: Class A has $12$ students with mean mark $58$; class B has $18$ students with mean $63$. (a) Show that the mean of the combined group is $61$. (b) A third group of $10$ students joins and the mean of all $40$ students becomes $64$. Find the mean of the third group.
challenge_questions.full_solution: (a) Combined total $=12\times58+18\times63=696+1134=1830$; combined count $=30$; mean $=1830\div30=61$. (b) Total of all $40=40\times64=2560$; subtracting the first $30$ students' total ($1830$) leaves $730$ for the $10$ new students; their mean $=730\div10=73$.

challenge_questions.statement: A set of seven numbers has mean $8$. When one number is removed, the mean of the remaining six is $7$. Find the number removed.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Original total $=7\times8=56$. New total $=6\times7=42$. Number removed $=56-42=14$.

challenge_questions.statement: For the table $x=1,2,3,4$ with frequencies $5,k,7,2$, the mean is $2.4$. Find $k$ and then the median.
challenge_questions.answer: $k=1$; median $=3$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: $\sum fx=5(1)+k(2)+7(3)+2(4)=5+2k+21+8=34+2k$. $\sum f=5+k+7+2=14+k$. $\dfrac{34+2k}{14+k}=2.4\Rightarrow34+2k=2.4(14+k)=33.6+2.4k\Rightarrow0.4=0.4k\Rightarrow k=1$. With $k=1$: $n=15$, frequencies $5,1,7,2$; running totals $5,6,13,15$; the median (8th value) falls in the $x=3$ group (running total reaches $13$ there): median $=3$.

challenge_questions.statement: Show that adding a new value equal to the current mean does not change the mean.
challenge_questions.answer: Proven algebraically: new mean $=\dfrac{nm+m}{n+1}=m$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Let the original total be $S$ over $n$ values, mean $m=S/n$, so $S=nm$. Adding a new value equal to $m$ gives a new total $S+m=nm+m$ over $n+1$ values. New mean $=\dfrac{nm+m}{n+1}=\dfrac{m(n+1)}{n+1}=m$: unchanged.

challenge_questions.statement: A set of data has median $14$, IQR $8$ and range $15$. Every value is multiplied by $3$ and then $2$ is added. Write down the new median, IQR and range, explaining why the IQR and range are not affected by the '$+2$'.
challenge_questions.answer: New median $=44$, new IQR $=24$, new range $=45$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Multiplying every value by $3$ scales the median, IQR and range all by $3$; adding $2$ afterwards shifts the median by $+2$, but has NO effect on the IQR or range, since both are DIFFERENCES between two values, and a constant shift added to both values of a difference cancels out exactly. New median $=14\times3+2=44$. New IQR $=8\times3=24$ (the $+2$ cancels in $Q_3-Q_1$). New range $=15\times3=45$ (the $+2$ cancels in max$-$min).

challenge_questions.statement: The table shows grouped data: $0<x\le10$ frequency $6$; $10<x\le20$ frequency $14$. Find the smallest and largest possible values of the true mean, and compare with the estimate.
challenge_questions.answer: The true mean is greater than $7$ and at most $17$; the midpoint estimate, $12$, lies between these limits.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Smallest possible: values can be just above each class's LOWER bound, giving a mean just above $\dfrac{0(6)+10(14)}{20}=\dfrac{140}{20}=7$ (the bounds $0$ and $10$ themselves are excluded by the $<$ signs). Largest possible: every value equals its class's UPPER bound: $\dfrac{10(6)+20(14)}{20}=\dfrac{340}{20}=17$. So $7<\text{true mean}\le17$. The midpoint-based estimate is $\dfrac{5(6)+15(14)}{20}=\dfrac{240}{20}=12$, which sits between these two extremes, as it always must since the midpoint lies between the two boundaries.

mcq.stem: A data set has smallest value $12$ and largest value $29$. What is the range?

options.why_wrong: This restates the two extreme values instead of calculating the single number the range actually requires: largest minus smallest.
This is the MIDPOINT of $12$ and $29$, not the range — the midpoint and the range measure completely different things.
This adds the two extreme values ($12+29$) instead of subtracting the smaller from the larger.

mcq.explanation: Range $=$ largest $-$ smallest $=29-12=17$: always a single subtracted number, never a description of the two extremes or their average.

mcq.stem: In a frequency table, the value $x=6$ occurs with frequency $11$, the highest frequency in the table. What is the mode?

options.why_wrong: This is the FREQUENCY of the mode (how many times it occurs), not the mode itself — the mode must always be a data value.
This is $6+11$, which has no meaning in this context and is not any of the standard summary statistics.

options.text: It cannot be determined without more information
options.why_wrong: The mode is fully determined once the value with the highest frequency is identified, which is already given here.

mcq.explanation: The mode is the data VALUE with the highest frequency, which is $x=6$ here — not the frequency number $11$ itself.

mcq.stem: A frequency table has $x=0,1,2,3$ with frequencies $2,8,5,1$. What is the mean?

options.text: $1.5$ (computed as the mean of $0,1,2,3$)
options.why_wrong: Averaging the four distinct $x$-values directly ($\tfrac{0+1+2+3}{4}=1.5$) ignores the frequencies entirely. Most of the data are $1$s and $2$s, so the weighted mean $\tfrac{\sum fx}{\sum f}$ is lower than $1.5$.
This is the mode (the value with the highest frequency, $8$), and also the median here, not the mean.
This is $\sum fx$ (the total of the $f\times x$ column) without dividing by $\sum f=16$, the total frequency.

mcq.stem: A small company's nine salaries are mostly similar, except for the managing director's salary, which is far higher than everyone else's. Which average best represents a 'typical' salary at this company?

options.text: The median
The mean, since it uses every salary in the calculation
options.why_wrong: Using every value is normally an advantage of the mean, but here that is exactly the problem: the one extreme salary pulls the mean well above what almost everyone actually earns.

options.text: The mode, since salaries are numerical data
options.why_wrong: With continuous-ish numerical salary data, no value may repeat at all, so a mode may not even exist — it is not a sensible choice here.

options.text: The range, since it shows how salaries differ
options.why_wrong: The range is a measure of SPREAD, not an average — it cannot answer 'what is a typical salary?' on its own.

mcq.explanation: The median is not affected by the single very high outlier, so it better represents what most employees actually earn; the mean would be pulled upward by the managing director's salary.

mcq.stem: A grouped frequency table has a class $20<x\le30$ with frequency $9$. What value of $x$ should be used in the $f\times x$ row when estimating the mean?

options.text: $9$ (the frequency)
options.why_wrong: This uses the class's FREQUENCY as if it were the data value, confusing 'how many values are in the class' with 'what value represents the class'.

options.text: $25$ (the midpoint)
$10$ (the class width)
options.why_wrong: The class width (upper boundary minus lower boundary) measures how wide the class is, not a representative data value inside it.

options.text: $30$ (the upper boundary)
options.why_wrong: Using only the upper boundary overestimates every value in the class; the standard method assumes values are spread evenly, so the MIDPOINT is used instead.

mcq.explanation: The estimated mean always uses the class midpoint, $\tfrac{20+30}{2}=25$, as the representative $x$-value for every value assumed to lie in that class.

flashcards.front: Mean, median, mode, range — one-line definitions
flashcards.back: Mean $=$ total $\div$ count. Median $=$ middle of ORDERED data. Mode $=$ most frequent value. Range $=$ largest $-$ smallest.

flashcards.front: Rearranged mean formula for 'missing value' problems
flashcards.back: total $=$ mean $\times$ number of values — the key to every missing-value or combined-group question.

flashcards.front: True or false: the range can be written as 'from 5 to 12'.
flashcards.back: False. The range is always a SINGLE number: largest $-$ smallest $=12-5=7$.

flashcards.front: Mean from a frequency table
flashcards.back: $\text{mean}=\dfrac{\sum fx}{\sum f}$ — each $x$-value weighted by its own frequency, never a plain average of the $x$-values.

flashcards.front: How do you find the median from a frequency table?
flashcards.back: Find the median's POSITION ($\tfrac{n+1}{2}$), then use running totals of frequency to see which $x$-value that position falls in.

flashcards.front: Mean vs median vs mode — when is each the best choice?
flashcards.back: Mean: every value matters, no extreme outliers. Median: an outlier is present. Mode: the data is categorical, or you need the single most common value.

flashcards.front: How do you find Q1 and Q3 from a list of raw data?
flashcards.back: Order the data, find the median, then take the median of the LOWER half (for $Q_1$) and the median of the UPPER half (for $Q_3$) — excluding the overall median itself if $n$ is odd.

flashcards.front: Interquartile range
flashcards.back: $\mathrm{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1$: the spread of the middle $50\%$ of the data, unaffected by extreme outliers.

flashcards.front: Does an outlier affect the IQR much?
flashcards.back: No — the IQR only looks at the middle half of the data, so a single extreme value at either end barely changes it (unlike the range, which is built entirely from the two extremes).

flashcards.front: Estimating the mean of grouped data
flashcards.back: $\text{estimated mean}=\dfrac{\sum f\times(\text{midpoint})}{\sum f}$, where midpoint $=\tfrac12$(lower boundary $+$ upper boundary) of each class.

flashcards.front: Why is a grouped mean always called an 'estimate'?
flashcards.back: Grouping hides the individual values; the calculation assumes every value equals its class midpoint, which is rarely exactly true.

flashcards.front: What is the modal class, and how do you find it?
flashcards.back: The class with the highest FREQUENCY (for equal class widths) in a grouped frequency table — not the class with the highest midpoint.

flashcards.front: A whole data set is multiplied by 3 and then has 2 added to every value. What happens to the median, IQR and range?
flashcards.back: All three get multiplied by 3; the median also shifts by $+2$, but the IQR and range are unaffected by the $+2$, since both are differences and the shift cancels out.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The range of a data set can be given as two numbers ('from 5 to 10'), or as the middle value between the extremes.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The two extreme values (smallest and largest) are naturally spoken about together ('the marks ranged from 5 to 10'), so the everyday phrase blurs into the mathematical definition, which is a single SUBTRACTED number.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner writes 'range $=5$ to $10$' or 'range $=7.5$' (the midpoint of $5$ and $10$) instead of $10-5=5$.
misconceptions.correct_model: The range is always a SINGLE number: largest value minus smallest value. 'The marks ranged from 5 to 10' describes the extremes in words; the range itself is the calculation $10-5=5$.
misconceptions.remediation: Whenever 'range' is asked for, immediately write 'largest $-$ smallest $=$' before putting in any numbers, to force the subtraction rather than a restatement of the two extremes.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The mode is the FREQUENCY of the most common value, not the value itself.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Finding the mode from a frequency table involves spotting the largest frequency number, and it is easy to report that number itself rather than the data value it belongs to.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner reports '7' as the mode when a frequency table shows the value $5$ occurring $7$ times (the largest frequency), when the mode should be $5$.
misconceptions.correct_model: The mode is always a DATA VALUE (the one that occurs most often), never a frequency. In a frequency table, find the largest frequency first, then report the value in THAT row, not the frequency number itself.
misconceptions.remediation: In a frequency table, circle the largest frequency, then draw an arrow sideways to the value in that same row, and report only that value as the mode.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The mean of a frequency table is found by averaging the $x$-values themselves, ignoring the frequencies (e.g. mean of $x=0,1,2,3,4$ is simply $2$).
misconceptions.why_it_appears: If the $x$-values happen to be listed in a neat row, it looks exactly like an ordinary list to average, and the frequency row underneath can be overlooked or treated as a separate, unrelated piece of information.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner computes the mean of a frequency table by averaging the distinct $x$-values ($0,1,2,3,4\to2$) instead of weighting each $x$-value by how often it actually occurs.
misconceptions.correct_model: Each $x$-value must be WEIGHTED by its frequency: mean $=\dfrac{\sum fx}{\sum f}$, found by adding an $f\times x$ row, totalling it, and dividing by the total frequency — not by the number of distinct $x$-values.
misconceptions.remediation: Before computing any frequency-table mean, physically add the $f\times x$ row to the table and total both rows, making the weighting step impossible to skip.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: When estimating the mean of grouped data, the class FREQUENCY is used as the $x$-value instead of the class MIDPOINT.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A grouped-data table has several numeric-looking columns (class boundaries, frequency, and eventually midpoint), and without a clear procedure it is easy to multiply frequency by frequency, or to use the frequency where the midpoint belongs.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner's 'midpoint' column is identical to the frequency column, or they compute $\sum f\times f$ instead of $\sum f\times x$ (midpoint).
misconceptions.correct_model: The estimated mean always uses $x=$ the MIDPOINT of each class (the value halfway between its lower and upper boundary), weighted by that class's frequency: estimated mean $=\dfrac{\sum f\times(\text{midpoint})}{\sum f}$.
misconceptions.remediation: Always add an explicit 'midpoint' column, computed as $\tfrac12$(lower boundary $+$ upper boundary), as a separate step BEFORE multiplying by frequency — never skip straight from boundaries to the $f\times x$ row.

common_mistakes.mistake: Finding the median before ordering the data.
common_mistakes.why: The data often looks already 'listed', so the ordering step feels optional or obvious rather than essential.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Make 'write the ordered list' the very first line of working on every median or quartile question, with no exceptions.

common_mistakes.mistake: Averaging the distinct x-values of a frequency table directly, ignoring the frequencies.
common_mistakes.why: The x-values are often listed in a single neat row, which looks exactly like an ordinary list to average.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always add and total the $f\times x$ row before attempting a frequency-table mean — never average the x-row alone.

common_mistakes.mistake: Calling a bare mean value 'the average' without checking whether an outlier makes it misleading.
common_mistakes.why: The mean is the most familiar average, so it is often reached for automatically without considering whether the question actually needs it.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Before reporting 'the average', scan the data for an obvious outlier; if one exists, check the median too before deciding which to report.

exam_notes: For a frequency-table mean, always show the $f\times x$ row and both totals ($\sum fx$ and $\sum f$) explicitly — the method marks sit in showing this working, even if the final division then goes wrong.
'Which average is most suitable?' questions need the NAME of the average AND a reason tied to the specific data in the question — a generic reason with no connection to the context loses marks.

For quartiles from a raw list, always show the ordered list and clearly mark where the median splits it into a lower and upper half — a bare final answer with no visible splitting can lose method marks.
'Estimate the mean' (grouped data) must use the word 'estimate' in your final answer statement — omitting it can lose a mark even when the calculation itself is entirely correct.

summary.big_idea: Every data set needs ONE average (mean, median or mode, chosen to suit the data and the question) paired with ONE measure of spread (range, or for Extended work the interquartile range), and both must be found from an ORDERED list or a properly weighted frequency table — never from raw, unsorted or unweighted data.
key_points: Mean $=$ total $\div$ count (so total $=$ mean $\times$ count for missing-value problems); median $=$ middle of ORDERED data; mode $=$ most frequent value; range $=$ largest $-$ smallest.
From a frequency table: mean $=\sum fx\div\sum f$; median located via running totals of frequency; mode has the highest frequency (never report the frequency itself as the mode).
Choose the average to suit the data and the question: mean when every value matters and there's no outlier; median when there is an outlier; mode for categorical data or 'most common' questions.
(Extended) $Q_1$ and $Q_3$ are the medians of the lower and upper halves of ordered data; $\mathrm{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1$ describes the spread of the middle $50\%$, barely affected by outliers.
(Extended) For grouped data, estimate the mean using class MIDPOINTS weighted by frequency; the modal class has the highest frequency.
formulas: \text{mean} = \dfrac{\sum x}{n} \quad\text{or, from a frequency table,}\quad \dfrac{\sum fx}{\sum f}
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Order the data (or weight a frequency table by $f\times x$) before calculating anything; pick the average that actually suits the question and the data (watch for outliers); and always pair an average with a measure of spread — range for Core, IQR for Extended when outliers are present.

objectives.statement: Extract information and draw inferences from tables and statistical diagrams, supporting each statement with a number from the data.
Compare two data sets using the mean (or median) together with the range, giving numerical comparisons and a conclusion in context.
Compare two data sets using the median together with the interquartile range when outliers or skewed data make the mean and range unreliable.
Recognise reasons a conclusion may be unreliable: small or biased samples, misleading graphs (truncated or unequal axes), and correlation without causation.

prerequisites.statement: Calculate the mean, median and range of a data set (Lesson 9.3).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every comparison in this lesson is built from averages and spreads already calculated exactly as in the previous lesson; this lesson adds the skill of comparing and interpreting them, not of calculating them.

prerequisites.statement: Calculate the lower quartile, upper quartile and interquartile range of a data set (Lesson 9.3).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Comparing with the IQR (Extended) requires the IQR to already be calculated correctly; any error here carries straight into a wrong comparison.

prerequisites.statement: Read values and totals from a two-way table and a bar chart (Lessons 9.1-9.2).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Interpreting tables and diagrams in this lesson assumes fluent reading of the table and chart structures built in the first two lessons of this unit.

diagnostic_items.question: Two data sets have the same mean. What additional information is needed to compare them fairly?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: A measure of spread (the range, or the interquartile range) is needed, so that how CONSISTENT each set is can also be compared, not just the typical size of the values.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Nothing more is needed — if the means are equal, the two data sets are basically the same.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Assumes a single summary statistic (the average) fully describes a data set, missing that two sets with identical means can still be wildly different in how spread out their values are.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks whether the learner understands that a full comparison always needs BOTH an average and a measure of spread, never one alone.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Show two short lists with the same mean but very different ranges side by side, and ask what is different between them despite the equal mean.

diagnostic_items.question: Does a smaller range always mean that a data set is 'better'?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: No. A smaller range only means the values are more consistent (less spread out); whether that is 'better' depends entirely on the context — consistent race times are good, but a consistently low test score is not.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Yes — a smaller range is always the preferable, more reliable result.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Treats 'spread' as inherently good or bad in itself, rather than recognising that spread is a neutral fact about the data whose desirability depends on what the data represents.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Tests whether the learner separates the MATHEMATICAL fact (smaller spread) from the CONTEXTUAL judgement (whether that is desirable here).
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Contrast two contexts side by side — sprint times (small spread is good) versus charity donations (small spread could just mean everyone gave little) — to show the same statistic needs different interpretations.

diagnostic_items.question: Why is the median a better average than the mean for describing typical house prices in an area with one very expensive mansion?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: The mean is pulled strongly upward by the one very expensive house (an outlier), making it unrepresentative of what a typical house actually costs; the median, which only depends on the middle position of the ordered data, is unaffected by that single extreme value.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The median is always the more 'proper' or 'official' average to use for money.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Memorises a rule about which average to use in which context without understanding the underlying reason (resistance to outliers), so the learner cannot generalise the idea to a new context.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that the learner can explain WHY the median resists outliers (it depends only on position, not on magnitude), not just recall that it is 'the right one to use for prices'.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Walk through a small worked list of house prices with one outlier, computing both mean and median, to see concretely how much the mean shifts and the median does not.

diagnostic_items.question: Give two reasons why a survey of 15 pupils outside a sports shop may not represent the whole school.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: The sample is small (only 15 pupils out of the whole school), and it is biased (pupils outside a sports shop are more likely to be interested in sport than the average pupil), so the results cannot safely be generalised to everyone.

common_wrong_answers.answer: It's fine, since 15 people is still a reasonable number to ask.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Judges sample reliability purely by size, missing the separate and often more serious problem of WHO was asked (sampling location/context introducing bias), not just how many.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that the learner identifies BOTH independent problems — small size and biased selection — rather than only one.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Ask the learner to redesign the survey so it is no longer biased (e.g. randomly selecting pupils from the whole school register), making the fix for bias concrete and separate from the fix for size.

diagnostic_items.question: Why can a bar chart whose vertical axis does not start at zero be misleading?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: When the axis is truncated, the bar heights are no longer proportional to the values they represent, so small real differences can look dramatically large — exaggerating the true scale of change.

common_wrong_answers.answer: It isn't misleading, since the axis labels still show the correct numbers.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Assumes that correct numeric labels are enough to prevent a false impression, missing that a chart's visual impact (bar heights, areas) is what most readers actually absorb, even when the labels are technically accurate.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that the learner connects the VISUAL proportionality of bar heights (not just the printed numbers) to the risk of misleading an at-a-glance reader.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Show the same data plotted with a truncated axis and with a zero-based axis side by side, and ask the learner to describe the two very different first impressions each gives.

theory_blocks.title: Three ingredients of a full comparison
theory_blocks.body: A comparison is a sentence with three ingredients: **(1)** a comparison of an *average*, **(2)** a comparison of the *spread*, and **(3)** the *meaning in context* ('on average, team B scored higher, but team A was more consistent'). [[red:Numbers alone, without words, do not earn full marks.]]

theory_blocks.title: Reading tables and diagrams carefully
theory_blocks.body: Tables and diagrams hold more information than the headline numbers. Before answering any question about one, read the **title**, the **axis labels**, the **units** and the **scale**. A two-way table lets you find a sub-total, a row total, a column total and a fraction of any group; a dual bar chart lets you compare two groups side by side at each category.

theory_blocks.title: Method for reading a diagram
theory_blocks.body:
1. Read the title, labels, units and the **scale** on each axis (does it start at $0$?).
2. Take exact values from the graph, and say which values you used.
3. Look for patterns: highest, lowest, trend over time, differences between groups.
4. Support each statement with a number from the data, then state what it means in context.

theory_blocks.title: Comparing with mean and range
theory_blocks.body: To compare two data sets, compute **one average** (usually the mean, or the median if there are outliers) and **one measure of spread** (the range) for each. A **larger average** means the values are typically larger; a **smaller spread** means the values are more consistent (more reliable).

theory_blocks.title: Three errors that break a comparison
theory_blocks.body:
- Writing 'A has a mean of $15$ and B has a mean of $15$' and stopping — you must *compare* ('equal', 'higher', 'lower') and *interpret*.
- Saying a smaller (or bigger) range automatically means 'better'. A range only tells you how [[blue:*spread out*]] the values are; whether a small spread is good or bad depends on the context (for a runner, small spread is good; for charity donations, it may just mean everyone gave little).
- Comparing a TOTAL with a mean: if the two groups have different sizes, compare the means, not the totals.

theory_blocks.title: The command word 'Compare'
theory_blocks.body: A full-mark answer to a 'compare' question contains *two* numerical comparisons, one for the average and one for the spread, each followed by a statement in words that refers to the situation in the question ('on average the bus takes longer', 'the times are more consistent').

theory_blocks.title: Samples and bias
theory_blocks.body: A conclusion is only as good as the data behind it. A **small sample** may not represent the whole group. A **biased sample** (for instance, surveying only members of the football club about school sports) systematically favours one answer. Data collected a long time ago, or in a different place, may not apply now.

theory_blocks.title: Small AND biased: two separate problems
theory_blocks.body: Concluding that 'most students in the school like football' from a survey of $20$ members of the school football team is flawed for TWO separate reasons: the sample is small, and it is biased (those students were more likely to like football regardless). A better sample would be chosen at random from all the students.

theory_blocks.title: How a graph can mislead
theory_blocks.body: Besides a truncated vertical axis, a graph can mislead by using unequal scale steps on an axis, three-dimensional pictures where the area or volume (not the height) changes, or showing only a very short time period chosen to display only the good news. Also beware of **correlation without cause**: two quantities can rise together without one causing the other.

theory_blocks.title: Questions to ask before trusting a graph or claim
theory_blocks.body: Before you trust a graph or a claim, ask yourself: Does the axis start at zero? Are the steps equal? What is the sample size, and who was asked? Is the data recent? Can the claim be checked against actual numbers from a table?

theory_blocks.title: Exam guidance for this lesson
theory_blocks.body: Exam answers on this topic are marked on WORDS as much as numbers: a bare pair of averages, with no comparison stated and no context sentence, typically earns no marks at all even if both numbers are correct. Always finish a comparison or a limitation answer with a sentence connecting the mathematics back to the situation described in the question.

theory_blocks.title: Comparing with median and IQR
theory_blocks.body: The mean and range are both strongly affected by extreme values. When the data contain outliers, or the distribution is lopsided, a fairer comparison uses the **median** and the **interquartile range**, since both resist the influence of a single extreme value.

theory_blocks.title: Choosing which pair of measures to use
theory_blocks.body:
- Symmetrical data without outliers: mean and range are fine.
- Outliers or skewed data: use median and IQR instead.
- Always say which pair of measures you used, and give the numerical value for each set.

theory_blocks.title: Why the median and IQR resist outliers
theory_blocks.body: Both the median and the quartiles are defined purely by POSITION in an ordered list, not by the actual size of the extreme values. Moving the largest value in a data set much further away changes the mean and range a great deal, but barely changes the median and IQR at all — this is exactly why they are the safer choice whenever outliers are present.

keywords.definition: A bar chart that places two groups' bars side by side at each category, so each pair can be compared directly.
A table that cross-tabulates two categorical variables, showing row totals, column totals and a grand total.
Describes a data set with a small spread (range or IQR), meaning the values are close together rather than widely scattered.
A statistic (such as the median or IQR) that is only slightly affected by extreme outliers in the data.
A systematic tendency for a sample to favour a particular answer, usually because of how or from whom it was collected.
A graph axis that does not start at zero, which can make bar heights disproportionate to the real values and exaggerate differences.
A tendency for two quantities to change together; it does not by itself prove that one causes the other.
A relationship where a change in one quantity directly brings about a change in another; cannot be established from correlation alone.

worked_examples.statement:
A two-way table. Ninety students chose their favourite sport.

| | Football | Tennis | Swimming | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Boys | 24 | 9 | 12 | 45 |
| Girls | 11 | 15 | 19 | 45 |
| Total | 35 | 24 | 31 | 90 |

(a) What fraction of the boys chose tennis? (b) Which sport is the most popular overall? (c) Is it true that 'more than half of the girls prefer tennis or swimming'?
knowns: two-way table of 90 students by sport and gender
unknowns: fraction, most popular sport overall, truth of a stated claim
reasoning: (a) Find the boys-tennis cell ($9$) and the boys total ($45$), then write the fraction and simplify.
(b) Compare the three column totals (Football $35$, Tennis $24$, Swimming $31$) to find the largest.
(c) Add the girls' tennis and swimming cells, compare this to half of the girls' total ($45\div2=22.5$).
worked_examples.solution: (a) $\tfrac{9}{45}=\tfrac15$. (b) Football, with $35$ students, is the most popular overall. (c) $15+19=34$ girls out of $45$ chose tennis or swimming, and $34>22.5$, so the statement is true.
worked_examples.interpretation: Every answer here comes directly from reading the right cell or total in the table and comparing it to another number from the same table — no outside calculation is needed, only careful, exact reading.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Dividing by the sport's column total (24) instead of the boys' row total (45) in part (a), which answers a different question (what fraction of tennis-choosers are boys).

worked_examples.statement: A dual bar chart. The chart shows quarterly sales (thousands) for Shop A and Shop B over four quarters: Q1 $40/30$, Q2 $55/35$, Q3 $70/80$, Q4 $45/60$ (A/B). Use the chart to compare the two shops' sales pattern over the year.
knowns: quarterly sales for Shop A and Shop B, as a dual bar chart
unknowns: which shop sold more overall, and how the pattern changed across the year
reasoning: Read each pair of bars quarter by quarter: in Q1 and Q2, Shop A's bar is taller; in Q3 and Q4, Shop B's bar is taller.
Add each shop's four values to find the whole-year total: A $=40+55+70+45$; B $=30+35+80+60$.
Compare the two yearly totals, and connect the early-year/late-year pattern to the final totals.
worked_examples.solution: Shop A sold more in the first two quarters, Shop B in the last two. A's total $=210$ thousand, B's total $=205$ thousand: over the whole year the shops were almost level, although Shop B sold more in the second half of the year.
worked_examples.interpretation: A dual bar chart's real value is in the QUARTER-BY-QUARTER comparison, which a single whole-year total would hide completely — reading the pattern across categories is as important as reading any single bar's height.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Comparing only the final quarter's bars (Shop B ahead) and concluding Shop B 'did better overall', without adding up the full year's totals first.
