worked_examples.statement: Comparing two teams. The points scored by two teams in six matches are: Team A: $12,14,15,15,16,18$; Team B: $5,9,15,17,21,23$. Compare the performances of the teams.
knowns: 6 match scores for each of two teams
unknowns: mean and range for each team, and a worded comparison
reasoning: Add each team's six scores and divide by $6$ to find each mean.
Find each team's range (largest $-$ smallest).
Compare the two means (are they equal, or is one bigger?), then compare the two ranges, then write a sentence connecting both comparisons to what they mean for the teams.
worked_examples.solution: Team A: mean $=\dfrac{90}{6}=15$, range $=18-12=6$. Team B: mean $=\dfrac{90}{6}=15$, range $=23-5=18$. The two teams have the same mean, so on average they score equally well. Team A has a much smaller range ($6<18$), so Team A is more consistent, while Team B's scores are much more variable.
worked_examples.interpretation: Equal means can completely hide a big difference in consistency; only by also comparing the spread does the real difference between the two teams become visible.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Stopping after finding that both means equal $15$ and concluding the teams 'performed the same', without comparing the ranges at all.

assets.caption: Dot plots of the two teams' scores: both are centred on the same mean of 15, but Team B's dots are spread over three times as much of the axis as Team A's.
assets.purpose: Reuse the legacy dot-plot comparison to make the equal-mean/unequal-spread point visually, matching the worked solution.

worked_examples.statement: Comparing journey times. The journey times (minutes) of two bus routes over $11$ days are: Route A: $22,24,25,26,27,28,29,30,31,33,35$; Route B: $18,20,21,24,26,28,30,33,37,40,45$. Compare the two routes using medians and interquartile ranges.
knowns: 11 journey times for each of two bus routes
unknowns: median, Q1, Q3, IQR for each route, and a worded comparison
reasoning: Both lists already have $n=11$ (odd), so the median is the $6$th ordered value and each half (excluding the median) has five values.
Route A: median is the 6th value; $Q_1$ is the median of the first five values; $Q_3$ is the median of the last five values.
Route B: same method applied to its own ordered list.
Compare the two medians, then the two IQRs, then write a sentence connecting both to reliability of each route.
worked_examples.solution: Route A: median $=28$, $Q_1=25$, $Q_3=31$, $\mathrm{IQR}=6$. Route B: median $=28$, $Q_1=21$, $Q_3=37$, $\mathrm{IQR}=16$. The medians are equal, so the typical journey takes the same time on both routes ($28$ minutes). The IQR for route B ($16$) is much bigger than for route A ($6$), so route A's journey times are more consistent and route B is less predictable.
worked_examples.interpretation: Even with equal typical journey times, the IQR reveals that one route is far more PREDICTABLE than the other — exactly the kind of difference a mean-and-range comparison alone could also show, but here median and IQR are the safer choice if the data contain outliers.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Including the median value itself in one of the two halves before finding $Q_1$ or $Q_3$, which shifts both quartiles for an odd-sized list.

assets.caption: The thick bar in each row marks the interquartile range (the middle half of the data); the thin line continues to the smallest and largest value. Both rows are centred at the same median, but Route B's thick bar is far longer.
assets.purpose: Reuse the legacy simplified box-plot style diagram to show the IQR visually alongside the worked comparison.

worked_examples.statement: A misleading bar chart. A company's sales over three years were $52$, $55$ and $58$ thousand. One chart plots the vertical axis starting at $50$; another plots it starting at $0$. (a) In the truncated chart, roughly how many times taller does the third bar look compared with the first? (b) Calculate the real percentage increase from year 1 to year 3. (c) Explain why the truncated chart is misleading.
knowns: sales of 52, 55, 58 thousand over three years
one chart with axis from 50, one from 0
unknowns: apparent height ratio in the truncated chart, real percentage increase, explanation
reasoning: (a) In the truncated chart, the bars only show the part ABOVE $50$: $2$ units for year 1, $8$ units for year 3; compare these two heights directly.
(b) Use the real values ($52$ and $58$) with the percentage change formula: $\dfrac{58-52}{52}\times100$.
(c) Compare the dramatic-looking height ratio from (a) with the modest real percentage change from (b).
worked_examples.solution: (a) The third bar is $8$ units tall above the truncated base versus $2$ units for the first bar: it looks four times as tall. (b) Real increase $=\dfrac{58-52}{52}\times100\approx11.5\%$ (3 s.f.). (c) The chart is misleading because cutting off the bottom of the axis makes a modest $11.5\%$ real increase look like a fourfold jump, since the bar heights are no longer proportional to the actual sales values.
worked_examples.interpretation: The SAME three numbers produce two completely different visual impressions purely because of where the vertical axis starts — recomputing the real percentage change from the actual values is the only reliable way to see past a misleading chart.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Reading the apparent 'four times taller' impression from the truncated chart as if it were the real percentage increase in sales.

guided_exercises.statement: Two classes sat the same test. Class X: $58,62,65,68,72$; Class Y: $50,55,70,75,85$. Compare the two classes' results using the mean and the range.
hints: Find each class's mean and range separately before attempting any comparison sentence.
Your final answer needs a sentence for EACH of the average and the spread — a bare pair of numbers is not a complete comparison.
guided_exercises.answer: X: mean $=65$, range $=14$. Y: mean $=67$, range $=35$. Class Y scored slightly higher on average, but Class X's results were far more consistent.
guided_exercises.full_solution: Class X: mean $=\tfrac{58+62+65+68+72}{5}=\tfrac{325}{5}=65$; range $=72-58=14$. Class Y: mean $=\tfrac{50+55+70+75+85}{5}=\tfrac{335}{5}=67$; range $=85-50=35$. Comparing: Class Y's mean ($67$) is a little higher than Class X's ($65$), so Class Y did slightly better on average; however Class X's range ($14$) is much smaller than Class Y's ($35$), so Class X's marks were far more consistent.
common_errors: Giving only the two means and two ranges without a worded comparison sentence linking them to 'higher/lower' and 'more/less consistent'.

guided_exercises.statement: A student asks $25$ people leaving a cinema whether they enjoy going to the cinema, and finds that $23$ say yes. She concludes 'almost everyone enjoys going to the cinema'. Explain why this conclusion is unreliable, then suggest a better way to collect the data.
hints: Think about WHO was asked, not just how many people were asked.
A better method should remove the bias, not just increase the sample size.
guided_exercises.answer: The sample is biased: everyone asked had just chosen to go to the cinema, so they were already more likely to enjoy it. A better method would survey a random sample of the general population, not just cinema-goers.
guided_exercises.full_solution: Every person in this sample had just voluntarily attended the cinema, which makes them far more likely to enjoy it than a randomly chosen member of the public (someone who dislikes the cinema is unlikely to be standing outside one). The sample is therefore biased, regardless of its size. A better method would randomly sample people from the wider population — for example, a random selection of names from the local area — so that people who never go to the cinema have an equal chance of being asked.
common_errors: Suggesting only 'ask more people' as the fix, which increases the sample size but does nothing to remove the underlying bias in WHO is being asked.

guided_exercises.statement: Two sets of delivery times (minutes) are: Set M: $10,12,13,14,15,16,18,20,45$; Set N: $11,13,14,15,16,17,18,19,20$. Compare the two sets using the median and interquartile range, and explain why this is a fairer comparison here than mean and range.
hints: Both sets have $n=9$ (odd); find the median first, then split the remaining 8 values into two halves of 4 (excluding the median).
Look carefully at Set M's largest value before deciding which pair of measures is fairer.
guided_exercises.answer: M: median $=15$, $Q_1=12.5$, $Q_3=19$, IQR $=6.5$. N: median $=16$, $Q_1=13.5$, $Q_3=18.5$, IQR $=5$. The medians are close, and the IQRs show Set N is slightly more consistent; median/IQR are fairer here because Set M contains an outlier (45) that would distort its mean and range.
guided_exercises.full_solution: Set M ordered: $10,12,13,14,15,16,18,20,45$ ($n=9$). Median (5th value) $=15$. Lower half $10,12,13,14$: $Q_1=\tfrac{12+13}{2}=12.5$. Upper half $16,18,20,45$: $Q_3=\tfrac{18+20}{2}=19$. IQR $=19-12.5=6.5$. Set N ordered: $11,13,14,15,16,17,18,19,20$ ($n=9$). Median (5th value) $=16$. Lower half $11,13,14,15$: $Q_1=\tfrac{13+14}{2}=13.5$. Upper half $17,18,19,20$: $Q_3=\tfrac{18+19}{2}=18.5$. IQR $=18.5-13.5=5$. Set M contains an extreme outlier ($45$, a very delayed delivery) that would badly distort its mean and range; the median and IQR are far less affected by it, making them the fairer choice here.
common_errors: Using the mean and range despite the obvious outlier (45) in Set M, producing a distorted comparison.

exercises.statement: Rainfall (mm) in five months: Town P: $30,42,35,38,45$; Town Q: $20,60,10,55,45$. Calculate the mean and the range for each town and compare them.
exercises.answer: P: mean $38$, range $15$. Q: mean $38$, range $50$. Same average rainfall, but P is far more consistent while Q varies much more.
exercises.full_solution: P: mean $=\tfrac{30+42+35+38+45}{5}=\tfrac{190}{5}=38$; range $=45-30=15$. Q: mean $=\tfrac{20+60+10+55+45}{5}=\tfrac{190}{5}=38$; range $=60-10=50$. Both towns have the same mean rainfall ($38$\,mm), so on average they receive the same amount; but Town P's range ($15$) is far smaller than Town Q's ($50$), so Town P's rainfall is much more consistent month to month.
common_errors: Stopping after finding the equal means without comparing the ranges at all.

exercises.statement: Ana's test marks: $6,7,7,8,9$. Ben's test marks: $4,5,8,10,10$. Find the mean and range for each and say who is more consistent.
exercises.answer: Ana: mean $7.4$, range $3$. Ben: mean $7.4$, range $6$. Same average mark; Ana is more consistent.
exercises.full_solution: Ana: mean $=\tfrac{6+7+7+8+9}{5}=\tfrac{37}{5}=7.4$; range $=9-6=3$. Ben: mean $=\tfrac{4+5+8+10+10}{5}=\tfrac{37}{5}=7.4$; range $=10-4=6$. Both have the same mean mark, but Ana's range ($3$) is half of Ben's ($6$), so Ana's marks are more consistent.
common_errors: Treating the equal means as proof the two students performed 'identically', ignoring the different ranges.

exercises.statement: Two sprinters' times (s) over five races: Ravi: $12.1,12.3,12.2,12.4,12.5$; Sam: $11.8,12.9,12.0,13.1,11.7$. Find the mean and range for each. Which runner is more reliable? Explain.
exercises.answer: Ravi: mean $12.3$, range $0.4$. Sam: mean $12.3$, range $1.4$. Same average time; Ravi is more reliable (much smaller range).
exercises.full_solution: Ravi: mean $=\tfrac{12.1+12.3+12.2+12.4+12.5}{5}=\tfrac{61.5}{5}=12.3$; range $=12.5-12.1=0.4$. Sam: mean $=\tfrac{11.8+12.9+12.0+13.1+11.7}{5}=\tfrac{61.5}{5}=12.3$; range $=13.1-11.7=1.4$. Both runners have the same average time, but Ravi's range ($0.4$\,s) is far smaller than Sam's ($1.4$\,s), so Ravi's times are much more consistent and therefore more reliable.
common_errors: Concluding 'Sam is faster' from the equal means, which is not what the question asks (it asks about reliability/consistency, answered by the range).

exercises.statement:
The table shows a class's preferred pet.

| | Dog | Cat | Other | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Boys | 8 | 5 | 3 | 16 |
| Girls | 6 | 10 | 3 | 19 |
| Total | 14 | 15 | 6 | 35 |

(a) What fraction of the girls chose cat? (b) Which pet is preferred by more students overall? (c) Do more boys than girls prefer dogs?
exercises.answer: (a) $\tfrac{10}{19}$. (b) Cat ($15>14$). (c) Yes: $8$ boys vs $6$ girls prefer dogs.
exercises.full_solution: (a) $\tfrac{10}{19}$ (girls who chose cat, over the girls' total). (b) Column totals: Dog $14$, Cat $15$, Other $6$; Cat is preferred by more students overall. (c) Boys who chose dog $=8$; girls who chose dog $=6$; so MORE boys than girls prefer dogs ($8>6$).
common_errors: In (c), comparing the counts against the wrong row totals (16 vs 19) instead of comparing the two raw dog counts directly, as the question asks.

exercises.statement: A student surveys $20$ members of the school chess club and finds that $18$ enjoy chess. She concludes that 'most students in the school enjoy chess'. Give two reasons why this conclusion is not reliable.
exercises.answer: The sample is small (only 20 out of the whole school) and biased (chess club members are far more likely to enjoy chess than a random student).
exercises.full_solution: Reason 1 (size): only $20$ people were surveyed out of the whole school population, which is too small to safely represent everyone. Reason 2 (bias): every person surveyed was already a member of the chess CLUB, so they are far more likely to enjoy chess than a randomly chosen student elsewhere in the school — the sample was not random across the whole school.
common_errors: Giving only one reason (usually size) and missing the separate, equally important issue of bias in who was selected.

exercises.statement: A bar chart shows the profit of a company for two years. The vertical axis starts at $95$ instead of $0$, and the bars are $96$ and $99$ (thousands). Explain why the chart is misleading, and calculate the real percentage increase (1 d.p.).
exercises.answer: The chart is misleading because the truncated axis makes the second bar look four times as tall as the first; real increase $=3.1\%$.
exercises.full_solution: Above the truncated base of $95$, the bars measure $1$ unit ($96-95$) and $4$ units ($99-95$): the second bar looks four times as tall as the first, even though the real values are close together. Real percentage increase $=\dfrac{99-96}{96}\times100=3.125\%\approx3.1\%$ (1 d.p.).
common_errors: Computing the percentage increase using the truncated values (e.g. $4\div1$) instead of the real profit figures (96 and 99).

exercises.statement: Sales of ice cream and cases of sunburn both increase in July. Does eating ice cream cause sunburn? Explain.
exercises.answer: No. Both increase because of hot sunny weather (a third factor); correlation does not imply cause.
exercises.full_solution: Ice-cream sales and sunburn cases both rise in July, but neither causes the other directly — hot, sunny weather is the common underlying factor that increases both: people buy more ice cream to cool down, and they also spend more time in the sun and get burnt more often. This is a classic example of correlation without causation.
common_errors: Accepting the apparent link at face value and concluding one quantity directly causes the other, without considering a shared underlying cause.

exercises.statement: The mean height of $10$ girls is $162$\,cm and the mean height of $15$ boys is $170$\,cm. Find the mean height of all $25$ students.
exercises.full_solution: Total height $=10\times162+15\times170=1620+2550=4170$\,cm. Combined mean $=4170\div25=166.8$\,cm.
common_errors: Averaging the two given means directly ($\tfrac{162+170}{2}=166$), ignoring that the two groups have different sizes.

exercises.statement: Class 1 has mean mark $64$ and range $30$. Class 2 has mean mark $64$ and range $12$. Write two comparisons in context.
exercises.answer: The average marks of the two classes are equal. Class 2's marks are more consistent (range $12<30$), while Class 1's marks are more varied.
exercises.full_solution: Comparison 1 (average): both classes have the same mean mark ($64$), so on average the two classes performed equally well. Comparison 2 (spread): Class 2's range ($12$) is much smaller than Class 1's ($30$), so Class 2's marks were far more consistent, while Class 1 had a much wider variation in performance between its highest and lowest scorers.
common_errors: Giving only a numerical statement of the ranges without a worded 'more/less consistent' comparison in context.

exercises.statement: Set P: $5,8,9,11,12,13,15,16,20$. Set Q: $9,10,11,11,12,12,13,14,15$. Find the median, IQR and range of each and compare the sets.
exercises.answer: P: median $12$, IQR $7$, range $15$. Q: median $12$, IQR $3$, range $6$. Equal medians; Q is more consistent.
exercises.full_solution: Set P ($n=9$): median (5th value) $=12$. Lower half $5,8,9,11$: $Q_1=8.5$. Upper half $13,15,16,20$: $Q_3=15.5$. IQR $=15.5-8.5=7$. Range $=20-5=15$. Set Q ($n=9$): median (5th value) $=12$. Lower half $9,10,11,11$: $Q_1=10.5$. Upper half $12,13,14,15$: $Q_3=13.5$. IQR $=13.5-10.5=3$. Range $=15-9=6$. Both sets have the same median ($12$), so a typical value is the same in each; Set Q has a much smaller IQR and range, so it is far more consistent.
common_errors: Including the median (12) in the lower or upper half before computing the quartiles for either set.

exercises.statement: Mass (g) of eight apples: $150,152,155,156,158,160,162,220$. Find the range and IQR. Which describes the spread of typical apples better? Explain.
exercises.answer: Range $=70$, IQR $=7.5$. The IQR describes typical apples better; the range is distorted by the outlier $220$.
exercises.full_solution: Range $=220-150=70$. $n=8$ (even): lower half $150,152,155,156$, $Q_1=\tfrac{152+155}{2}=153.5$; upper half $158,160,162,220$, $Q_3=\tfrac{160+162}{2}=161$. IQR $=161-153.5=7.5$. The range ($70$) is almost entirely caused by the single unusually heavy apple ($220$\,g); the IQR ($7.5$) reflects the much smaller spread of the other seven, more typical apples.
common_errors: Leaving the outlier (220) out of the ordered list when finding the quartiles: it must stay in, and the point is that it dominates the range but barely affects the IQR.

exercises.statement: Two schools' exam marks: School A has median $62$, IQR $14$; school B has median $58$, IQR $8$. Compare the schools' performance.
exercises.answer: School A's typical mark is higher (62 vs 58), but School B's marks are more consistent (IQR 8 vs 14).
exercises.full_solution: School A's median ($62$) is higher than School B's ($58$), so a typical student at School A scored higher in this exam. However, School B's IQR ($8$) is smaller than School A's ($14$), so School B's marks were more tightly clustered together — School B's results were more consistent, even though its typical mark was lower.
common_errors: Concluding School A is simply 'better' overall, without separately acknowledging School B's advantage in consistency.

exercises.statement: The data $12,14,15,16,17,18,20$ are altered by adding an extra value of $60$. Find the median and IQR before and after, and comment.
exercises.answer: Before: median $16$, IQR $4$. After: median $16.5$, IQR $4.5$. Both measures barely change despite the huge new value.
exercises.full_solution: Before ($n=7$): ordered $12,14,15,16,17,18,20$; median (4th value) $=16$. Lower half $12,14,15$: $Q_1=14$. Upper half $17,18,20$: $Q_3=18$. IQR $=18-14=4$. After ($n=8$, adding $60$): ordered $12,14,15,16,17,18,20,60$; median $=\tfrac{16+17}{2}=16.5$. Lower half $12,14,15,16$: $Q_1=\tfrac{14+15}{2}=14.5$. Upper half $17,18,20,60$: $Q_3=\tfrac{18+20}{2}=19$. IQR $=19-14.5=4.5$. Even though $60$ is far larger than every other value, the median only rises by $0.5$ and the IQR only by $0.5$ — both measures are highly resistant to this extreme outlier.
common_errors: Expecting the median and IQR to shift dramatically just because an extreme value was added, rather than recognising their resistance to outliers.

exercises.statement: A newspaper says 'The mean time to run $100$\,m is $14.2$\,s, so almost everybody in the club can run under $15$\,s'. Write down one piece of information you would want to check the claim.
exercises.answer: e.g. the range or IQR (spread) of the times, or the median: a low mean can hide a few very slow runners.
exercises.full_solution: A mean alone tells you nothing about how SPREAD OUT the individual times are. Knowing the range (or IQR) of the runners' times — or checking the median instead — would reveal whether the times really do cluster below $15$\,s, or whether a few very fast runners are pulling a mean down while several much slower members take well over $15$\,s.
common_errors: Accepting the mean-based claim at face value without questioning whether a single average can really describe 'almost everybody'.

exercises.statement:
The dual bar chart shows the after-school club chosen by the $40$ students in Year 10 and by the $40$ students in Year 11.
(a) How many Year 11 students chose Chess?
(b) Which club shows the biggest difference between the two year groups, and how big is that difference?
(c) A student says 'Football is the most popular club in both year groups.' Use the chart to decide whether this is correct, quoting numbers from the chart.
exercises.answer: (a) $13$. (b) Art, a difference of $6$ students. (c) Not correct: Football is the most popular club in Year 10 ($14$ students), but in Year 11 the most popular club is Chess ($13$ students) against Football's $10$.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) Read the height of the Year 11 bar above Chess: $13$ students.
(b) The differences are Art $12-6=6$, Chess $13-8=5$, Drama $11-6=5$, Football $14-10=4$. The biggest difference is at Art, where $6$ more Year 10 students than Year 11 students chose the club.
(c) The claim is not correct. In Year 10 Football is indeed the tallest bar ($14$ students, more than Art $12$, Chess $8$, Drama $6$). In Year 11, however, Chess is the tallest bar ($13$ students) and Football has only $10$, so Football is not the most popular club in both year groups. Both year groups have $40$ students, so the bar heights may be compared directly.
common_errors: Comparing the Year 10 bars only and assuming the Year 11 pattern must be the same.
Giving the taller bar's height as the 'difference' instead of subtracting the two heights.

exam_questions.statement:
The number of customers served per hour at two cafes over six hours was: Cafe North: $18,22,20,25,19,24$; Cafe South: $10,30,15,35,12,26$.
(a) Calculate the mean and range for each cafe. [3]
(b) Compare the two cafes' customer numbers, writing two full comparisons in context. [2]
exam_questions.answer: (a) North: mean $=21.3$, range $=7$. South: mean $=21.3$, range $=25$. (b) Equal average customers per hour; North is far more consistent, South's numbers vary a lot hour to hour.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) North: sum $=18+22+20+25+19+24=128$, mean $=128\div6=21.33\ldots\approx21.3$ (3 s.f.); range $=25-18=7$. South: sum $=10+30+15+35+12+26=128$, mean $=128\div6=21.33\ldots\approx21.3$ (3 s.f.); range $=35-10=25$. (b) The two cafes serve the same average number of customers per hour ($21.3$), so on average their busyness is the same; however North's range ($7$) is far smaller than South's ($25$), so North's customer numbers are much more consistent hour to hour, while South experiences far bigger swings between quiet and busy hours.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for correct sum(s); A1 for both means $=21.3$ (accept $21.33\ldots$ or $\tfrac{64}{3}$); A1 for both ranges correct (North 7, South 25)
(b) B1 for a correct comparison of the means stated in words (not just numbers); B1 for a correct comparison of the ranges stated in words, connected to consistency/variability in context.
common_errors: In (a), rounding the mean too early and carrying the rounded value into further working, rather than keeping sufficient precision until the final answer.

exam_questions.statement:
The weekly earnings (\$) of nine employees at two small shops are: Shop East: $280,310,320,330,340,350,360,370,520$; Shop West: $300,315,325,335,345,355,365,375,385$.
(a) Find the median and interquartile range for each shop. [4]
(b) Explain, with a reason, which shop's earnings data is better compared using the median and IQR rather than the mean and range. [2]
(c) State what the two medians tell you about typical pay at the two shops. [1]
exam_questions.answer: (a) East: median $340$, IQR $50$. West: median $345$, IQR $50$. (b) Shop East, because of the outlier $520$. (c) Typical pay is very similar at both shops.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Shop East ($n=9$): ordered as given; median (5th value) $=340$. Lower half $280,310,320,330$: $Q_1=315$. Upper half $350,360,370,520$: $Q_3=365$. IQR $=365-315=50$. Shop West ($n=9$): median (5th value) $=345$. Lower half $300,315,325,335$: $Q_1=320$. Upper half $355,365,375,385$: $Q_3=370$. IQR $=370-320=50$. (b) Shop East's data contains an outlier ($520$), which would badly distort its mean and range; the median and IQR are much less affected by this single very high earner, making them the fairer choice for Shop East specifically (and a consistent choice to use for both, for a fair comparison). (c) The two medians ($340$ and $345$) are very close, so a typical employee earns almost the same amount at either shop.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for correctly ordering and splitting each shop's data into lower and upper halves (excluding the median); A1 for both medians correct ($340$ and $345$); A1 for East's $Q_1=315$, $Q_3=365$ and IQR $=50$; A1 for West's $Q_1=320$, $Q_3=370$ and IQR $=50$
(b) B1 for identifying the outlier (520) in Shop East's data; B1 for a correct reason linking the outlier to why mean/range would be distorted but median/IQR would not
(c) B1 for a correct contextual statement that the medians (and hence typical pay) are close/similar.
common_errors: In (a), computing a mean-based comparison instead of a median/IQR-based one, missing what the question specifically asks for.

exam_questions.statement:
A company's advert states: 'Sales have grown massively!' and shows a bar chart with a vertical axis starting at \$180,000, with bars at \$182,000 and \$188,000 for two consecutive years.
(a) Calculate the real percentage increase in sales, to 1 decimal place. [2]
(b) Explain why the bar chart gives a misleading impression of this growth. [2]
exam_questions.answer: (a) $3.3\%$. (b) The truncated axis makes the second bar look many times taller than the first, even though the real increase is modest.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Real percentage increase $=\dfrac{188000-182000}{182000}\times100=\dfrac{6000}{182000}\times100\approx3.3\%$ (1 d.p.). (b) Above the truncated base of $\$180{,}000$, the bars measure $\$2{,}000$ and $\$8{,}000$ respectively — making the second bar look four times as tall as the first — even though the real sales increase is only about $3.3\%$. The bar heights are no longer proportional to the true values, exaggerating the apparent growth far beyond what actually happened.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for a correct percentage-change calculation using the real values (182000, 188000); A1 for $3.3\%$
(b) B1 for identifying that the axis does not start at zero/is truncated; B1 for connecting this to bar heights no longer being proportional to the real values, exaggerating the apparent change.
common_errors: In (a), using the truncated-axis heights (2000 and 8000) directly in a percentage-change calculation relative to each other, rather than computing the real percentage change from the original sales figures.

exam_questions.statement:
The back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram shows the times, in seconds, taken by the $15$ students in Class A and the $15$ students in Class B to solve a puzzle.
(a) Find the median and the range of the Class A times. [2]
(b) Find the median and the range of the Class B times. [2]
(c) Make two comparisons between the times of the two classes. [2]
exam_questions.answer: (a) Median $38$ seconds, range $40$ seconds. (b) Median $47$ seconds, range $24$ seconds. (c) Class A was quicker on average (median $38$ s against $47$ s), but Class B was more consistent (range $24$ s against $40$ s).
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a) Reading the Class A leaves outwards from the stem gives $24,27,28,31,33,35,36,38,42,44,45,47,51,53,64$. With $15$ values the median is the $\tfrac{15+1}{2}=8$th value, which is $38$ seconds. The range is $64-24=40$ seconds.
(b) The Class B times are $34,36,38,41,43,45,46,47,48,49,50,52,55,57,58$. The median is again the $8$th value, $47$ seconds, and the range is $58-34=24$ seconds.
(c) Class A was quicker on average: its median time of $38$ seconds is $9$ seconds less than Class B's median of $47$ seconds. Class B's times were more consistent: its range of $24$ seconds is smaller than Class A's range of $40$ seconds.
mark_scheme: (a) B1 for median $=38$; B1 for range $=64-24=40$
(b) B1 for median $=47$; B1 for range $=58-34=24$

(c) B1 for a comparison of the medians in context (Class A quicker on average, with both values quoted); B1 for a comparison of the ranges in context (Class B more consistent, with both values quoted)
common_errors: Reading the Class A leaves left to right, so the smallest Class A time is given as $48$ instead of $24$.
Giving the median as the $7.5$th or $8.5$th value, or quoting the middle stem instead of a data value.
Writing only the four numbers in part (c) without saying what they mean about the two classes.

assets.caption: Back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram of the puzzle times (seconds) for Class A and Class B: the stems are the tens digit, and the Class A leaves are read outwards from the stem, so they increase from right to left.
assets.purpose: An exam-style item on LO-STA-04-1 and LO-STA-04-2 that requires reading an actual diagram before the median and range comparison.

challenge_questions.statement: Team X has mean score $14$ and range $10$; team Y has mean score $14$ and range $4$. Priya says 'Team Y is better'. Explain whether she is right.
challenge_questions.answer: Not necessarily. The means are equal (same average scoring); Y is more consistent, but that does not automatically make it 'better' overall.
challenge_questions.full_solution: The two teams score equally well on average, since their means are both $14$; Priya is right that Team Y is more CONSISTENT, since its range ($4$) is much smaller than Team X's ($10$). But 'more consistent' is not automatically the same as 'better' — whether consistency is an advantage depends on the context (e.g. if occasional very high scores from Team X are valuable, its larger range could even be an advantage). Priya's claim is only partly justified: Y is more consistent, not simply 'better'.

challenge_questions.statement: A headmaster says 'The mean mark rose from $60$ to $65$, so every student improved.' Give an example with $4$ students showing that the statement can be false.
challenge_questions.answer: e.g. marks $50,60,70,60\to80,80,80,20$: the mean rises from $60$ to $65$, but one student's mark falls from $60$ to $20$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Before: $50,60,70,60$, total $=240$, mean $=60$. After: $80,80,80,20$, total $=260$, mean $=65$. The overall mean did rise from $60$ to $65$, exactly as claimed, yet the student who scored $60$ before now scores only $20$ — a large FALL, not an improvement. A rising mean describes the group as a whole; it says nothing about every individual student.

challenge_questions.statement: Group 1 has $4$ values with mean $10$; group 2 has $6$ values with mean $20$. Ali says that the overall mean is $\frac{10+20}{2}=15$. Show that he is wrong and find the correct value.
challenge_questions.answer: Ali is wrong (he ignores the different group sizes); the correct overall mean is $16$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Group 1's total $=4\times10=40$. Group 2's total $=6\times20=120$. Combined total $=40+120=160$, over $4+6=10$ values. Correct overall mean $=160\div10=16$. Ali's method (averaging the two means directly) only works when the two groups are the SAME size; here group 2 is larger, so it should pull the overall mean closer to $20$ than to $10$, which is exactly what $16$ (rather than $15$) reflects.

challenge_questions.statement: A newspaper bar chart draws profits of \$2.00m and \$2.10m with the vertical axis starting at \$1.98m. How many times taller does the second bar look than the first? What is the real percentage increase?
challenge_questions.answer: The second bar looks $6$ times taller; the real increase is $5\%$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Above the truncated base of $\$1.98$m, the bars measure $2.00-1.98=0.02$ and $2.10-1.98=0.12$. Apparent height ratio $=0.12\div0.02=6$: the second bar looks six times as tall as the first. Real percentage increase $=\dfrac{2.10-2.00}{2.00}\times100=5\%$ — a far more modest change than the chart visually suggests.

challenge_questions.statement: The data $12,14,15,16,17,18,20$ ($n=7$) have an extra value $60$ added. Show that the mean changes by $5.5$ while the median changes by $0.5$ and the IQR by $0.5$. What does this tell you about which measures are robust?
challenge_questions.answer: Mean changes by $5.5$; median changes by $0.5$; IQR changes by $0.5$. The median and IQR are robust to outliers; the mean and range are not.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Before ($n=7$): mean $=\tfrac{12+14+15+16+17+18+20}{7}=\tfrac{112}{7}=16$; median $=16$; $Q_1=14$, $Q_3=18$, IQR $=4$; range $=20-12=8$. After adding $60$ ($n=8$): mean $=\tfrac{172}{8}=21.5$ (change $=21.5-16=5.5$); median $=\tfrac{16+17}{2}=16.5$ (change $=0.5$); $Q_1=14.5$, $Q_3=19$, IQR $=4.5$ (change $=0.5$); range $=60-12=48$ (change $=40$). The single new value of $60$ changes the mean by $5.5$ and the range by a huge $40$, but it only nudges the median and IQR by $0.5$ each: this confirms that the median and IQR are ROBUST (resistant) to outliers, while the mean and especially the range are heavily distorted by them.

mcq.stem: Team P and Team Q both have a mean score of $20$. A student writes 'the mean of P is 20 and the mean of Q is 20' and stops. What is missing from this as a full comparison?

options.text: Nothing — since the means are equal, the comparison is already complete
options.why_wrong: Stating that the averages are equal is only ONE of the three required ingredients of a comparison; the spread and a contextual sentence are both still missing.

options.text: The median of each team, which must always be given alongside the mean
options.why_wrong: A median is not automatically required alongside a mean; what's missing here is a measure of SPREAD (such as the range), not a second measure of average.

options.text: A comparison of the spread (e.g. the range), plus a sentence stating what the equal means and the spread comparison mean in context
The total score of each team, to check the means were calculated correctly
options.why_wrong: Showing a total might support the mean calculation but it does not provide the comparison of CONSISTENCY that a full answer needs.

mcq.explanation: A full comparison needs three ingredients: a comparison of the average (already given here, and equal), a comparison of the spread (missing), and a sentence connecting both back to the context (also missing).

mcq.stem: Data set X has a smaller range than data set Y. Which statement is correct?

options.text: X is automatically the 'better' data set, since a smaller range is always preferable
options.why_wrong: A smaller range is a neutral fact about consistency, not an automatic judgement of quality; whether it is desirable depends entirely on what the data actually measures.

options.text: X must also have a smaller mean than Y
options.why_wrong: The range (spread) and the mean (average) are independent measures; knowing one tells you nothing about the other.

options.text: X and Y cannot be meaningfully compared unless their ranges are equal
options.why_wrong: Different ranges can absolutely still be compared — that comparison itself (which is bigger, and what it means) is exactly the point of this kind of question.

options.text: X's values are more consistent than Y's; whether that is a good thing depends on what the data represents

mcq.explanation: A smaller range means more consistent values; it does not by itself make a data set 'better', since whether consistency is desirable depends on the context.

mcq.stem: Group A has $5$ values with a total of $100$. Group B has $8$ values with a total of $144$. Which group has the higher average?

options.text: Group A, since its mean ($100\div5=20$) is higher than Group B's mean ($144\div8=18$)
Group B, because its total ($144$) is bigger than Group A's ($100$)
options.why_wrong: Comparing raw totals ignores that the two groups have different sizes (5 vs 8 values); a bigger total can simply mean a bigger group, not a higher average.

options.text: They must be equal, since no further information is given
options.why_wrong: The means can be calculated directly from the totals and sizes given, so there's no need to assume equality without checking.

options.text: It cannot be determined from the information given
options.why_wrong: The means ARE fully determined here: mean $=$ total $\div$ count for each group, using the numbers already provided.

mcq.explanation: Group A's mean $=100\div5=20$; Group B's mean $=144\div8=18$. Even though Group B has the bigger raw TOTAL, Group A has the higher AVERAGE, because its total is spread over fewer values.

mcq.stem: A study finds that towns with more cafes also have more bookshops. Which conclusion is correctly justified by this finding alone?

options.text: Opening more cafes directly causes more bookshops to open
options.why_wrong: A correlation between two quantities does not by itself prove that one causes the other; a third factor (such as a generally busier, wealthier town centre) could explain both.

options.text: The two quantities are correlated, but this alone does not show that one causes the other
Opening more bookshops directly causes more cafes to open
options.why_wrong: This reverses the same unjustified causal claim; correlation alone cannot establish the direction of causation, or that causation exists at all.

options.text: The finding must be a coincidence with no explanation at all
options.why_wrong: Dismissing the pattern as pure coincidence goes too far in the other direction; a genuine common cause (e.g. a busy town centre) is a perfectly reasonable explanation that a correlation alone cannot rule in or out.

mcq.explanation: The finding shows a correlation between cafes and bookshops, but correlation alone never establishes causation in either direction — a third factor (such as overall town centre activity) could easily explain both trends.

mcq.stem: Data set M contains a single extreme outlier; data set N has no outliers. Which pair of measures gives the FAIREST comparison between M and N?

options.text: Mean and range, since they use every data value
options.why_wrong: Using every value is normally a strength of the mean and range, but here it is exactly the weakness: both are heavily distorted by the single outlier in set M.

options.text: Mode and range
options.why_wrong: The mode often does not exist for this kind of numerical data, and even when it does, it ignores almost all of the data — it is not a useful average for this comparison.

options.text: Median and interquartile range
Total and mean, since they allow checking each other
options.why_wrong: A total does not help here at all; it is not a measure of spread, and does nothing to address the outlier problem the mean already has.

mcq.explanation: Since Set M has an outlier, the mean and range would both be distorted by it; the median and IQR are far more resistant to extreme values, making them the fairest choice for comparing the two sets here.

mcq.stem: A bar chart's vertical axis runs from $40$ to $50$ instead of from $0$ to $50$. What effect does this have?

options.text: It has no effect, as long as the axis numbers printed on the chart are accurate
options.why_wrong: Accurate printed numbers do not prevent a visual distortion; the bar HEIGHTS, which is what a reader notices at a glance, are no longer proportional to the real values once the axis is truncated.

options.text: It makes the chart more accurate, since it zooms in on the relevant range of values
options.why_wrong: Zooming in does not add accuracy to the underlying numbers; it specifically breaks the proportionality between bar height and value, which is what causes the misleading impression.

options.text: It only affects charts with negative values, not charts like this one
options.why_wrong: Truncating the axis distorts proportionality regardless of whether any values are negative; this effect applies here even though all the chart's values are positive.

options.text: It exaggerates the apparent differences between the bars, since the bar heights are no longer proportional to the real values

mcq.explanation: Starting the vertical axis above zero breaks the proportionality between bar height and actual value, so small real differences can look dramatically larger than they really are.

flashcards.front: What three ingredients does a full 'compare' answer need?
flashcards.back: (1) A comparison of the average; (2) a comparison of the spread; (3) a sentence stating what this means in the context of the question.

flashcards.front: Two data sets have equal means. Does that mean they are 'the same'?
flashcards.back: No. They could have very different spreads; the mean alone never fully describes a data set — always check the spread too.

flashcards.front: Is a smaller range always 'better'?
flashcards.back: No — a smaller range just means more consistent values; whether that's desirable depends entirely on the context (consistent race times: good; consistently low scores: bad).

flashcards.front: Two groups have different sizes. Can you compare their totals to decide which did better?
flashcards.back: If two groups have DIFFERENT sizes, only the means (or medians) can be fairly compared — never compare raw totals.

flashcards.front: When should you use median/IQR instead of mean/range to compare two data sets?
flashcards.back: When the data contains outliers, or is skewed/lopsided — the median and IQR resist the influence of extreme values far better than the mean and range.

flashcards.front: Why are the median and IQR 'robust' to outliers?
flashcards.back: They are defined by POSITION in an ordered list, not by the actual size of the extreme values, so moving an outlier further away barely changes them.

flashcards.front: Mean+range vs median+IQR: which pair is more resistant to a single very extreme value?
flashcards.back: Median and IQR are far more resistant; the mean and range (especially the range) can be dramatically distorted by just one outlier.

flashcards.front: Give two reasons a sample might not represent a whole population.
flashcards.back: It may be too SMALL, and/or it may be BIASED (chosen in a way that favours a particular answer, e.g. only asking members of a relevant club).

flashcards.front: If a bar chart's axis numbers are all correct, can the chart still mislead?
flashcards.back: Yes — if the axis doesn't start at zero, the bar HEIGHTS are no longer proportional to the values, exaggerating differences even though every printed number is accurate.

flashcards.front: List three ways (besides a truncated axis) a graph can be misleading.
flashcards.back: Unequal scale steps on an axis; 3D pictures where area/volume (not height) changes; showing only a short time period chosen to show only good news.

flashcards.front: Two quantities rise together over time. Does one necessarily cause the other?
flashcards.back: No — this is correlation, not proof of causation; a third factor could explain both, or the link could be coincidence.

flashcards.front: Before trusting a graph, what five questions should you ask?
flashcards.back: Does the axis start at zero? Are the steps equal? What is the sample size, and who was asked? Is the data recent? Can the claim be checked against actual numbers?

flashcards.front: A school's mean mark rises from 60 to 65. Does this prove every student improved?
flashcards.back: No — a rising mean describes the group as a whole; individual students can still have gone down even while the overall mean rises.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Stating that two averages are equal (or that one is bigger) is, by itself, a complete comparison of two data sets.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Finding and stating the averages feels like the main calculation, so once that number is produced it can feel like the task is finished, especially under time pressure in an exam.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner writes 'A has a mean of 15 and B has a mean of 15' and stops, without comparing the spread or giving any contextual sentence.
misconceptions.correct_model: A full comparison always needs THREE ingredients: (1) a comparison of the average, (2) a comparison of the spread, and (3) a sentence that states what this means in the context of the question.
misconceptions.remediation: Before submitting any 'compare' answer, check it against the three-ingredient checklist: average compared? spread compared? context sentence included?

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A smaller range (or IQR) is always the 'better' or more desirable result, regardless of what the data represents.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: In many familiar exam contexts (race times, test consistency) a smaller spread genuinely is the better outcome, so the pattern gets over-generalised to every context without checking what the data actually measures.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner automatically writes 'so data set X is better' whenever its range or IQR is smaller, without considering whether small spread is actually desirable here.
misconceptions.correct_model: A smaller spread only means the values are more CONSISTENT; whether consistency is a good thing depends entirely on the context of the question — it is a neutral mathematical fact, not an automatic verdict of 'better'.
misconceptions.remediation: Before calling a smaller spread 'better', ask explicitly: 'in this situation, is being consistent actually a good thing?'

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Two groups of different sizes can be compared directly using their TOTALS rather than their means.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A total is often the first number computed (e.g. when finding a mean), and if the two group sizes are close or forgotten, comparing totals can look like a valid shortcut.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner compares two groups' overall totals (e.g. 'Group X has a bigger total so it did better') without checking or accounting for the number of values in each group.
misconceptions.correct_model: When two groups have DIFFERENT sizes, only the MEANS (or medians) can be fairly compared — a bigger total might simply mean a bigger group, not better individual performance.
misconceptions.remediation: Before comparing two groups, always check their sizes are stated; if they differ at all, compare the means, never the raw totals.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: If two quantities rise and fall together (correlation), one of them must be causing the change in the other.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A shared trend over time (both quantities going up together) intuitively feels like cause and effect, especially when a plausible-sounding story can be told to connect them.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner concludes 'X causes Y' purely from the fact that X and Y increased together, without considering a third, common factor or pure coincidence.
misconceptions.correct_model: Correlation only shows that two quantities tend to change together; it does NOT show that one causes the other. A third factor (e.g. hot weather causing both ice-cream sales and sunburn to rise) can explain the link just as well, or the link may be coincidence.
misconceptions.remediation: Whenever a correlation is given, ask explicitly: 'could a third factor explain both changes, rather than one causing the other?'

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A bar chart cannot be misleading as long as the axis numbers printed on it are accurate.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Checking the printed numbers feels like a complete check of 'honesty', without separately considering whether the VISUAL heights of the bars still represent the data fairly.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner inspects only the axis labels for correctness and concludes a truncated-axis chart is 'not misleading' because the numbers themselves are accurate.
misconceptions.correct_model: A chart is misleading whenever bar heights are no longer PROPORTIONAL to the values (for example, a truncated axis), even if every printed number on it is completely accurate — the visual impression, not just the labels, is what misleads a quick reader.
misconceptions.remediation: For any bar chart, check specifically whether the vertical axis starts at zero; if it does not, recompute the real percentage change from the actual numbers rather than trusting the apparent bar heights.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stating two averages are equal (or that one is bigger) and treating that as a complete comparison.
common_mistakes.why: Finding the averages is the main calculation, so once that number is produced the task can feel finished.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check every 'compare' answer against the three-ingredient checklist: average, spread, and a context sentence.

common_mistakes.mistake: Comparing two groups' raw totals instead of their means when the groups have different sizes.
common_mistakes.why: A total is often the first number calculated, and if group sizes are close or forgotten, comparing totals can look like a valid shortcut.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Before comparing two groups, check their sizes are stated; if they differ at all, compare means (or medians), never totals.

common_mistakes.mistake: Concluding one quantity causes another purely because they rise and fall together.
common_mistakes.why: A shared trend over time intuitively feels like cause and effect, especially with a plausible-sounding story to connect them.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Whenever a correlation is given, ask explicitly whether a third factor could explain both changes.

exam_notes: 'Compare' questions are marked on WORDS as much as numbers: a bare pair of averages with no comparison sentence and no context typically earns no marks at all, even if the numbers themselves are correct.

When asked to explain why a sample or conclusion is unreliable, give a reason tied to the SPECIFIC scenario in the question (e.g. 'chess club members are more likely to enjoy chess') rather than a generic statement like 'the sample might be biased'.
For a misleading-graph question, always recompute the REAL percentage change from the actual values given, rather than estimating from the apparent bar heights.

For 'correlation without cause' questions, naming a plausible THIRD FACTOR (not just saying 'correlation isn't causation') earns full marks; a bare assertion without a specific alternative explanation may not.

summary.big_idea: A full comparison of two data sets always combines an average, a measure of spread, and a sentence of meaning in context; choose mean+range for ordinary data but switch to median+IQR (Extended) whenever outliers or skew are present; and before trusting any graph or conclusion, check for small or biased samples, misleading axes, and correlation mistaken for causation.
key_points: A full comparison always needs three ingredients: a comparison of average, a comparison of spread, and a contextual sentence connecting both to the situation — bare numbers alone are never a complete comparison.
A larger average means typically larger values; a smaller spread means more consistent values; whether consistency is 'good' depends entirely on context.
When two groups have different sizes, only their means (or medians) can be fairly compared, never their raw totals.
(Extended) The median and IQR are far more resistant to outliers than the mean and range, so they give a fairer comparison whenever extreme values or skewed data are present.
A conclusion is only as reliable as the data behind it: check for small or biased samples, truncated or unequal axes, and correlation that does not prove causation.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Never give an average on its own as a 'comparison' — always pair it with a measure of spread and a sentence in context; switch to median and IQR when outliers are present; and always question a sample's size and bias, and a graph's axis, before trusting its conclusion.

objectives.statement: Plot points on a scatter diagram and describe the type (positive, negative, zero) and strength (strong, weak) of correlation.
Draw a sensible line of best fit by eye through the mean point, and use it to estimate values by interpolation.
Find the equation of a line of best fit from two points on it, and interpret its gradient and intercept in the context of the data.
Identify outliers, explain why extrapolation is unreliable, and explain why correlation does not prove causation.

prerequisites.statement: Plot coordinates $(x,y)$ accurately on a pair of axes.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every scatter diagram in this lesson is built from individually plotted coordinate pairs; an inaccurate plot produces a misleading pattern before any statistics is even applied.

prerequisites.statement: Calculate the mean of a list of values (Lesson 9.3).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A good line of best fit is checked against the mean point $(\bar x,\bar y)$, so this lesson assumes the mean can already be calculated fluently for both the $x$-values and the $y$-values.

prerequisites.statement: Find the gradient of a line through two given points, and write the equation of a straight line in the form $y=mx+c$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Finding the equation of a line of best fit from two points on it is ordinary coordinate-geometry gradient work applied to a new context; without it, only the 'by eye' reading skills in this lesson are accessible.

diagnostic_items.question: On a grid where the $x$-axis is numbered every $10$ units and the $y$-axis every $5$ units, with $5$ small squares between each pair of printed numbers, exactly where do you mark the point $(34,12)$?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: One small square is $10\div5=2$ units across and $5\div5=1$ unit up. So go to $30$ on the $x$-axis and count on $2$ more small squares to reach $34$, then go up to $10$ on the $y$-axis and count up $2$ more small squares to reach $12$, and mark a small cross where the two meet.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Two small squares to the right of $30$ and two small squares above $10$, taking every small square as $1$ unit on both axes, which gives $(32,12)$.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Assumes one small square is worth $1$ unit on every axis instead of working the scale out from the printed numbers, so the reading is wrong on any axis whose numbering is not in ones.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that the learner works out the value of one small square on each axis separately before plotting, which is what makes the points of a scatter diagram land in the right places.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Before plotting anything, write the value of one small square beside each axis (axis step $\div$ number of small squares) and use those two numbers for every point.

diagnostic_items.question: Find the mean of $3$, $7$ and $8$.

common_wrong_answers.answer: $7$, because it is the middle number of the three.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Gives the median instead of the mean: the middle value of an ordered list is found rather than the total divided by how many values there are.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that the mean can be calculated fluently, since the mean point $(\bar x,\bar y)$ is used throughout this lesson to position and check a line of best fit.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Say the method in words before calculating: 'add all the values, then divide by how many there are', and contrast it with 'the median is the middle one'.

diagnostic_items.question: Find the mean point $(\bar x,\bar y)$ of the four points $(2,5)$, $(4,6)$, $(6,10)$ and $(8,11)$.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: $\bar x=\dfrac{2+4+6+8}{4}=\dfrac{20}{4}=5$ and $\bar y=\dfrac{5+6+10+11}{4}=\dfrac{32}{4}=8$, so the mean point is $(5,8)$.

common_wrong_answers.answer: $(6,10)$, by picking the plotted point nearest the middle of the list.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Looks for the mean point among the given points instead of calculating it, missing that the mean point is worked out from the $x$-values and the $y$-values separately and need not be one of the data points at all.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that the learner can average the $x$-values and the $y$-values separately, which is exactly the calculation used to find the point a line of best fit should pass through.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Write the $x$-values in one row and the $y$-values in another, find the mean of each row on its own, and only then put the two answers together as a coordinate pair.

diagnostic_items.question: Find the gradient of the straight line through $(1,4)$ and $(5,12)$.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Gradient $=\dfrac{12-4}{5-1}=\dfrac{8}{4}=2$.

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Divides the change in $x$ by the change in $y$, which turns the gradient upside down; the gradient is always the change in $y$ divided by the change in $x$.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks the gradient calculation from two points, which is the whole of the work needed to find the equation of a line of best fit in this lesson.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Write 'gradient $=$ change in $y\,\div\,$change in $x$' at the top of the working every time, and label which number came from which axis before dividing.

diagnostic_items.question: A straight line has gradient $3$ and crosses the $y$-axis at $(0,5)$. Write its equation in the form $y=mx+c$.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: $y=3x+5$ (gradient $m=3$, intercept $c=5$).

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Swaps the gradient and the intercept, putting the intercept in front of $x$; in $y=mx+c$ the number multiplying $x$ is always the gradient and the number added on is always the $y$-intercept.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that the learner can assemble $y=mx+c$ from a gradient and an intercept, which is the final step when the equation of a line of best fit is asked for.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Label the two numbers '$m=$' and '$c=$' before writing anything, then substitute them into the printed form $y=mx+c$.

theory_blocks.title: What a scatter diagram answers
theory_blocks.body: A scatter diagram answers the question 'when one variable changes, what tends to happen to the other?'. [[blue:The PATTERN of the crosses]], not any single point, carries the message. Everything in this lesson is about reading that pattern: its direction, its tightness, and how far it can be trusted.
