theory_blocks.title: What a cumulative frequency is
theory_blocks.body: The **cumulative frequency** of a class is the total number of values up to and including the UPPER class boundary of that class. It is found by adding the frequencies as you go down the table (a running total). The last cumulative frequency always equals the total frequency $n$.

theory_blocks.title: Checking a cumulative frequency table
theory_blocks.body: The final cumulative frequency must equal the total number of data values, and the cumulative frequencies must never decrease down the table. Writing a $0$ at the lower boundary of the first class gives the curve's starting point.

theory_blocks.title: Method for drawing a cumulative frequency curve
theory_blocks.body:
1. Complete the cumulative frequency table.
2. Draw axes: the variable (with units) on the horizontal axis, cumulative frequency on the vertical axis, with the scale going up to $n$.
3. Plot each point at the UPPER class boundary with the corresponding cumulative frequency, as a small cross: $(10,4),(20,16),\ldots$, and the starting point at the LOWER boundary of the first class with cumulative frequency $0$ (here $(0,0)$, because the first class starts at $0$).
4. Join the points with a SMOOTH curve drawn freehand (not with straight segments).

theory_blocks.title: Four errors that break a cumulative frequency diagram
theory_blocks.body:
- Plotting the points at the MIDPOINTS or LOWER boundaries of the classes. [[blue:It must be the upper class boundary.]]
- Joining the points with a zig-zag of straight lines. For the syllabus, the points are joined with a smooth curve.
- Plotting the FREQUENCY of each class instead of the running total.
- Choosing an uneven vertical scale, or one that stops before $n$.

theory_blocks.title: Reading the median, quartiles and percentiles
theory_blocks.body:
For a cumulative frequency curve of $n$ values:

- **Median**: the value read across at cumulative frequency $\tfrac12n$.
- **Lower quartile** $Q_1$: at $\tfrac14n$. **Upper quartile** $Q_3$: at $\tfrac34n$.
- **Interquartile range** $=Q_3-Q_1$.
- The $p$th **percentile**: the value at cumulative frequency $\tfrac{p}{100}n$ (so $Q_1$ is the $25$th percentile and the median is the $50$th).

**Method:** go across from the vertical axis to the curve, then straight down to the horizontal axis, and read the value.

theory_blocks.title: Why $\tfrac n2$, not $\tfrac{n+1}{2}$, on a curve
theory_blocks.body: For a cumulative frequency curve the positions used are $\tfrac12n$, $\tfrac14n$ and $\tfrac34n$ (not $\tfrac{n+1}{2}$ and so on, as used for a short raw list in Lesson 9.3). For large $n$ the numerical difference is negligible, and the curve itself is only an estimate anyway, so this small distinction does not affect the accuracy of a reading taken from it.

theory_blocks.title: Counting values above or below a given value
theory_blocks.body: Reverse the usual procedure: start at the horizontal axis at the given value, go UP to the curve, then ACROSS to the vertical axis to read the cumulative frequency there.

theory_blocks.title: 'More than x' needs a subtraction
theory_blocks.body: 'How many took MORE THAN $x$?' needs a subtraction: read the cumulative frequency at $x$ (the number UP TO $x$) and subtract it from $n$. Reading the value at $x$ and stopping there gives the wrong group entirely.

theory_blocks.title: Unequal class widths
theory_blocks.body: Cumulative frequency does not depend on the class widths, even though the classes in a table may be unequal. The method stays exactly the same: running total, plotted at the upper boundary of each class, whatever its width.

theory_blocks.title: Comparing two distributions
theory_blocks.body: The curves of two data sets can be drawn on the same axes. The curve that is FURTHER TO THE RIGHT belongs to the set with larger values overall. The curve that rises MORE STEEPLY in the middle belongs to the set with smaller spread (its values are more tightly concentrated).

theory_blocks.title: Exam guidance for this lesson
theory_blocks.body: These questions are Extended content, so they can appear on Paper 2 (non-calculator) or Paper 4 (calculator). Use a ruler and draw the read-off lines on the graph: a correct reading with no visible construction lines can lose the method mark. Say 'estimate' and give values to the accuracy the grid allows (usually to the nearest small square). A question may give a partly printed grid: always check the scale of both axes before reading from it.

keywords.definition: The running total of frequencies up to and including a class's upper boundary.
A smooth curve joining points plotted at each class's upper boundary against its cumulative frequency, always rising from 0 to n.
The value at a given cumulative-frequency position expressed as a percentage of n; the pth percentile is at cumulative frequency (p/100)n.
Estimating a value between two known points on a cumulative frequency table or curve by assuming a straight-line change between them.

worked_examples.statement: Building the table. The times $t$ (minutes) taken by $80$ students to solve a puzzle are grouped: $0<t\le10$ freq $4$; $10<t\le20$ freq $12$; $20<t\le30$ freq $24$; $30<t\le40$ freq $22$; $40<t\le50$ freq $12$; $50<t\le60$ freq $6$. Complete the cumulative frequency table.
knowns: grouped frequency table with 6 classes, total 80 students
unknowns: cumulative frequency at each upper class boundary
reasoning: Start the running total at $0$ (the lower boundary of the first class).
Add each class's frequency to the running total so far, recording the new total at that class's upper boundary.
Check the final running total equals the given overall count of $80$.
worked_examples.solution: Cumulative frequency table: $t\le0$: $0$; $t\le10$: $4$; $t\le20$: $16$; $t\le30$: $40$; $t\le40$: $62$; $t\le50$: $74$; $t\le60$: $80$. For example $4+12=16$ students took $20$ minutes or less, and $16+24=40$ took $30$ minutes or less. The last value is $80=n$, so the table is consistent.
worked_examples.interpretation: Each new cumulative total is simply 'everything counted so far plus this class's frequency' — the running-total structure means a single arithmetic slip early in the table propagates through every later value, so checking the final total against $n$ is an essential habit.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Writing each class's own frequency again at each row (instead of adding it to the previous running total), which produces a table that does not actually accumulate at all.

worked_examples.statement: Drawing and reading the curve. Using the puzzle data's cumulative frequency table ($n=80$), draw the cumulative frequency curve and estimate the median, the lower and upper quartiles, and the interquartile range.
knowns: cumulative frequency table from the related idea, n=80
unknowns: median, Q1, Q3, IQR, read from the curve
reasoning: Plot each point at its class's upper boundary with the matching cumulative frequency, plus the starting point $(0,0)$, and join them with a smooth curve.
Compute the three target cumulative-frequency positions: $\tfrac12n=40$, $\tfrac14n=20$, $\tfrac34n=60$.
For each position, go across from the vertical axis to the curve, then down to the horizontal axis, and read the value.
worked_examples.solution: At cumulative frequency $40$ the curve is at $t\approx30$: median $\approx30$ minutes. At $20$: $Q_1\approx22$ minutes. At $60$: $Q_3\approx39$ minutes. $\mathrm{IQR}\approx39-22=17$ minutes. Because the values are read from a hand-drawn curve, answers within about $\pm1$ minute are accepted.
worked_examples.interpretation: The SAME curve answers three different questions just by reading it at three different heights ($\tfrac14n$, $\tfrac12n$, $\tfrac34n$) — once the curve is correctly drawn, no further calculation is needed for any of these estimates.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Reading the quartiles' positions as $20$ and $60$ correctly, but then going UP from the horizontal axis to the curve instead of ACROSS from the vertical axis, reversing the correct reading direction.

assets.caption: Cumulative frequency curve for the puzzle-solving times, with dashed construction lines showing how the median, lower quartile and upper quartile are read off.
assets.purpose: Reproduce the legacy puzzle-curve figure exactly, including its quartile read-off construction lines, matching the worked reading method.

worked_examples.statement: Counting and percentiles. Using the puzzle data ($n=80$): (a) Estimate how many students took more than $45$ minutes. (b) Estimate the $90$th percentile.
knowns: the same puzzle cumulative frequency curve, n=80
unknowns: number of students taking more than 45 minutes, and the 90th percentile
reasoning: (a) Go up from $t=45$ on the horizontal axis to the curve, then across to read the cumulative frequency there; this gives the number taking $45$ minutes OR LESS, so subtract from $n$ for 'more than'.
(b) Compute the target cumulative frequency for the 90th percentile: $\tfrac{90}{100}\times80$; then read across at that height to find the corresponding time.
worked_examples.solution: (a) Going up from $t=45$, the curve is at about $68$: so about $68$ students took $45$ minutes or less, and $80-68=12$ took MORE THAN $45$ minutes. (b) The 90th percentile position is $\tfrac{90}{100}\times80=72$; reading across at $72$ gives $t\approx48$: $90\%$ of the students finished in about $48$ minutes or less.
worked_examples.interpretation: Both parts use the SAME curve and the same basic reading skill, but part (a) needs an extra subtraction step ($n-{}$reading) that part (b) does not — recognising which questions need that extra step is as important as reading the curve correctly in the first place.
worked_examples.common_mistake: In part (a), reporting $68$ (the number taking $45$ minutes or less) as the final answer, forgetting the question asked for MORE than $45$ minutes.

worked_examples.statement: From a cumulative table back to frequencies. The masses $m$ kg of parcels are given as a cumulative frequency table: $m\le0$: $0$; $m\le2$: $8$; $m\le5$: $30$; $m\le10$: $60$; $m\le20$: $70$. Find the frequency of each class and estimate the median mass.
knowns: a cumulative frequency table with unequal class widths, n=70
unknowns: the frequency of each class, and the median mass
reasoning: Find each class's frequency by subtracting each cumulative value from the one before it.
Find the median's target cumulative frequency, $\tfrac12n$, and identify which class it falls inside.
Use linear interpolation within that class (since the class widths here are unequal, the class's own width must be used directly) to estimate where the median falls.
worked_examples.solution: Frequencies: $8-0=8$; $30-8=22$; $60-30=30$; $70-60=10$. Total $=70=n$, confirming the table. Median position $=\tfrac12\times70=35$, which lies between $m=5$ (cumulative $30$) and $m=10$ (cumulative $60$). By linear interpolation: $5+\dfrac{35-30}{60-30}\times5=5+\dfrac{5}{30}\times5\approx5.8$\,kg; plotting and reading from the smooth curve gives a similar estimate of about $6$\,kg.
worked_examples.interpretation: Unequal class widths change nothing about the METHOD — the running total is still a running total, and the median position is still $\tfrac12n$ — only the interpolation arithmetic within the median class needs to use that class's own width.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Using the wrong class width when interpolating inside the median class (for example $10$, the width of the next class $10<m\le20$, or $3$, the width of the class before) instead of the median class's own width, $10-5=5$.

worked_examples.statement: Comparing two distributions. Two groups of $80$ students each solved the same puzzle. For group A, $Q_1\approx22$, $Q_3\approx39$ (median $30$); for group B, $Q_1\approx24$, $Q_3\approx36$ (median also $30$). Compare the two groups' performance.
knowns: two cumulative frequency curves, both n=80, both passing through the same median point
unknowns: IQR for each group, and a worded comparison
reasoning: Calculate each group's IQR from its given quartiles.
Compare the two medians first (are they equal, or is one bigger?).
Compare the two IQRs, then write a sentence connecting both comparisons to what they mean for the groups' consistency.
worked_examples.solution: $\mathrm{IQR}_A\approx39-22=17$; $\mathrm{IQR}_B\approx36-24=12$. The medians are equal ($30$ minutes), so the typical student takes the same time in both groups. Group B has the smaller interquartile range, so its times are more consistent (more tightly clustered) than those of group A.
worked_examples.interpretation: Two curves that share the same median can still look very different: the curve that is STEEPER around the median (here, group B's) always corresponds to the smaller IQR and the more consistent group, exactly as the visual steepness rule predicts.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Concluding the groups 'performed identically' purely because their medians are equal, without also comparing the two IQRs.

assets.caption: Cumulative frequency curves for two groups of $80$ students on the same axes. Both curves are smooth and pass through the same median point $(30,40)$, but Group B rises more steeply around the median: reading across at a cumulative frequency of $20$ and of $60$ gives $Q_1\approx22$ and $Q_3\approx39$ for Group A, and $Q_1\approx24$ and $Q_3\approx36$ for Group B.
assets.purpose: Reproduce the legacy two-curve comparison figure exactly, matching the worked reasoning about equal medians but different interquartile ranges.

guided_exercises.statement: The ages $x$ (years) of $60$ members of a gym are grouped: $18<x\le25$ freq $14$; $25<x\le35$ freq $20$; $35<x\le50$ freq $18$; $50<x\le70$ freq $8$. Build the cumulative frequency table.
hints: Start the running total at $0$, at the lower boundary of the first class ($x=18$).
Add each class's frequency to the PREVIOUS running total, not to the original frequency column again.
guided_exercises.full_solution: Running total: $0$ (at $x=18$); $0+14=14$ (at $x=25$); $14+20=34$ (at $x=35$); $34+18=52$ (at $x=50$); $52+8=60$ (at $x=70$). The final value $60$ matches the total number of members, confirming the table is correct.
common_errors: Plotting or recording each class's own frequency again instead of the accumulated running total.

guided_exercises.statement: A cumulative frequency curve for $60$ gym members passes through $(18,0)$, $(25,14)$, $(35,34)$, $(50,52)$, $(70,60)$ (as built in the related idea). Estimate the median age and the interquartile range, using linear interpolation between the given points.
hints: Find the target positions first: $\tfrac12\times60=30$ for the median, $\tfrac14\times60=15$ for $Q_1$, $\tfrac34\times60=45$ for $Q_3$.
For each position, identify which pair of given points it falls between before interpolating.
guided_exercises.answer: Median $\approx33$, $Q_1\approx25.5$, $Q_3\approx44.2$, IQR $\approx18.7$.
guided_exercises.full_solution: Median (position $30$) lies between $(25,14)$ and $(35,34)$: $25+\dfrac{30-14}{34-14}\times10=25+\dfrac{16}{20}\times10=25+8=33$. $Q_1$ (position $15$) lies between $(25,14)$ and $(35,34)$: $25+\dfrac{15-14}{34-14}\times10=25+0.5=25.5$. $Q_3$ (position $45$) lies between $(35,34)$ and $(50,52)$: $35+\dfrac{45-34}{52-34}\times15=35+\dfrac{11}{18}\times15\approx44.2$. IQR $\approx44.2-25.5=18.7$. (Values given to the nearest $0.1$; accept the equivalent values obtained by careful by-eye curve reading.)
common_errors: Identifying the correct target position (e.g. 30 for the median) but then interpolating between the wrong pair of points (not checking which interval the position actually falls inside).

guided_exercises.statement: Using the same gym cumulative frequency curve as the related idea ($n=60$, points as given), estimate how many members are older than $40$.
hints: First find the cumulative frequency AT $x=40$ by interpolating between the two surrounding given points.
Remember the final step: 'more than' needs a subtraction from $n$, not just the reading itself.
guided_exercises.answer: Cumulative frequency at $40\approx40$; members older than $40\approx20$.
guided_exercises.full_solution: $x=40$ lies between $(35,34)$ and $(50,52)$: cumulative frequency $\approx34+\dfrac{40-35}{50-35}\times(52-34)=34+\dfrac{5}{15}\times18=34+6=40$. So about $40$ members are aged $40$ or younger, meaning $60-40=20$ members are OLDER than $40$.
common_errors: Reporting the reading at $x=40$ (about 40) directly as the final answer, without subtracting from $n=60$ to find the number older than 40.

exercises.statement: The heights $h$ (cm) of $50$ students are grouped: $140<h\le150$ freq $4$; $150<h\le160$ freq $11$; $160<h\le170$ freq $19$; $170<h\le180$ freq $12$; $180<h\le190$ freq $4$. (a) Complete a cumulative frequency table. (b) Estimate the median and the interquartile range (by interpolation).
common_errors: Plotting the cumulative frequencies at the class midpoints instead of the upper boundaries when drawing the curve this table would produce.

exercises.statement: The table gives cumulative frequencies for marks in a test taken by $100$ students: mark $\le0$: $0$; $\le20$: $5$; $\le40$: $18$; $\le60$: $46$; $\le80$: $82$; $\le100$: $100$. (a) Find the number of students in each class. (b) Estimate the median mark. (c) The pass mark is $45$. Estimate how many students passed.
exercises.answer: (a) $5,13,28,36,18$. (b) Median $\approx62.2$. (c) About $75$ passed.
common_errors: In (c), reporting the reading at mark 45 (about 25) as the number who PASSED, instead of subtracting it from 100 to count those scoring above the pass mark.

exercises.statement: A cumulative frequency curve for $120$ values passes through $(10,0)$, $(20,10)$, $(30,35)$, $(40,70)$, $(50,105)$, $(60,120)$. Estimate the median, $Q_1$, $Q_3$ and the IQR, interpolating between the given points.
exercises.answer: Median $\approx37.1$, $Q_1=28$, $Q_3\approx45.7$, IQR $\approx17.7$.
common_errors: Using $n=6$ (the number of given points) instead of $n=120$ (the actual total) when computing the target positions.

exercises.statement: Using the heights data from the related idea, estimate (a) the $90$th percentile; (b) how many students are taller than $175$\,cm.
exercises.answer: (a) $\approx179.2$\,cm. (b) About $10$ students.
exercises.full_solution: (a) 90th percentile position $=\tfrac{90}{100}\times50=45$. This falls between $(170,34)$ and $(180,46)$: $170+\dfrac{45-34}{46-34}\times10\approx179.2$\,cm. (b) Cumulative frequency at $175$ falls between $(170,34)$ and $(180,46)$: $34+\dfrac{175-170}{180-170}\times(46-34)=34+0.5\times12=40$; so about $50-40=10$ students are taller than $175$\,cm.
common_errors: In (b), forgetting the final subtraction from the total (50), reporting the cumulative frequency at 175 itself (about 40) as the number taller than 175.

exercises.statement: In two schools: School A has median $52$, $Q_1=40$, $Q_3=66$; School B has median $52$, $Q_1=45$, $Q_3=58$. Compare the results of the two schools.
exercises.answer: Same median; School B is more consistent (IQR 13 vs School A's IQR 26).
exercises.full_solution: Both schools have the same median mark ($52$), so a typical student scored the same in each. School A's IQR $=66-40=26$; School B's IQR $=58-45=13$. School B's IQR is much smaller, so School B's marks were far more consistent (tightly clustered), while School A's marks were much more spread out despite having the same typical (median) mark.
common_errors: Concluding the schools 'performed the same' purely from the equal medians, without comparing the two IQRs at all.

exercises.statement: Parcel masses (kg): $0<m\le2$ freq $8$; $2<m\le5$ freq $22$; $5<m\le10$ freq $30$; $10<m\le20$ freq $10$. Build a cumulative frequency table and estimate the median mass.
exercises.answer: Cumulative frequencies $8,30,60,70$ at $m=2,5,10,20$. Median $\approx5.8$-$6$\,kg.
common_errors: Using a fixed interpolation width (e.g. 10, copied from the next class) instead of this specific class's own width (10-5=5).

exercises.statement: In a cumulative frequency table, $t\le10$: $6$; $t\le20$: $21$; $t\le30$: $x$; $t\le40$: $69$; $t\le50$: $80$. The class $30<t\le40$ has frequency $24$. Find $x$ and the frequency of each class.
exercises.full_solution: Since the class $30<t\le40$ has frequency $24$, and its cumulative frequency at $t=40$ is $69$: $x=69-24=45$. Frequencies: $6-0=6$ (first class, assuming $t\le0$ is $0$); $21-6=15$; $45-21=24$; $69-45=24$; $80-69=11$.
common_errors: Computing $x$ by adding rather than subtracting the given class frequency from the t≤40 cumulative value (69+24 instead of 69-24).

exercises.statement: Describe what the shape of a cumulative frequency curve tells you about the data where it is (a) steep; (b) flat.
exercises.answer: (a) Many values packed into a narrow range. (b) Few values in that range.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Where the curve is steep, the cumulative total rises quickly over a small change in $x$, meaning many data values are packed closely together in that interval. (b) Where the curve is flat, the cumulative total barely changes over that interval, meaning very few (or no) data values lie there.
common_errors: Reversing the two descriptions (associating 'steep' with few values and 'flat' with many), rather than connecting steepness directly to how fast the running total grows.

exam_questions.statement:
The masses $m$ (kg) of $90$ parcels are grouped: $0<m\le5$ freq $10$; $5<m\le10$ freq $24$; $10<m\le15$ freq $30$; $15<m\le20$ freq $18$; $20<m\le30$ freq $8$.
(a) Complete the cumulative frequency table. [2]
(b) Estimate the median mass, using linear interpolation. [2]
(c) Estimate the interquartile range. [3]
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for a correct running total; A1 for all the cumulative values correct (0, 10, 34, 64, 82, 90)
(b) M1 for correctly identifying the median's position (45) and the interval it falls in; A1 for a reasonable estimate (accept a range, e.g. 11.5-12.0)

(c) M1 for correctly identifying both $Q_1$ and $Q_3$ positions and intervals; A1 for both quartile estimates; A1 for the correct IQR calculation from the candidate's own values (accept a sensible range).
common_errors: In (c), finding $Q_1$ and $Q_3$ correctly but then adding them instead of subtracting to find the IQR.

exam_questions.statement:
A cumulative frequency curve for the ages (in years) of $150$ people at a concert shows that $45$ people are aged $20$ or younger, and $120$ people are aged $35$ or younger.
(a) Estimate how many people are aged between $20$ and $35$. [1]
(b) Estimate how many people are older than $35$. [1]
(c) Given that the median age is $25$, state what this tells you about the ages of the people at the concert. [2]
exam_questions.answer: (a) $75$. (b) $30$. (c) Half the people are aged 25 or younger, and half are older than 25.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Number aged between $20$ and $35$ $=120-45=75$. (b) Number older than $35=150-120=30$. (c) A median age of $25$ means that, of the $150$ people, half ($75$) are aged $25$ or younger and the other half are older than $25$ — $25$ is the 'typical middle' age for this concert's audience.
mark_scheme: (a) B1 for $75$ (correct subtraction of the two given cumulative values)
(b) B1 for $30$ (correct subtraction from the total, 150-120)
(c) B1 for stating that half the people are aged 25 or younger (or equivalent); B1 for stating the other half are older than 25, i.e. a correct and complete contextual interpretation of the median.
common_errors: In (a), subtracting in the wrong order (45-120, giving a negative or nonsensical result) instead of 120-45.

challenge_questions.statement: A student draws the puzzle curve ($n=80$) by plotting the cumulative frequencies at the class midpoints $5,15,25,\ldots$ instead of the upper boundaries. What value would they obtain for the median, and by how much is it wrong?
challenge_questions.answer: They would read a median of about $25$ instead of $30$: an error of about $5$ minutes ($17\%$).
challenge_questions.full_solution: Plotting at midpoints instead of upper boundaries means the point that should be at $(30,40)$ (upper boundary $30$, cumulative frequency $40$) is instead plotted at $(25,40)$ (midpoint of the $20<t\le30$ class). Reading the median (cumulative frequency $40$) from this shifted curve gives $t\approx25$ instead of the correct $t\approx30$: an error of about $5$ minutes, or $\dfrac{5}{30}\times100\approx17\%$. This error applies to every percentile read from the mistaken curve, not just the median, since the whole curve is shifted.

challenge_questions.statement: Group A has cumulative frequencies $0,4,16,40,62,74,80$ and Group B has $0,1,6,40,74,79,80$ at $t=0,10,20,30,40,50,60$. By linear interpolation find $Q_1$, $Q_3$ and the IQR of each group and decide which group is more consistent.
challenge_questions.answer: A: $Q_1\approx21.7$, $Q_3\approx39.1$, IQR $\approx17.4$. B: $Q_1\approx24.1$, $Q_3\approx35.9$, IQR $\approx11.8$. B is more consistent.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Group A ($n=80$): $Q_1$ position $=20$, between $(20,16)$ and $(30,40)$: $20+\dfrac{20-16}{40-16}\times10=20+\dfrac{4}{24}\times10\approx21.7$. $Q_3$ position $=60$, between $(30,40)$ and $(40,62)$: $30+\dfrac{60-40}{62-40}\times10=30+\dfrac{20}{22}\times10\approx39.1$. IQR$_A\approx39.1-21.7=17.4$. Group B: $Q_1$ position $=20$, between $(20,6)$ and $(30,40)$: $20+\dfrac{20-6}{40-6}\times10=20+\dfrac{14}{34}\times10\approx24.1$. $Q_3$ position $=60$, between $(30,40)$ and $(40,74)$: $30+\dfrac{60-40}{74-40}\times10=30+\dfrac{20}{34}\times10\approx35.9$. IQR$_B\approx35.9-24.1=11.8$. Since IQR$_B<$IQR$_A$, Group B is more consistent.

challenge_questions.statement: For $200$ values, $Q_1=24$, the median is $30$, $Q_3=40$ and the $80$th percentile is $45$. Estimate (a) how many values are between $30$ and $45$; (b) what percentage of the values lie between $24$ and $40$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: (a) The median ($30$) corresponds to cumulative frequency $\tfrac12\times200=100$; the 80th percentile ($45$) corresponds to cumulative frequency $\tfrac{80}{100}\times200=160$. Values between $30$ and $45$ $=160-100=60$. (b) $24$ is $Q_1$ and $40$ is $Q_3$; by definition, the interquartile range always contains the MIDDLE $50\%$ of the data, regardless of the actual values of $n$.

challenge_questions.statement: The cumulative frequency curve of a data set is a straight line from $(0,0)$ to $(60,120)$. Describe the distribution and find the median, quartiles and IQR.
challenge_questions.answer: Uniform distribution: values are evenly spread from $0$ to $60$. Median $=30$, $Q_1=15$, $Q_3=45$, IQR $=30$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: A straight-line cumulative frequency curve means the running total increases at a perfectly constant rate, so the underlying data is spread EVENLY (uniformly) across the whole range $0$ to $60$ — no interval is more 'crowded' than any other. Since the line is straight, each target cumulative-frequency position maps directly and proportionally onto the $t$-axis: median (position $60$, half of $120$) $=30$; $Q_1$ (position $30$, a quarter of $120$) $=15$; $Q_3$ (position $90$, three-quarters of $120$) $=45$. IQR $=45-15=30$.

challenge_questions.statement: Some books use $\tfrac{n+1}{2}$ for the median position. For $n=80$, compare this with $\tfrac n2$ and explain why the difference does not matter when reading from a curve.
challenge_questions.answer: $\tfrac{81}{2}=40.5$ versus $40$: half a value out of $80$. On a curve this shifts the reading by a negligible amount.
challenge_questions.full_solution: $\tfrac{n+1}{2}=\tfrac{81}{2}=40.5$, compared with $\tfrac n2=40$: a difference of just $0.5$ out of a total of $80$ values. On a smooth, continuously rising cumulative frequency curve, moving the target cumulative-frequency position by such a tiny amount (0.5 out of 80) shifts the resulting reading on the horizontal axis by far less than the precision with which a hand-drawn curve can realistically be read (typically to the nearest unit or so) — so the choice between the two formulas makes no practical difference here, even though it would matter for an exact calculation from a short raw list.

mcq.stem: A grouped frequency table has a class $20<t\le30$ with cumulative frequency $40$ at that point. At which $t$-value should this cumulative frequency be plotted on the cumulative frequency diagram?

options.text: $t=25$ (the class midpoint)
options.why_wrong: The midpoint is used when estimating a MEAN from grouped data, not when plotting a cumulative frequency, which must be plotted at the upper boundary of the class it counts up to.

options.text: $t=30$ (the upper class boundary)
$t=20$ (the lower class boundary)
options.why_wrong: At the lower boundary, none of the values in this class have been counted yet; the cumulative total of 40 specifically includes every value up to the UPPER boundary, 30.

options.text: It does not matter, as long as it is plotted somewhere within the class
options.why_wrong: The plotting position is tied to the exact meaning of the cumulative frequency value (everything up to a specific boundary), so it is not an arbitrary choice within the class.

mcq.explanation: A cumulative frequency of 40 means '40 values are less than or equal to this point', which is only true at the class's upper boundary (30), since that is where every value in the class has finally been counted.

mcq.stem: After plotting the points of a cumulative frequency table, how should they be joined to form the diagram?

options.text: With straight line segments joining each consecutive pair of points
options.why_wrong: Straight segments are correct for some other graph types, but a cumulative frequency diagram specifically requires a smooth curve, reflecting that values could occur anywhere within each class.

options.text: They should not be joined at all; the diagram is just the plotted points
options.why_wrong: A cumulative frequency DIAGRAM specifically requires the points to be joined into a curve, which is what makes continuous reading (for the median, quartiles, percentiles) possible.

options.text: With a single smooth curve drawn freehand
With a bar for each class, like a histogram
options.why_wrong: Bars belong to a histogram, which shows frequency density, not cumulative frequency; a cumulative frequency diagram is a curve, not a set of bars.

mcq.explanation: A cumulative frequency diagram's points are joined with a single smooth curve, not straight segments or bars, since the underlying grouped data could take any value within each class.

mcq.stem: A learner's cumulative frequency diagram has heights that go up and down between classes instead of rising continuously. What has most likely gone wrong?

options.text: The axes were simply drawn the wrong way round
options.why_wrong: Swapped axes would distort the whole shape of the diagram, but would not specifically cause the plotted heights themselves to decrease between classes.

options.text: The curve was drawn with too sharp a pencil
options.why_wrong: The sharpness of the pencil affects only how neatly the curve is drawn, not whether the underlying plotted VALUES themselves rise or fall.

options.text: A percentage scale was used instead of a frequency scale
options.why_wrong: Switching between a frequency scale and a percentage scale only rescales the vertical axis; it would not make the curve decrease, since percentages of a running total still accumulate upward too.

options.text: The ordinary class frequencies were plotted instead of the running total (cumulative frequencies)

mcq.explanation: A cumulative frequency curve must always rise (never decrease), because it is a running total; heights going up and down signal that individual class frequencies were plotted instead of the accumulated running total.

mcq.stem: For $n=150$ values, the cumulative frequency read at $x=60$ is $110$. How many values are greater than $60$?

options.why_wrong: This is the number of values UP TO (less than or equal to) 60, not the number greater than 60; the question needs a further subtraction from the total, $n=150$.
Adding the two values has no meaning here; the correct operation is to SUBTRACT the reading at 60 from the total n, not to add them.

options.text: It cannot be determined without reading the curve again at a different value
options.why_wrong: The reading at 60 (110) together with the known total (150) is already sufficient to answer the question, using a single subtraction.

mcq.explanation: The reading at $x=60$ (110) gives the number of values up to and including 60; subtracting this from the total $n=150$ gives the number of values greater than 60: $150-110=40$.

mcq.stem: A student finds the median position for a cumulative frequency curve with $n=80$ by calculating $\tfrac{n+1}{2}=40.5$, exactly as they would for a short raw list. What is the correct position to use instead for reading the curve?

options.text: $\tfrac{n+1}{2}=40.5$ is correct; the same formula is always used regardless of context
options.why_wrong: The $\tfrac{n+1}{2}$ formula is specifically for a short, discretely ordered raw list; for a smooth cumulative frequency curve, the standard position used is $\tfrac n2$ instead.

options.text: $\tfrac n2=40$

options.why_wrong: This is neither the raw-list formula nor the curve-reading convention; the correct curve position is simply $\tfrac n2$.

options.text: $n=80$ itself
options.why_wrong: Using the full total $n$ would read the position for the MAXIMUM value in the data, not the median, which is at half of n.

mcq.explanation: For a cumulative frequency curve, the standard positions are $\tfrac n2$ for the median, $\tfrac n4$ for $Q_1$ and $\tfrac{3n}{4}$ for $Q_3$ — not the $\tfrac{n+1}{2}$ formula used for a short raw list, though the tiny numerical difference rarely matters in practice.

flashcards.front: What is a cumulative frequency?
flashcards.back: A running total: the number of values up to and including a given class's upper boundary.

flashcards.front: At which x-value should each cumulative frequency be plotted?
flashcards.back: At the UPPER class boundary — never the midpoint or lower boundary.

flashcards.front: Should the points on a cumulative frequency diagram be joined with straight segments?
flashcards.back: No — they are joined with a single smooth curve drawn freehand, never a zig-zag of straight lines.

flashcards.front: What cumulative-frequency position gives the median, Q1 and Q3 on a curve?
flashcards.back: Median at $\tfrac n2$; $Q_1$ at $\tfrac n4$; $Q_3$ at $\tfrac{3n}{4}$ (not $\tfrac{n+1}{2}$, which is for a short raw list).

flashcards.front: How do you find the p-th percentile's cumulative-frequency position?
flashcards.back: $\dfrac{p}{100}\times n$, then read across from that height to the curve and down to the axis.

flashcards.front: To find how many values are MORE than x, is it enough to read the curve at x?
flashcards.back: No — reading at x gives the number UP TO x; subtract that reading from n to get the number more than x.

flashcards.front: How do you count values above or below a given value from a curve?
flashcards.back: Go UP from that value on the horizontal axis to the curve, then ACROSS to read the cumulative frequency (the reverse of the usual median/quartile reading direction).

flashcards.front: What does a steep stretch of a cumulative frequency curve tell you about the data there?
flashcards.back: Many values are packed closely together in that interval (the running total rises quickly).

flashcards.front: Comparing two cumulative frequency curves: what does a curve further to the right, or a steeper curve, tell you?
flashcards.back: Further right = that group's values are typically larger; steeper (around the median) = that group's values are more concentrated (smaller spread).

flashcards.front: Two groups' cumulative frequency curves share the same median. Does that mean the groups are the same?
flashcards.back: No — compare their IQRs too; a steeper curve around the median means a smaller IQR and more consistent values, even with an equal median.

flashcards.front: What must the final value in a cumulative frequency table always equal?
flashcards.back: The total number of data values, $n$.

flashcards.front: A cumulative frequency curve is a perfectly straight line. What does this tell you about the distribution?
flashcards.back: The data is spread perfectly evenly (uniformly) across the whole range — no interval is more crowded than any other.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Cumulative frequency points should be plotted at the midpoint or the lower boundary of each class, rather than the upper boundary.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Earlier grouped-data work (estimating a mean) uses the class MIDPOINT as the representative value, so that habit can be carried over incorrectly into cumulative frequency, where the boundary used has a completely different meaning.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner plots the cumulative frequency value against the class midpoint (or lower boundary) instead of the upper boundary, shifting the whole curve to the left (or further left).
misconceptions.correct_model: Cumulative frequency points are always plotted at the UPPER class boundary, because the cumulative frequency is defined as the running total of values up to and including that exact boundary.
misconceptions.remediation: Before plotting any point, state out loud which boundary (upper) the cumulative frequency value belongs to, and confirm it matches the $x$-coordinate being used.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The points on a cumulative frequency diagram should be joined with straight zig-zag line segments, the same way an ordinary bar-chart-based frequency polygon is drawn.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Joining points with straight segments is a familiar, simpler technique from other graph types, and it can feel more 'precise' or rule-based than freehand curve drawing.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner's cumulative frequency diagram shows sharp angular corners at each plotted point instead of one continuously smooth, rising curve.
misconceptions.correct_model: For a cumulative frequency diagram, the plotted points are joined with a single SMOOTH curve drawn freehand, reflecting that the underlying grouped data could in principle take any value within each class.
misconceptions.remediation: After plotting all points, practise drawing one continuous smooth curve through them in a single unbroken pencil stroke, rather than ruling straight segments between consecutive points.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The height plotted for each class on a cumulative frequency diagram is that class's own FREQUENCY, not a running total.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A grouped frequency table's frequency column is the most immediately visible number for each class, so plotting it directly (rather than first computing a running total) can look like the obvious thing to do.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner's plotted heights go up and down between classes (matching the raw frequencies) instead of rising continuously from $0$ to $n$.
misconceptions.correct_model: The height plotted at each class's upper boundary is the CUMULATIVE (running total) frequency up to that point, not the frequency of that one class alone; a cumulative frequency curve can never decrease.
misconceptions.remediation: Before plotting, add an explicit 'running total' row underneath the ordinary frequency row in the table, computed by repeated addition, and plot only from that row.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: To find 'how many values are greater than $x$', it is enough to read the cumulative frequency at $x$ and report that number.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Reading a value off the curve at the given $x$ feels like it has already answered the question, especially under time pressure, without checking whether the reading itself represents 'up to $x$' or 'more than $x$'.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner reads the cumulative frequency at $x$ (the count up to and including $x$) and submits that number directly as the answer for 'more than $x$'.
misconceptions.correct_model: The cumulative frequency read at $x$ gives the number of values UP TO (less than or equal to) $x$; to find the number GREATER than $x$, this value must be SUBTRACTED from the total $n$.
misconceptions.remediation: Whenever a question asks for 'more than' or 'greater than' a value, write 'answer $=n-{}$(reading)' as an explicit extra line before giving a final numeric answer.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The median position on a cumulative frequency curve should be found using $\tfrac{n+1}{2}$, exactly as for a short raw list of data (Lesson 9.3).
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The $\tfrac{n+1}{2}$ position was the correct and memorised rule for finding the median of a short ordered list, so it is natural to try to reuse the same formula here without checking whether the context (a smooth curve, not a discrete ordered list) has changed.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner computes $\tfrac{n+1}{2}$ (rather than $\tfrac{n}{2}$) as the vertical position to read across from when finding the median from a cumulative frequency curve.
misconceptions.correct_model: For a cumulative frequency CURVE, the standard positions used are $\tfrac12n$ for the median, $\tfrac14n$ for $Q_1$, and $\tfrac34n$ for $Q_3$ (not $\tfrac{n+1}{2}$ and so on); for large $n$ the tiny numerical difference between $\tfrac n2$ and $\tfrac{n+1}{2}$ is negligible compared to the accuracy of reading a hand-drawn curve anyway.
misconceptions.remediation: Before reading any position from a cumulative frequency curve, write the three target positions explicitly as $\tfrac14n$, $\tfrac12n$, $\tfrac34n$, rather than reaching for the raw-list formula from Lesson 9.3.

common_mistakes.mistake: Plotting cumulative frequencies at the class midpoint instead of the upper boundary.
common_mistakes.why: Grouped-mean work (Lesson 9.3) correctly uses the midpoint, and the habit carries over incorrectly.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Before plotting any point, state out loud which boundary (upper) the cumulative frequency value belongs to.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reading the cumulative frequency at a value x and reporting it directly as the answer for 'more than x'.
common_mistakes.why: The reading step feels complete once a number has been found on the curve, so the required further subtraction can be forgotten.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Write 'answer = n - (reading)' explicitly whenever a question asks for 'more than' or 'greater than'.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the raw-list median position formula (n+1)/2 when reading a cumulative frequency curve.
common_mistakes.why: The (n+1)/2 formula was the correct, memorised rule in the previous lesson, so it is carried over without checking whether the context has changed.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Write the three curve-specific positions (n/4, n/2, 3n/4) explicitly before reading any value from a cumulative frequency curve.

exam_notes: Always draw the construction lines (to and from the curve) for every reading taken from a cumulative frequency diagram: a correct final value with no visible lines can lose the method mark.

State 'estimate' explicitly in any answer read from a cumulative frequency curve, and give it to the accuracy the grid allows (usually to the nearest small square), since the curve itself is only an approximation of the true distribution.
For 'how many/what percentage are more than x' questions, always show the subtraction from n as a separate explicit line of working, not just the final number.
When comparing two distributions from their cumulative frequency curves, a full-mark answer compares BOTH the medians and the IQRs, each followed by a sentence in context, exactly as in Lesson 9.4.

summary.big_idea: A cumulative frequency curve turns a grouped frequency table into a running-total picture of the whole data set: plotted at each class's upper boundary and joined with a smooth curve, it lets the median, quartiles, IQR and any percentile be estimated by reading across, and lets the number of values above or below a given point be found by reading up then subtracting from n when needed.
key_points: Cumulative frequency is a running total, plotted at each class's UPPER boundary, always rising from 0 to n; never plot the frequency alone or use the midpoint.
Join the points with a single smooth curve, never straight zig-zag segments.
Median at cumulative frequency n/2, Q1 at n/4, Q3 at 3n/4, IQR = Q3 - Q1; the pth percentile is at (p/100)n.
'How many more than x': read the cumulative frequency at x (the number up to x), then subtract from n.
Comparing two curves: a curve further right means larger typical values; a steeper curve around the median means a smaller IQR and more consistent data.
formulas: \text{median position} = \tfrac12 n, \quad Q_1\ \text{position} = \tfrac14 n, \quad Q_3\ \text{position} = \tfrac34 n
\text{number more than } x = n - (\text{cumulative frequency at } x)
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Plot at the upper class boundary, join with a smooth curve; read the median/quartiles/percentiles by going across at n/2, n/4, 3n/4 or (p/100)n; and remember the extra subtraction from n whenever a question asks for 'more than'.

07_Histograms.json.title: Histograms
07_Histograms.json.subject: Mathematics
07_Histograms.json.course_label: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 · Statistics · Extended only

objectives.statement: Calculate frequency density (frequency divided by class width) and draw a histogram for data with unequal class widths.
Find frequencies from a histogram's bar heights and widths, and find a missing height, width or scale from the others.
Estimate the number of values in part of a class, and estimate the mean, from a histogram.
Identify the modal class of a histogram correctly (by frequency density, not by frequency), and avoid the common errors that come from treating a histogram like an ordinary bar chart.

prerequisites.statement: Read and build a grouped frequency table, including finding class boundaries and widths (Lesson 9.1).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A histogram is built directly from a grouped frequency table; finding each class's width (upper boundary minus lower boundary) correctly is the first and most essential step in finding frequency density.

prerequisites.statement: Draw and read an ordinary bar chart with equal class widths (Lesson 9.2).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A histogram looks superficially similar to a bar chart, and this lesson is largely about the specific ways that similarity becomes MISLEADING once class widths are unequal.

prerequisites.statement: Estimate the mean of grouped data using class midpoints (Lesson 9.3).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Estimating the mean from a histogram uses exactly the same midpoint-weighted method, applied to frequencies recovered from the histogram's bars rather than read directly from a table.

diagnostic_items.question: Why is frequency not used for the height of the bars when classes have unequal widths?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: A wider class would look bigger on the diagram simply because it is wider, not because it genuinely contains more values; using frequency density instead makes the AREA of each bar (not its height) proportional to the frequency, so wide and narrow classes are compared fairly.

common_wrong_answers.answer: It doesn't really matter, as long as the frequencies are labelled on the bars.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Assumes that a correct numeric label can fix a visually misleading bar height, missing that the whole point of a histogram is for the VISUAL area itself to represent frequency fairly, without needing to read any label.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks whether the learner understands the root cause of the problem (unequal widths distorting a height-only comparison), not just that 'frequency density is the rule to use'.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Show the same library data plotted both ways (height = frequency, and height = frequency density) side by side, and ask which one makes the $60$-$100$ class look more crowded than it really is.

diagnostic_items.question: A class has width $5$ and frequency $30$. What is its frequency density?

common_wrong_answers.answer: $5\div30\approx0.17$.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Inverts the frequency density formula, dividing the width by the frequency instead of the frequency by the width.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks fluent, correctly-ordered use of the frequency density formula (frequency $\div$ width, not width $\div$ frequency).
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Rehearse the formula in both directions (frequency density $=$ frequency $\div$ width; frequency $=$ frequency density $\times$ width) until the correct order becomes automatic.

diagnostic_items.question: What does the area of a bar in a histogram represent?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: The frequency of that class (the number of data values in it).

common_wrong_answers.answer: The height of the bar represents the frequency, just like in an ordinary bar chart.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Carries over the bar-chart convention (height = frequency) directly into histograms, missing the entire point of using frequency density: in a histogram it is specifically the AREA, not the height, that equals the frequency.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Tests the single most important definitional fact of this lesson: that area (height $\times$ width), not height alone, represents frequency in a histogram.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Pick two bars of different widths with the same height and ask which represents more data — if the learner says 'the same', walk through the area calculation to show they are not equal.

diagnostic_items.question: Two adjacent classes have the same bar height but one is three times as wide. How do their frequencies compare?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: The wider class has three times the frequency, since both classes have the same frequency density (height) but the wider one spans three times the width, giving three times the area.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Their frequencies must be equal, since the bars are the same height.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Judges frequency purely by height (as in an ordinary bar chart), ignoring that in a histogram, frequency is given by AREA (height times width), so equal heights with different widths give different frequencies.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that the learner applies the area relationship correctly even when only comparing two classes qualitatively, without being given explicit numbers to calculate with.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Substitute concrete numbers (e.g. height $4$, widths $5$ and $15$) and calculate both areas explicitly, to make the 'same height does not mean same frequency' point unmistakable.

diagnostic_items.question: How is the modal class found from a histogram?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: It is the class with the tallest bar — that is, the highest frequency DENSITY — which is not necessarily the class with the largest frequency.

common_wrong_answers.answer: It is the class with the largest frequency (the largest bar area).
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Confuses the modal class (defined by the highest CONCENTRATION of values, i.e. frequency density) with the class containing the most values overall, which can easily be a different, wider class.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Tests the specific and often-confused distinction between 'most crowded' (modal class, by density) and 'most values overall' (largest frequency), which can point to two different classes.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Use the library data example, where the modal class (10-20, density 3) and the class with the largest frequency (20-40, frequency 50) are deliberately different classes, to make the distinction concrete.

theory_blocks.title: Area, not height, represents frequency
theory_blocks.body: In a histogram [[blue:the AREA of a bar is proportional to the frequency]]. If a class is twice as wide, the same number of values is spread over twice the width, so the bar must be only half as tall. Frequency density measures 'how crowded' the class is: the number of values PER UNIT of the variable (per year, per kg, per minute).
