theory_blocks.title: Frequency density
theory_blocks.body:
$$\text{frequency density}=\frac{\text{frequency}}{\text{class width}}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \text{frequency}=\text{frequency density}\times\text{class width}.$$

In a histogram the horizontal axis is a CONTINUOUS scale (no gaps between bars) and the vertical axis is labelled 'Frequency density'. The area of each bar equals the frequency of its class.

theory_blocks.title: Method for drawing a histogram
theory_blocks.body:
1. Write down the class boundaries and calculate each CLASS WIDTH.
2. Calculate FREQUENCY DENSITY $=$ frequency $\div$ width for every class.
3. Draw the horizontal axis as a continuous scale marked at the class boundaries; label the vertical axis 'Frequency density'.
4. Choose a vertical scale that fits the largest density; draw bars with NO GAPS (adjacent classes touch).

theory_blocks.title: Why not just use frequency for the bar height?
theory_blocks.body: If the same data is drawn with bar heights equal to the plain frequency, the wide classes look much bigger than they truly are. For the library data, a frequency-height diagram makes the last bar ($60$-$100$) look even larger than the $40$-$60$ bar (it is twice as wide and two-thirds as tall), suggesting there are more people over $60$ than aged $40$-$60$ — whereas a correct frequency-density diagram shows there are fewer, spread thinly across a much wider range.

theory_blocks.title: Four errors that break a histogram
theory_blocks.body:
- Plotting FREQUENCY on the vertical axis when the classes have unequal widths.
- Leaving gaps between bars, or labelling the axis just 'Frequency'. The label must be 'Frequency density'.
- Dividing by the MIDPOINT or by the number of classes instead of the class WIDTH.
- Using the class-limit numbers incorrectly: for $20<a\le40$ the width is $40-20=20$, not $40$.

theory_blocks.title: Reading a frequency from a histogram
theory_blocks.body: To read a histogram, MULTIPLY: frequency $=$ height $\times$ width (the area of the bar). This works for any bar, whatever its individual width.

theory_blocks.title: Estimating a part of a class
theory_blocks.body: When a range does not match the class boundaries, it is assumed that the values are spread EVENLY inside the class, so the number of values in a part of the class is (frequency density) $\times$ (width of that part). This assumption is exactly why such answers are only ESTIMATES, not exact counts.

theory_blocks.title: Finding a missing height, width or scale
theory_blocks.body: Often only some bars (or no vertical scale at all) are given. Because frequency $=$ density $\times$ width, any ONE unknown among frequency, density and width can be found once the other two (or a relationship such as a known total frequency, or one bar's known frequency) are available.

theory_blocks.title: Checking a histogram
theory_blocks.body: Always check a histogram by adding the frequencies obtained from (height $\times$ width) for every bar: the total must equal the number of data values. A quick sense check: the class with the HIGHEST BAR is the most crowded class, which may not be the class with the largest frequency overall.

theory_blocks.title: The modal class is found from density, not frequency
theory_blocks.body: The MODAL CLASS of a histogram is the class with the highest [[blue:FREQUENCY DENSITY]], not necessarily the class with the highest [[red:frequency]]. In the library data, the modal class is $10<a\le20$ (density $3$), although $20<a\le40$ has the larger frequency ($50$).

theory_blocks.title: Exam guidance for this lesson
theory_blocks.body: Histograms are Extended content, so they can appear on Paper 2 (non-calculator) or Paper 4 (calculator). Show the working row (class width, frequency density) in your table, use a ruler, and label both axes; the vertical axis must read 'Frequency density'. Marks are given for correct bar widths, correct heights, and for a correct total frequency.

keywords.definition: Frequency divided by class width; the quantity plotted as the height of a histogram bar.
A statistical diagram for grouped data (often with unequal class widths) in which the AREA of each bar, not its height, represents the frequency of that class.
The upper class boundary minus the lower class boundary; used as the divisor when calculating frequency density.
The class with the highest frequency density (the tallest bar) in a histogram; not necessarily the class with the largest frequency.

worked_examples.statement: Drawing a histogram. The ages $a$ (years) of $150$ people visiting a library are grouped: $0<a\le10$ freq $20$; $10<a\le20$ freq $30$; $20<a\le40$ freq $50$; $40<a\le60$ freq $30$; $60<a\le100$ freq $20$. Calculate the frequency densities and draw a histogram.
knowns: grouped frequency table with 5 unequal-width classes, total 150 people
unknowns: class width and frequency density for each class, and the histogram itself
reasoning: Add a class-width row: upper boundary minus lower boundary for each class.
Add a frequency-density row: frequency divided by class width for each class.
Draw a bar over each class with height equal to its frequency density, with no gaps between adjacent bars.
worked_examples.solution: Widths: $10,10,20,20,40$. Frequency densities: $\tfrac{20}{10}=2$, $\tfrac{30}{10}=3$, $\tfrac{50}{20}=2.5$, $\tfrac{30}{20}=1.5$, $\tfrac{20}{40}=0.5$. The widest class ($60$-$100$) has a low bar although it contains $20$ people; the same $20$ people are spread over $40$ years. The $10$-$20$ class has the tallest bar because it packs $30$ people into only $10$ years.
worked_examples.interpretation: The same frequency (20) can correspond to a tall, narrow bar OR a short, wide bar depending entirely on the class width — only the frequency density (and hence the bar's height) tells you how crowded each class actually is, which plain frequency alone cannot show.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Using the frequency itself (20, 30, 50, 30, 20) as each bar's height, ignoring that the classes have very different widths.

assets.caption: Histogram of library visitors' ages, drawn with frequency density as the bar height; the number inside each bar is its actual frequency.
assets.purpose: Reproduce the legacy library-ages histogram exactly, showing how unequal class widths produce a correctly-scaled set of bar heights.

worked_examples.statement: Wrong versus right. The library data from Example 1 is plotted two ways: once with bar height equal to plain frequency, and once with bar height equal to frequency density. Explain what is misleading about the first diagram.
knowns: the same library data plotted with two different height conventions
unknowns: why the frequency-height version is misleading
reasoning: Compare the two diagrams' $60$-$100$ bar specifically, since it has by far the widest class.
Check what each diagram's bar height is actually proportional to (frequency in one, frequency density in the other).
Connect the visual impression each diagram gives to the true crowdedness of each age group.
worked_examples.solution: In the frequency-height diagram, the last bar ($60$-$100$) is two-thirds as tall as the $40$-$60$ bar but twice as wide, so it has the LARGER area and looks bigger, suggesting there are more visitors over $60$ than aged $40$-$60$. In reality there are fewer ($20$ against $30$), and they are spread over $40$ years (density $0.5$), while the $30$ people aged $40$-$60$ are packed into just $20$ years (density $1.5$, three times as crowded) — exactly what the frequency-density diagram correctly shows.
worked_examples.interpretation: Both diagrams are built from the exact same data, yet only ONE of them tells the truth about crowdedness at a glance — this is precisely why frequency density, not frequency, is the required convention whenever class widths are unequal.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming a visually taller or wider-looking bar in the wrong (frequency-height) diagram must mean 'more crowded', when it may really just mean 'wider class'.

assets.caption: The same library data drawn two ways: height equal to frequency (wrong, left) makes the widest class look misleadingly large; height equal to frequency density (right) correctly shows it is sparsely spread.
assets.purpose: Reproduce the legacy side-by-side wrong-vs-right comparison exactly, to make the frequency-vs-frequency-density distinction visually unmistakable.

worked_examples.statement: From a histogram to a table. A histogram shows the waiting times $t$ (minutes) of customers at a call centre: bars of height $4,6,5,1.5,0.5$ over the classes $0$-$5$, $5$-$10$, $10$-$20$, $20$-$40$, $40$-$60$. (a) Find the frequency of each class and the total number of customers. (b) Estimate the number of customers who waited between $15$ and $30$ minutes. (c) Estimate the mean waiting time.
knowns: a histogram with 5 bars of given heights over 5 classes of different widths
unknowns: each class's frequency, the total, a partial-class estimate, and the estimated mean
reasoning: (a) For each class, multiply height $\times$ width to recover its frequency, then add all five frequencies.
(b) Split the range $15$ to $30$ into the two parts it actually overlaps (part of $10$-$20$, and part of $20$-$40$), and estimate each part separately assuming an even spread.
(c) Use the class midpoints, weighted by the frequencies found in (a), exactly as for any grouped-data mean estimate.
worked_examples.solution: (a) Frequencies: $4\times5=20$; $6\times5=30$; $5\times10=50$; $1.5\times20=30$; $0.5\times20=10$. Total $=140$ customers. (b) From $15$ to $20$ (half of the $10$-$20$ class): $5\times5=25$. From $20$ to $30$ (half of the $20$-$40$ class): $1.5\times10=15$. Total $\approx25+15=40$ customers. (c) Using midpoints $2.5,7.5,15,30,50$: mean $\approx\dfrac{20(2.5)+30(7.5)+50(15)+30(30)+10(50)}{140}=\dfrac{2425}{140}\approx17.3$ minutes.
worked_examples.interpretation: Three different kinds of question (total frequency, a partial-class count, and an estimated mean) all come from the SAME histogram once the frequencies have been recovered by (height $\times$ width) — the hardest part is usually splitting a part-way range into the correct pieces, as in part (b).
worked_examples.common_mistake: In part (b), using the FULL class frequency for $10$-$20$ (50) or $20$-$40$ (30) instead of only the HALF of each class that actually falls within $15$-$30$.

assets.caption: Histogram of call-centre waiting times, with the shaded region from 15 to 30 minutes (used in part (b)) split across two classes.
assets.purpose: Reproduce the legacy call-centre histogram exactly, including the shaded partial-class region, matching the worked part (b) reasoning.

worked_examples.statement: Missing bar. A histogram has total frequency $90$. The bars for $0<x\le10$, $10<x\le15$, $15<x\le25$ and $25<x\le45$ have heights $1.2$, $4.0$, $h$ and $0.5$. Find $h$.
knowns: 4 class heights (one unknown, h), total frequency 90
unknowns: the missing height h
reasoning: Write each class's frequency as height $\times$ width, leaving $h$ as an unknown where needed.
Set the sum of all four frequencies equal to the given total, $90$.
Solve the resulting linear equation for $h$.
worked_examples.solution: Frequencies: $1.2\times10=12$; $4.0\times5=20$; $h\times10=10h$; $0.5\times20=10$. Sum $=90$: $12+20+10h+10=90\Rightarrow10h=48\Rightarrow h=4.8$.
worked_examples.interpretation: A 'missing bar' problem is really just total $=$ sum of all the (height $\times$ width) terms, rearranged for the one unknown — exactly the same total-based reasoning used for a missing value in a mean (Lesson 9.3), just applied to areas instead of a single sum.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Using the wrong width for the third class ($15<x\le25$, width $10$), for example mistakenly using $25$ (the upper limit alone) instead of $25-15=10$.

worked_examples.statement: No scale on the vertical axis. In a histogram the bar for $10<x\le20$ has height $6$\,cm (measured on the page) and represents $30$ values. Another bar, for $20<x\le50$, has height $4$\,cm. How many values does it represent?
knowns: bar 1: width 10, height 6cm, represents 30 values
bar 2: width 30, height 4cm
unknowns: how many values bar 2 represents
reasoning: Find bar 1's area in these page units (width $\times$ height), and use the known frequency it represents to find 'values per area unit'.
Find bar 2's area in the same page units.
Scale bar 2's area by the 'values per area unit' rate found from bar 1.
worked_examples.solution: Bar 1: area $=10\times6=60$ units, representing $30$ values, so $1$ area unit represents $0.5$ values. Bar 2: area $=30\times4=120$ units, so it represents $120\times0.5=60$ values.
worked_examples.interpretation: Even with no numerical scale printed on the vertical axis at all, area is STILL proportional to frequency — one known bar is enough to convert every other bar's area (in whatever units it was measured) into an actual frequency.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Comparing the two bars' HEIGHTS alone (e.g. $4\div6\times30=20$) instead of their full AREAS (which also account for the different widths, $10$ versus $30$).

guided_exercises.statement: The lengths $\ell$ (cm) of $100$ fish caught in a survey are grouped: $0<\ell\le10$ freq $8$; $10<\ell\le15$ freq $27$; $15<\ell\le20$ freq $35$; $20<\ell\le40$ freq $30$. Calculate the frequency density of each class.
hints: Write an explicit class-width row first: upper boundary minus lower boundary for each class.
Divide each frequency by ITS OWN class's width, not a width copied from a neighbouring class.
guided_exercises.answer: Widths $10,5,5,20$; frequency densities $0.8,5.4,7,1.5$.
common_errors: Dividing the second or third class's frequency by 10 (copied from the first class) instead of its own, narrower width of 5.

guided_exercises.statement: A histogram has bars of heights $3$, $5$, $2$, $0.5$ over the classes $0<x\le4$, $4<x\le8$, $8<x\le16$, $16<x\le30$. (a) Find the frequency of each class and the total. (b) Estimate the number of values between $6$ and $12$.
hints: For (a), multiply each height by its own class's width to get that class's frequency.
For (b), identify which TWO classes the range 6 to 12 actually overlaps, and estimate only the overlapping portion of each.
guided_exercises.full_solution: (a) $3\times4=12$; $5\times4=20$; $2\times8=16$; $0.5\times14=7$. Total $=12+20+16+7=55$. (b) From $6$ to $8$ (part of the $4$-$8$ class): $5\times2=10$. From $8$ to $12$ (part of the $8$-$16$ class): $2\times4=8$. Total $\approx10+8=18$.
common_errors: In (b), using the full frequency of the 8-16 class (16) instead of only the part from 8 to 12 (half of that class's width).

guided_exercises.statement: A histogram has frequency densities $2.5$ (over $0$-$10$), $4$ (over $10$-$15$), $1$ (over $15$-$35$). Find the frequency of each class, and state the modal class.
hints: Find each class's frequency first (density times width) before deciding anything about which class is 'biggest'.
The modal class is found from the HEIGHT (density), not from whichever class turns out to have the largest frequency.
guided_exercises.answer: Frequencies $25,20,20$; modal class is $10<x\le15$ (density $4$, the tallest bar), even though it does not have the largest frequency.
guided_exercises.full_solution: Frequencies: $2.5\times10=25$; $4\times5=20$; $1\times20=20$. Although $0$-$10$ has the largest frequency ($25$), the modal class is defined by the highest frequency DENSITY, which is $4$ for the class $10<x\le15$ — this is the tallest bar, and therefore the modal class, even though its frequency (20) is smaller than the first class's.
common_errors: Naming the class with the largest frequency (0-10, frequency 25) as the modal class, instead of the class with the highest density (10-15, density 4).

exercises.statement: The heights $h$ (cm) of plants are grouped: $0<h\le10$ freq $12$; $10<h\le25$ freq $45$; $25<h\le30$ freq $20$; $30<h\le50$ freq $18$. Work out the frequency density of each class.
common_errors: Using the wrong width for the third class (25-30, width 5) by mistakenly subtracting incorrectly or copying a neighbouring width.

exercises.statement: A histogram has bars with frequency densities: $0<x\le4$: $5$; $4<x\le10$: $3$; $10<x\le20$: $2$; $20<x\le40$: $0.4$. (a) Find the frequency of each class and the total frequency. (b) Estimate the number of values between $7$ and $15$. (c) Estimate the mean (3 s.f.).
common_errors: In (c), using the class boundaries instead of midpoints as the x-values when estimating the mean.

exercises.statement: In a histogram, a bar over $5<x\le15$ has height $2.4$. (a) How many values does it represent? (b) A class $15<x\le20$ contains $18$ values. What is the height of its bar?
exercises.full_solution: (a) Frequency $=2.4\times10=24$. (b) Height $=18\div5=3.6$.
common_errors: In (b), dividing by the wrong class width (e.g. 10, copied from the first class) instead of the correct width of 5 for 15<x≤20.

exercises.statement: In a histogram, the bar for $0<x\le5$ has height $8$\,cm and represents $20$ values. Another bar of width $10$ has height $3$\,cm. How many values does it represent?
exercises.full_solution: Bar 1: area $=5\times8=40$, representing $20$ values, so $0.5$ values per area unit. Bar 2: area $=10\times3=30$, so it represents $30\times0.5=15$ values.
common_errors: Comparing the two bars' heights alone (3/8 x 20) rather than their full areas (which account for the different widths, 5 versus 10).

exercises.statement: A student draws a histogram of the plant-height data in the related idea using bar height equal to frequency. Explain why this is wrong and which class appears misleadingly large.
exercises.answer: Unequal widths mean area (not height) must represent frequency; the wide class 10<h≤25 (frequency 45) looks misleadingly large.
exercises.full_solution: Since the class widths are unequal, using height $=$ frequency means a wide class will automatically produce a tall bar simply because it is wide, not because it is especially crowded. Here the class $10<h\le25$ (frequency $45$, width $15$) would look by far the largest bar, even though its frequency DENSITY ($3$) is lower than the narrow class $25<h\le30$ (frequency $20$, density $4$) — the narrow class's true crowding would be hidden by its small-looking bar.
common_errors: Assuming the class with the biggest-looking (frequency-height) bar must also be the most crowded class, rather than checking the frequency density.

exercises.statement: Use the library histogram of this lesson (the related idea) to estimate (a) the number of people aged between $30$ and $50$; (b) the number aged over $50$ and the percentage of the total that this represents (1 d.p.).
exercises.full_solution: (a) From $30$ to $40$ (half of $20$-$40$, density $2.5$): $2.5\times10=25$. From $40$ to $50$ (half of $40$-$60$, density $1.5$): $1.5\times10=15$. Total $\approx25+15=40$. (b) From $50$ to $60$ (half of $40$-$60$): $1.5\times10=15$. From $60$ to $100$ (all of $60$-$100$): $0.5\times40=20$. Total $\approx15+20=35$; percentage $=\dfrac{35}{150}\times100\approx23.3\%$.
common_errors: In (a), using the FULL class 20-40 (frequency 50) instead of only the half of it (30 to 40) that falls within the requested range.

exercises.statement: Use the library data to estimate the mean age (3 s.f.).
exercises.answer: $\approx34.3$ years.
common_errors: Using the class boundaries rather than the midpoints as the representative x-value for each class.

exercises.statement: A histogram has total frequency $60$. Bars: $0<x\le5$ height $2$; $5<x\le10$ height $h$; $10<x\le30$ height $0.5$. Find $h$.
exercises.full_solution: Frequencies: $2\times5=10$; $h\times5=5h$; $0.5\times20=10$. Sum $=60$: $10+5h+10=60\Rightarrow5h=40\Rightarrow h=8$.
common_errors: Using the wrong width for the third class (10-30, width 20) by mistakenly using 30 (the upper limit alone).

exam_questions.statement:
The table shows the time $t$ (minutes) spent on homework each evening by $120$ students.
$$\begin{array}{l|ccccc}
\text{Time},\ t & 0<t\le15 & 15<t\le30 & 30<t\le45 & 45<t\le75 & 75<t\le120\\\hline
\text{Frequency} & 18 & 36 & 30 & 24 & 12
\end{array}$$
(a) Calculate the frequency density for each class. [3]
(b) State which class is the modal class, explaining your reasoning. [2]
(c) A new student says 'the class $45<t\le75$ has more students than the class $0<t\le15$, so it must be the more crowded class.' Explain why this reasoning is flawed. [2]
exam_questions.answer: (a) Densities: $1.2, 2.4, 2, 0.8, 0.267$ (3 s.f.). (b) $15<t\le30$ (density $2.4$, the highest). (c) 'Crowded' means frequency density, not frequency: $45<t\le75$ has more students ($24$ against $18$) but spread over $30$ minutes, so its density ($0.8$) is lower than that of $0<t\le15$ ($1.2$).
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Widths $15,15,15,30,45$. Densities: $18\div15=1.2$; $36\div15=2.4$; $30\div15=2$; $24\div30=0.8$; $12\div45\approx0.267$. (b) The modal class is the one with the highest frequency density, which is $15<t\le30$ with density $2.4$ — this is the tallest bar on the histogram. (c) The student is confusing frequency with frequency density ('crowdedness'). Although $45<t\le75$ has more students ($24$) than $0<t\le15$ ($18$), its class width ($30$) is twice that of $0<t\le15$ ($15$), so its density ($24\div30=0.8$) is actually lower than that of $0<t\le15$ ($18\div15=1.2$). Ranking classes by frequency alone, rather than density, gives the wrong order of crowdedness whenever widths differ.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for correct class widths; A1 for at least 3 correct densities; A1 for all 5 correct (accept 3 s.f. for the last)
(b) B1 for correctly identifying 15<t≤30 as modal; B1 for a reason referencing highest DENSITY (not frequency)
(c) B1 for identifying the frequency/frequency-density confusion; B1 for a correct comparison showing $45<t\le75$'s density ($0.8$) is in fact lower than $0<t\le15$'s ($1.2$).
common_errors: In (b), naming the class with the largest raw frequency (15<t≤30, which happens to coincide here, but for the wrong reason) without checking density explicitly.

exam_questions.statement:
A histogram shows the masses $m$ (kg) of $80$ parcels, with bars of height $3$ over $0<m\le4$, height $5$ over $4<m\le8$, height $2.5$ over $8<m\le16$, and height $h$ over $16<m\le30$.
(a) Show that the value of $h$ is $2$. [3]
(b) Estimate the number of parcels with mass between $6$ and $12$\,kg. [3]
exam_questions.answer: (a) Shown: $h=2$. (b) $\approx20$.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Frequencies: $3\times4=12$; $5\times4=20$; $2.5\times8=20$; $h\times14=14h$. Sum $=80$: $12+20+20+14h=80\Rightarrow14h=28\Rightarrow h=2$. (b) From $6$ to $8$ (part of the $4$-$8$ class): $5\times2=10$. From $8$ to $12$ (part of the $8$-$16$ class): $2.5\times4=10$. Total $=10+10=20$ parcels.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for correct frequency expressions; M1 for setting the sum equal to 80; A1 for solving correctly for $h$
(b) M1 for correctly splitting the range into its two overlapping classes; M1 for correct partial-area calculations; A1 for the correct total, $20$.
common_errors: In (a), using the wrong width for the final class (16-30, width 14) by mistakenly using 30 alone.

exam_questions.statement:
A histogram for the ages of $125$ festival attendees has frequency densities $3$ (over $10<a\le20$), $6$ (over $20<a\le25$), $4$ (over $25<a\le35$) and $1$ (over $35<a\le60$).
(a) Find the frequency of each class. [2]
(b) Estimate the mean age (3 s.f.). [2]
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for correct width identification; A1 for all four frequencies correct
(b) M1 for correct midpoints and weighted sum; A1 for correct final mean (follow-through from candidate's own frequencies).
common_errors: Using the class boundaries instead of midpoints when estimating the mean.

challenge_questions.statement: Estimate the median age of the $150$ library visitors from this lesson. (Hint: find the class containing the $75$th value and assume an even spread.)
challenge_questions.answer: $\approx30$ years.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Cumulative frequencies: $20$ (at $a=10$), $50$ (at $a=20$), $100$ (at $a=40$), $130$ (at $a=60$), $150$ (at $a=100$). The $75$th value lies in the class $20<a\le40$ (cumulative frequency reaches $50$ before this class and $100$ by its end): $25$ values into a class of $50$, which is halfway through, so median $\approx20+\dfrac{25}{50}\times20=30$ years.

challenge_questions.statement: The bars of a histogram for classes of widths $5$, $10$ and $30$ have heights in the ratio $4:3:1$. The total frequency is $160$. Find the frequency of each class.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Taking heights as $4k,3k,k$ for some constant $k$, the areas (frequencies) are in ratio $4k\times5:3k\times10:k\times30=20k:30k:30k=2:3:3$. Total frequency $=160$ over $2+3+3=8$ parts: each part $=20$. Frequencies: $2\times20=40$; $3\times20=60$; $3\times20=60$.

challenge_questions.statement: A student says 'a frequency density of $3$ means that there are $3$ people in the class'. Explain what it really means when the class is ages in years, and why the number of people in the class $10<a\le20$ is $30$.
challenge_questions.answer: It means 3 people PER YEAR of age; the class is 10 years wide, so the number of people is 3x10=30.
challenge_questions.full_solution: A frequency density of $3$ (with age measured in years) means there are approximately $3$ people for EVERY YEAR of age within that class, not simply '3 people in the class' — density is a RATE, not a count. For the class $10<a\le20$, the class width is $10$ years, so the total number of people in it is found by multiplying the rate by the width: $3\times10=30$ people, matching the frequency given in the original library data.

challenge_questions.statement: Two adjacent bars: $5<x\le10$ has height $6$; the bar for $10<x\le30$ has area three times that of the first bar. Find its height.
challenge_questions.full_solution: First bar's area $=5\times6=30$. Second bar's area $=3\times30=90$. Second bar's width $=30-10=20$, so its height $=90\div20=4.5$.

challenge_questions.statement: The frequency density of a class $20<x\le50$ is $d$ and the frequency density of the class $50<x\le80$ is $\tfrac d3$. If the total number of values in these two classes is $80$, find $d$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Frequencies: $d\times30=30d$ (first class, width $30$); $\tfrac d3\times30=10d$ (second class, width $30$). Sum $=30d+10d=40d=80\Rightarrow d=2$.

mcq.stem: In a histogram, Class A (width $4$) and Class B (width $12$) both have the same bar height. How do their frequencies compare?

options.text: Their frequencies are equal, since the bars have the same height
options.why_wrong: Equal heights only mean equal frequency DENSITY; since the widths differ, the actual frequencies (areas) are not equal — the wider class has a bigger area.

options.text: Class A's frequency is three times Class B's
options.why_wrong: This reverses the correct relationship; the WIDER class (B) has the greater area and therefore the greater frequency, not the narrower one.

options.text: Class B's frequency is three times Class A's, since B is three times as wide
It cannot be determined without knowing the actual height value
options.why_wrong: The RATIO of the two frequencies can be found from the ratio of the widths alone, since the (equal) heights cancel out in that ratio.

mcq.explanation: Frequency is given by area (height $\times$ width); with equal heights, the frequencies are in the same ratio as the widths, so Class B (three times as wide) has three times Class A's frequency.

mcq.stem: A class is written as $20<x\le45$ and has frequency $75$. What is its frequency density?

options.text: $75\div32.5=2.3$ (dividing by the class midpoint)
options.why_wrong: The midpoint (32.5) is used for estimating a mean, not for frequency density; frequency density must be divided by the class WIDTH, which is 45-20=25, not the midpoint.

options.text: $75\div45=1.67$ (dividing by the upper limit alone)
options.why_wrong: The class width is upper boundary MINUS lower boundary (45-20=25), not the upper limit by itself (45).

options.text: $45-20=25$ (the width itself, mistaken for the density)
options.why_wrong: This finds the correct class width, but stops there instead of actually dividing the frequency by it to get the density.

mcq.explanation: Frequency density $=$ frequency $\div$ class width $=75\div(45-20)=75\div25=3$.

mcq.stem: Which of these is a correct feature of a histogram (as opposed to an ordinary bar chart)?

options.text: The bars touch with no gaps, and the vertical axis is labelled 'Frequency density'
The bars have small gaps between them, like a bar chart, and the vertical axis is labelled 'Frequency'
options.why_wrong: A histogram's horizontal axis is a continuous numerical scale, so bars must touch with no gaps, and the vertical axis specifically must read 'Frequency density', not 'Frequency'.

options.text: The bars are always the same width, regardless of the class boundaries
options.why_wrong: A histogram's bar widths follow the actual class widths directly, which are often unequal — this is precisely why frequency density (not frequency) is needed as the height.

options.text: The vertical axis always starts above zero to save space
options.why_wrong: There is no such convention for histograms; like most statistical diagrams, the vertical axis should start at zero to avoid a misleading appearance.

mcq.explanation: A histogram's horizontal axis is continuous, so its bars touch with no gaps between them, and its vertical axis must be labelled 'Frequency density', not 'Frequency'.

mcq.stem: A class is given as $15<t\le45$. What is its class width?

options.text: $45$ (the upper limit alone)
options.why_wrong: The upper limit by itself is not the class width; the width requires the subtraction of the lower boundary too: 45-15=30, not 45.

options.text: $15$ (the lower limit alone)
options.why_wrong: The lower limit alone is not the class width either; both boundaries must be used in the subtraction.

options.text: $45+15=60$ (the sum of the two limits)
options.why_wrong: Adding the two limits does not give the width; the width is the DIFFERENCE between the upper and lower boundaries: 45-15=30, not 60.

mcq.explanation: Class width is always upper boundary minus lower boundary: $45-15=30$.

mcq.stem: A histogram has classes with frequencies $40$, $36$, $30$ and frequency densities $2$, $6$, $1$ respectively. Which is the modal class?

options.text: The class with frequency $40$ (the largest frequency)
options.why_wrong: The modal class of a histogram is defined by the highest frequency DENSITY (the tallest bar), not the largest frequency, which can easily belong to a different (wider) class.

options.text: All three classes are equally modal, since each has a reasonably large frequency
options.why_wrong: The modal class is a single, specific class — the one with the clearly highest frequency density — not a judgement that several classes are all 'similarly large'.

options.text: The class with frequency density $6$
The class with frequency density $1$ (the lowest), since it is the most spread out
options.why_wrong: A LOW frequency density means the class is the LEAST crowded, which is the opposite of what defines a modal class (the most crowded, highest-density class).

mcq.explanation: The modal class of a histogram is the one with the highest frequency density (the tallest bar), which here is the class with density $6$ — not necessarily the class with the largest frequency (which is a different class here, with frequency $40$).

flashcards.front: Frequency density formula
flashcards.back: $\text{frequency density}=\dfrac{\text{frequency}}{\text{class width}}$, so $\text{frequency}=\text{frequency density}\times\text{class width}$.

flashcards.front: What does the AREA of a histogram bar represent?
flashcards.back: The frequency of that class — not the height alone, since class widths may be unequal.

flashcards.front: Can you read a histogram's frequency directly from its bar height?
flashcards.back: No — frequency = height x width (the area); the height alone only gives the frequency density.

flashcards.front: How do you find a class's width?
flashcards.back: Upper class boundary MINUS lower class boundary — never the upper limit alone, and never the midpoint.

flashcards.front: What two visual features must a histogram have (unlike an ordinary bar chart)?
flashcards.back: Bars touching with no gaps (continuous horizontal axis); vertical axis labelled 'Frequency density'.

flashcards.front: Is the modal class of a histogram the one with the largest frequency?
flashcards.back: No — it is the class with the highest frequency DENSITY (the tallest bar), which may be a different, narrower class.

flashcards.front: How do you estimate the number of values in part of a histogram class (not matching the class boundaries)?
flashcards.back: Assume an even spread within the class: count = frequency density x (width of that part).

flashcards.front: How do you estimate the mean from a histogram?
flashcards.back: Recover each class's frequency (height x width), then use class midpoints weighted by those frequencies, exactly as for any grouped-data mean.

flashcards.front: Bar chart (equal widths) vs histogram (unequal widths): what represents frequency in each?
flashcards.back: Bar chart: height represents frequency directly. Histogram: AREA (height x width) represents frequency; height alone is only frequency density.

flashcards.front: A histogram has no numbers on its vertical axis, but one bar's frequency is known. How do you find another bar's frequency?
flashcards.back: Find the known bar's area and the 'values per area unit' rate; apply that same rate to the other bar's area.

flashcards.front: What should you always check after completing a histogram's frequency table?
flashcards.back: That the sum of all (height x width) frequencies equals the total number of data values given.

flashcards.front: Two classes have the same frequency but very different widths. What does that tell you about their frequency densities?
flashcards.back: The narrower class has the higher frequency density (more crowded); the wider class has the lower density, since the same count is spread over more width.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The height of a histogram bar represents the frequency of its class, exactly as in an ordinary bar chart, even when class widths are unequal.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Every other bar-style diagram studied so far (simple bar charts, dual bar charts) uses height to represent frequency directly, so this habit transfers naturally — until unequal class widths make it silently wrong, since the height no longer tells the whole story on its own.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner reads a histogram's bar heights directly as frequencies (or compares two bars' heights to decide which class has more data) without multiplying by each bar's width.
misconceptions.correct_model: A histogram's vertical axis shows FREQUENCY DENSITY, not frequency; the AREA of each bar (height $\times$ width), not its height alone, is what equals the frequency of that class. A tall, narrow bar and a short, wide bar can represent the very same frequency.
misconceptions.remediation: Before reading any frequency off a histogram, always write 'frequency $=$ height $\times$ width' and multiply through, never read the height alone as the answer.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Frequency density is found by dividing the frequency by the class MIDPOINT, or by the number of classes in the table, rather than by the class width.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Class midpoints are the number most recently used for a different grouped-data calculation (estimating a mean, in Lesson 9.3), so they can be substituted in by mistake wherever another division by a 'class-related number' is needed.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner computes frequency density using the class's midpoint value (or a count of how many classes there are) in the denominator, instead of (upper boundary $-$ lower boundary).
misconceptions.correct_model: Frequency density $=$ frequency $\div$ CLASS WIDTH, where class width $=$ upper class boundary $-$ lower class boundary — never the midpoint, and never the number of classes in the table.
misconceptions.remediation: Before calculating any frequency density, write out the class width explicitly as a separate subtraction (upper $-$ lower) in its own table row, so it cannot be confused with the midpoint.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A histogram can be drawn with small gaps between the bars, and its vertical axis can simply be labelled 'Frequency', the same as an ordinary bar chart.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Ordinary bar charts for categorical data (Lesson 9.2) deliberately use gaps between bars to show the categories are separate and unordered; this habit, and the familiar axis label, can be carried over even though a histogram's horizontal axis is a CONTINUOUS numerical scale.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner's histogram shows visible gaps between adjacent bars, or the vertical axis is labelled 'Frequency' instead of 'Frequency density'.
misconceptions.correct_model: A histogram's bars must touch with NO GAPS (since the horizontal axis is a continuous numerical scale, not separate categories), and the vertical axis must be labelled 'Frequency density', never just 'Frequency'.
misconceptions.remediation: Before drawing a histogram, say out loud: 'continuous axis, bars touching, vertical axis says Frequency density' as a three-part checklist.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: For a class written as $20<a\le40$, the class width is $40$ (the upper limit alone), not $40-20=20$.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The upper class-limit number is the most visually prominent number directly beside the class on the table, so it can be mistaken for 'the width' without the subtraction step being performed explicitly.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner uses the raw upper-boundary number as the class width in a frequency-density calculation, rather than subtracting the lower boundary from it first.
misconceptions.correct_model: Class width is always UPPER boundary MINUS LOWER boundary; for $20<a\le40$ the width is $40-20=20$, not $40$.
misconceptions.remediation: Add an explicit 'class width' row to every grouped table, computed as a visible subtraction, before attempting any frequency density calculation.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The modal class of a histogram is the class with the largest frequency (the widest or tallest-area bar), the same rule used for an ordinary frequency table.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: In Lesson 9.3, the modal class of grouped data (with equal class widths) genuinely IS the class with the largest frequency, since frequency and frequency density agree exactly when widths are equal; this correct earlier rule becomes incorrect here, where widths are unequal.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner identifies the modal class of a histogram by scanning for the class with the largest frequency (area), rather than the tallest bar.
misconceptions.correct_model: The modal class of a histogram is the class with the highest FREQUENCY DENSITY (the tallest bar) — that is, the most crowded class — which is not necessarily the class with the largest frequency. In the library data, the modal class is $10<a\le20$ (density $3$), even though $20<a\le40$ has the larger frequency ($50$).
misconceptions.remediation: For a histogram's modal class, scan specifically for the TALLEST bar (highest density), and deliberately check that this is not simply the class with the biggest frequency number.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reading a histogram's bar height directly as its frequency, ignoring the class width.
common_mistakes.why: Every other bar-style diagram studied uses height to represent frequency directly, so the habit transfers by default.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always write 'frequency = height x width' before reading any value off a histogram.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dividing frequency by the class midpoint, or by the number of classes, instead of the class width when finding frequency density.
common_mistakes.why: Midpoints were the key number in the grouped-mean calculation (Lesson 9.3), and the habit can carry over to a different formula.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Add an explicit class-width row (upper minus lower) before attempting any frequency density calculation.

common_mistakes.mistake: Identifying the modal class of a histogram as the one with the largest frequency, rather than the highest density.
common_mistakes.why: This was the correct rule for equal-width grouped data (Lesson 9.3), and it is easy to apply the same rule without checking whether widths are now unequal.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: For a histogram's modal class, always scan for the tallest bar (highest density), and explicitly check this is not simply the class with the biggest frequency number.

exam_notes: Always show an explicit class-width row and a frequency-density row in your working table before drawing or reading any histogram — method marks are specifically awarded for this working.
The vertical axis of any histogram you draw must be labelled 'Frequency density', never just 'Frequency' — using the wrong label can lose a mark even if every bar is otherwise drawn correctly.
For 'estimate the number of values in part of a class' questions, always state the assumption explicitly: 'assuming an even spread within the class'.
When identifying a modal class, state explicitly that you are using frequency DENSITY (not frequency) as the basis for your answer, to make the correct reasoning visible to the marker.

summary.big_idea: When grouped data has unequal class widths, a histogram replaces an ordinary bar chart: its vertical axis shows frequency density (frequency divided by class width), so the AREA of each bar, not its height, represents the frequency of that class, letting frequencies, partial-class estimates, the mean and the (density-based) modal class all be recovered correctly.
key_points: Frequency density = frequency / class width; frequency = frequency density x class width = the area of the bar.
A histogram's horizontal axis is continuous (bars touch, no gaps); the vertical axis must be labelled 'Frequency density', not 'Frequency'.
To read a frequency from a histogram, multiply height by width; for a missing height, width or scale, use the same relationship with the other two known quantities.
For part of a class, assume an even spread: count = frequency density x (width of that part); this is why such answers are only estimates.
The modal class is the class with the highest frequency density (tallest bar), which may not be the class with the largest frequency.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: In a histogram, AREA represents frequency, not height; always calculate and show class width and frequency density explicitly, and find the modal class from the tallest bar (highest density), not the largest frequency.
